entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Love does not judge of resentment, nor resentment of love.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Smith argues that no single passion has the right to judge another; only conscience can stand above them.

interpretation.en: Smith is defending the authority of the moral faculties against writers who treated them as just one more appetite with no special right to rule. His point is that ordinary passions only push against each other: love and resentment can conflict, but neither can approve or condemn the other. Judging is a separate job, and Smith compares conscience to a sense whose objects are the other passions, the way the eye has the final word on colour.
interpretation.zh: 斯密在这里为道德能力的权威辩护，反驳那些把它看作与其他欲望地位相同、并无特别统辖权的说法。他的意思是，普通的激情只会彼此冲撞：爱与怨恨可以对立，但谁也无权赞许或谴责对方。评判是另一种职能，斯密把良心比作一种感官，它的对象就是其他激情，正如眼睛对颜色有最终的发言权。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing but exemplary morals can give dignity to a man of small fortune.
entries.work: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
entries.context: In The Wealth of Nations, Smith observes that clergy on modest incomes earn respect only through the example of their conduct.

interpretation.en: The line comes from Smith's discussion of how churches are endowed, where he notes some good effects of benefices that are all roughly equal and modest. A clergyman without much money cannot win standing through display, and the vices of vanity would make him ridiculous and ruin him, so his own situation pushes him toward the strict morals ordinary people respect. Smith's argument is about incentives: modest pay makes good conduct the clergyman's interest as well as his duty, and earns him the affection of his parishioners.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自斯密讨论教会俸禄的部分，他指出各教职俸禄大致相等且都不丰厚时，会带来一些好的效果。收入微薄的教士无法靠排场赢得地位，轻浮和虚荣会让他显得可笑并使他破产，所以他的处境推动他遵守普通民众最尊重的严格道德。斯密的论证着眼于利益激励：微薄的俸禄使良好操守既是教士的义务，也符合他自身的利益，并为他赢得教众的亲近。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: There is something agreeable even in the weakness of friendship and humanity.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, on why even excessive tenderness and generosity are regarded kindly rather than with aversion.

interpretation.en: Smith is sorting the passions by how spectators react to them, and here he turns to the amiable ones, such as tenderness and generosity. Even when these run to excess, onlookers feel a mix of pity and love rather than contempt; the overly soft parent or friend is blamed gently and with sympathy. This contrasts with the unsocial passions like hatred, which Smith treats as disagreeable to observers even in proper measure.
interpretation.zh: 斯密在按照旁观者的反应对激情进行分类，这里谈的是温和可亲的一类，如慈爱与慷慨。即使这些情感过度，旁观者感到的也是怜惜与爱意交织，而不是轻蔑；过于心软的父母或朋友会受到温和而同情的责备。这与仇恨之类的不合群的激情形成对照，斯密认为后者即便适度，也令旁观者不快。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Our sympathy with sorrow, though not more real, has been more taken notice of than our sympathy with joy.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments opens its discussion of sympathy by noting that we attend more to shared grief than to shared happiness.

interpretation.en: This opens Smith's chapter on the difference between sympathy with joy and sympathy with sorrow. He notes that the word itself originally meant fellow-feeling with suffering, and that a recent philosopher, often identified as Hume, felt the need to argue that sympathy with joy is real, while no one ever thought compassion needed proof. Smith goes on to argue that sympathy with joy is real but has been overlooked, which complicates the common picture of sympathy as mainly pity.
interpretation.zh: 这是斯密讨论同情快乐与同情悲伤之差别一章的开头。他指出，这个词的本义是对他人痛苦的同感；又说一位近来的哲学家（通常认为指休谟）觉得有必要论证对快乐的同情确实存在，而从没有人觉得怜悯需要证明。斯密接着论证，对快乐的同情同样真实，只是一直被忽视，这使通常把同情只理解为怜悯的看法变得复杂。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: It is evident, however, that we are anxious about our own beauty and deformity only on account of its effect upon others.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, arguing that concern for how we look, and for how we behave, exists only because other people see us.

interpretation.en: Smith uses physical appearance as a model for how moral self-judgment arises. People check themselves in a mirror to see themselves as others see them, and Smith claims that a person cut off from all society would care nothing about looking handsome or deformed. The broader argument is that conscience develops the same way: people learn to judge their own conduct by imagining how an impartial spectator would see it, so self-assessment is social in origin.
interpretation.zh: 斯密以外貌为例，说明道德上的自我评判是如何产生的。人们照镜子，是为了像别人那样看自己；斯密认为，一个完全脱离社会的人根本不会在意自己是美是丑。更大的论点是，良心也以同样的方式形成：人通过想象一位公正的旁观者会如何看待自己，学会评判自己的行为，所以自我评价起源于社会。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing tends so much to corrupt mankind as dependency, while independency still increases the honesty of the people.
entries.work: Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and Arms
entries.context: From student notes of Smith's Glasgow lectures on law and government, on why dependence on patrons corrupts people more than any police can correct.

interpretation.en: The text survives as a student's notes of Smith's lectures, not as his own written prose. Smith is explaining why crime is higher where many people live as dependants: he points to feudal retainers turned out with no living, and contrasts Paris and Edinburgh, with their large households of servants, against Glasgow, where few keep more than one. His conclusion is that it is less the police that prevent crime than having few people living off others, and the passage is often read as an early statement of the link between commerce, independence and good conduct.
interpretation.zh: 这段文字是学生记录的斯密讲课笔记，并非斯密亲手写成。斯密在解释为什么依附他人为生的人多的地方犯罪也多：他举出被遣散后无以为生的封建家臣，并把仆役众多的巴黎和爱丁堡，同几乎无人雇用一名以上仆人的格拉斯哥作对比。他的结论是，防止犯罪的主要不是治安，而是尽量减少依附他人为生的人；这段话常被视为对商业、独立与良好品行之间关系的早期表述。

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing is so soon forgot as pain.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, explaining why we sympathise little with bodily pain: once it has passed, it is hardly remembered.

interpretation.en: Smith is explaining why spectators feel little sympathy for bodily pain compared with pain that comes through the imagination. Once physical pain ends, even the sufferer can no longer re-enter it, whereas a careless word from a friend keeps hurting because it lives on as an idea. His point is that sympathy works through imagination, so passions rooted in the imagination are easier for others to share than those rooted in the body.
interpretation.zh: 斯密在解释，为什么旁观者对身体疼痛的同情，远不如对源于想象的痛苦的同情。肉体的疼痛一旦过去，连受苦者本人也无法再体会；而朋友一句不经意的话会持续刺痛，因为它作为一个观念留在心里。他的意思是，同情是通过想象进行的，所以源于想象的情感比源于身体的情感更容易被他人分担。

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: The man who disassociates his ambition, however disinterested, from the coöperation of his fellows, always takes this risk of ultimate failure.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: In Democracy and Social Ethics, Addams writes about reformers who act alone rather than alongside the people they mean to help.

interpretation.en: Addams writes this near the end of her discussion of a benevolent employer who planned improvements for his workers without them. Her claim is that reform done for people rather than with them is fragile, however unselfish the reformer, because it does not draw on the shared effort that keeps a project alive. She concedes that collective effort is clumsier than one capable person acting alone, but argues it calls out deeper social capacities and is the only safe keeper of things meant for common use.
interpretation.zh: 亚当斯在讨论一位仁慈雇主的末尾写下这句话，这位雇主为工人规划种种改善，却不让工人参与。她的观点是，为人而不是与人一起进行的改革是脆弱的，无论改革者多么无私，因为它没有借助能让事业延续下去的共同努力。她承认集体行动比一个能干的人单独行事更笨拙，但认为它能唤起更深的社会能力，而且只有公众本身才能可靠地守护供公共使用的东西。

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: It is not comfortable to outrage the conventions of those among whom we live, and, if our social life be a narrow one, it is still more difficult.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, on the pressure poor families feel to follow their neighbours' customs even when outsiders call them wasteful.

interpretation.en: Addams is describing what a middle-class charity visitor learns over time in a poor household. The visitor first sees spending on mourning clothes, while the living children go short, as simple waste; Addams explains that the whole street enforces this custom, and a mother who skipped it would face blame and exclusion. The passage argues that the visitor's own moral standards are not neutral, and that judging the poor requires understanding the narrow social world whose rules they cannot easily defy.
interpretation.zh: 亚当斯在描写一位中产阶级慈善访问员在贫困家庭中逐渐明白的事情。访问员起初把为死去的孩子置办丧服、却让活着的孩子缺衣少食看作纯粹的浪费；亚当斯解释说，整条街的人都维护这一习俗，不遵守的母亲会受到指责和排斥。这段话指出，访问员自己的道德标准并不中立，要评判穷人，就得理解他们所处的那个狭小社会，其规矩他们很难违背。

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: It is impossible to bring about the higher development by any self-assertion or breaking away of the individual will.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, on the friction between daughters and families: growth comes through the family's claims, not by breaking from them.

interpretation.en: This comes from Addams's chapter on the tension between educated daughters who want to serve society and families who still claim them for domestic duty. She grants that the family must grow in each generation, but argues that real progress does not come from a daughter simply breaking away; it comes from carrying the whole family into the wider life. Her image is a plant pressing against a sheath that both confines and protects it, and readers have debated whether this counsel is wisely patient or too accommodating.
interpretation.zh: 这段话出自亚当斯讨论受过教育、想服务社会的女儿与仍要求她们尽家务义务的家庭之间矛盾的一章。她承认家庭必须在每一代人中有所发展，但认为真正的进步不来自女儿单方面的出走，而是让整个家庭一起走向更广阔的生活。她用的比喻是植物的新芽顶着既束缚又保护它的外鞘生长；这一主张究竟是明智的耐心还是过于迁就，读者看法不一。

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: There is no doubt that most of the misunderstandings of life are due to partial intelligence, because our experiences have been so unlike that we cannot comprehend each other.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics argues that people misjudge each other because their experiences of life have been so different.

interpretation.en: Addams is still discussing conflict between parents and children who live by different moral codes. She argues that misunderstanding mostly comes from partial knowledge, because people with very different experiences cannot grasp each other's reasons. Her remedy is shared experience: as family members take part in more of the same events and interests, the old clash of codes should fade, in line with her broader view that participation is the best education.
interpretation.zh: 亚当斯仍在讨论遵循不同道德准则的父母与子女之间的冲突。她认为误解大多源于片面的认识，因为经历截然不同的人无法理解彼此的理由。她给出的办法是共同的经验：家庭成员参与越来越多相同的事情和兴趣，旧有的准则冲突就会消退，这与她认为参与是最好的教育这一更大观点相一致。

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: We are constantly underestimating the amount of sentiment among simple people.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, written from Hull-House in Chicago, on the feeling for memory and old age in the songs immigrant neighbours loved.

interpretation.en: Addams is writing about the moral outlook of her working-class and immigrant neighbours, as seen in the songs and plays they love. She points out that these favour forgiveness, reconciliation and the generous rogue over strict justice, and argues that outsiders consistently underrate how much feeling such audiences have. The point feeds her wider argument that reformers misjudge the poor when they apply their own standards without first understanding what the poor actually value.
interpretation.zh: 亚当斯在写她的工人和移民邻居的道德观，这体现在他们喜爱的歌曲和戏剧中。她指出，这些作品偏爱宽恕、和解和慷慨的浪子，而不是严格的公正；她认为外人总是低估这些听众的情感之深。这一点服务于她更大的论证：改革者若不先了解穷人真正看重什么，就用自己的标准去衡量，便会误判他们。

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: Virtue then is in a sense a mean state, since it certainly has an aptitude for aiming at the mean.
entries.work: The Nicomachean Ethics
entries.context: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle sets out his doctrine that virtue lies in a mean between excess and deficiency.

interpretation.en: Aristotle has just argued that feelings and actions can go wrong by excess or by deficiency, and that the point between them is what gets praised. Virtue is therefore a mean in the sense that it is a settled disposition that aims at that middle point. He goes on to say the mean is relative to the person and situation rather than an arithmetic midpoint, and he notes that some actions, like murder, have no mean at all, so the doctrine is less a rule of moderation than a claim about getting things right.
interpretation.zh: 亚里士多德刚刚论证，情感和行为可能因过度或不足而出错，而两者之间的那一点才受到称赞。因此德性在这个意义上是一种中道：它是一种稳定的品质，以那个中间点为目标。他接着说，这个中道是相对于具体的人和情境而言的，并非算术上的中点；他还指出，有些行为如谋杀根本没有中道，所以这一学说与其说是节制的规则，不如说是关于做得恰当的主张。

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.
entries.work: Poetics
entries.context: The Poetics, on character in tragedy: a dramatic character shows itself in what a person chooses and what they avoid.

interpretation.en: In the Poetics Aristotle lists the parts of tragedy, and here he separates character from thought. Character is shown when a figure makes a choice that reveals what sort of person they are; speeches in which nobody chooses or refuses anything do not show character. Thought, by contrast, is shown in argument and general statements. The distinction reflects Aristotle's wider view, also found in his ethics, that choice is what reveals moral disposition.
interpretation.zh: 在《诗学》中，亚里士多德列举悲剧的组成部分，这里他把性格与思想区分开来。人物作出选择、显示自己是怎样的人时，性格就显现出来；人物什么也不选择、什么也不拒绝的言辞，则不能表现性格。相比之下，思想体现在论证和一般性的陈述中。这一区分反映了亚里士多德在伦理学中也持有的观点：选择最能显示一个人的道德品质。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Love is impatient and unless to her is given what is loved, grief has no limit.
entries.work: The Soliloquies of St. Augustine
entries.context: The Soliloquies, a dialogue between Augustine and Reason; here Augustine speaks as they turn to the second book.

interpretation.en: In the Soliloquies Augustine speaks as one voice in a dialogue with Reason, and this line is his transition into the second book. The love he means is his longing to know God and the soul, which the first book has stirred up, and he is impatient because the inquiry has paused. The line is less an argument than a statement of motive: the desire for truth is treated as a kind of love that suffers until it reaches what it loves.
interpretation.zh: 在《独语录》中，奥古斯丁以对话一方的身份与理性交谈，这句话是他转入第二卷的过渡。他所说的爱，是第一卷所激起的认识上帝与灵魂的渴望；因为探讨中断了，他感到急切。这句话与其说是论证，不如说是动机的表白：对真理的渴求被看作一种爱，在得到所爱之前一直受苦。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: No man loves what he endures, though he love to endure.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: In the Confessions, Augustine reflects that troubles are to be endured, not loved, even by someone who takes pride in bearing them.

interpretation.en: In Book X of the Confessions Augustine is examining his present state, divided between joys and sorrows, and asking whether human life is anything but trial. His point is that hardship is commanded to be endured, not loved: a person may be glad of being able to endure, yet would still prefer there were nothing to endure. He uses this to show that neither prosperity nor adversity offers rest, since each breeds fear or longing for the other.
interpretation.zh: 在《忏悔录》第十卷中，奥古斯丁审视自己当下的状态，在喜乐与忧苦之间挣扎，并追问人生是否无处不是试炼。他的意思是，苦难是被命令去忍受的，而不是去爱的：人可以因自己能够忍耐而欣喜，但仍宁愿没有什么需要忍受。他借此说明，顺境和逆境都不能带来安宁，因为每一种都会引起对另一种的恐惧或渴望。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: It is the decided opinion of all who use their brains, that all men desire to be happy.
entries.work: The City of God
entries.locator: OF PROVIDING MEN WITH ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS, BOOK I
entries.context: The City of God opens a long inquiry into happiness with a point Augustine takes as agreed by everyone.

interpretation.en: This opens Book X of the City of God, where Augustine starts from the one point he takes all philosophers to share: everyone wants to be happy. The disagreement, he says, is over who is happy and how happiness is reached. He uses that common ground to frame his real question, whether the worship of many gods or of the one God leads to the happy life, continuing his argument against the Platonists.
interpretation.zh: 这是《上帝之城》第十卷的开头，奥古斯丁从他认为所有哲学家都同意的一点出发：人人都想要幸福。他说，分歧在于谁是幸福的，以及怎样才能获得幸福。他借这个共同点引出真正的问题：通往幸福生活的，是敬拜众神，还是敬拜唯一的上帝，以此继续他对柏拉图主义者的论辩。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Nature is to be judged by capacity, education by knowledge, practice by its fruit.
entries.work: The City of God
entries.locator: OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS, BOOK I
entries.context: The City of God, on the three things every craftsman needs, which Augustine borrows to describe the parts of philosophy.

interpretation.en: Augustine is discussing the threefold division of philosophy into natural, rational and moral, which he links to Plato. He compares it with the three things any craftsman needs, natural ability, training and practice, and says how each is measured. He then shifts to the distinction between enjoying and using, arguing that temporal goods are to be used and only God is to be enjoyed, a distinction that is central to his ethics elsewhere.
interpretation.zh: 奥古斯丁在讨论哲学分为自然、理性和道德三部分的划分，并把这一划分与柏拉图联系起来。他把它与任何工匠都需要的三样东西——天赋、教育和练习——相比较，并说明各自以什么来衡量。随后他转到享用与使用的区分，认为尘世之物应当被使用，唯有上帝才应当被享用；这一区分在他的伦理思想中十分核心。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Every where the greater joy is ushered in by the greater pain.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: In the Confessions, Augustine wonders why recovering what was lost moves us more than never losing it.

interpretation.en: In Book VIII, around the story of Victorinus's conversion, Augustine asks why recovering something lost brings more joy than never having lost it. He gathers examples from ordinary life and from the parables of the lost and found, and states the pattern as a general law. He then turns it into a question for God, who rejoices without change, about why created things alternate between loss and recovery, and he leaves the question unresolved.
interpretation.zh: 在《忏悔录》第八卷，围绕维克托里努斯皈依的故事，奥古斯丁问：为什么失而复得比从未失去带来更大的喜乐？他从日常生活和失而复得的比喻中收集例子，把这一现象说成普遍的规律。接着他把它转成向上帝提出的问题：上帝的喜乐永恒不变，为什么受造之物却在失去与复得之间起伏？这个问题他没有给出答案。

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: The mind commands the mind, its own self, to will, and yet it doth not.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: The Confessions, Book VIII: Augustine puzzling over a will divided against itself in the months before his conversion.

interpretation.en: Augustine is describing his paralysis shortly before his conversion, when he wanted to change his life and still did not. He finds it monstrous that the body obeys the mind at once, while the mind cannot get itself to will. His answer is that the will is not whole: it commands only partly because it wills only partly. The passage is one of the classic early accounts of a divided will, and it is read both as autobiography and as an argument about the weakness of the will.
interpretation.zh: 奥古斯丁在描述自己皈依前不久的瘫痪状态：他想改变生活，却始终没有做到。他觉得这很怪异：身体对心灵的命令立即服从，而心灵却无法让自己去意愿。他的解释是，意志并不完整：它只是部分地命令，因为它只是部分地意愿。这段文字是关于分裂意志的经典早期论述之一，既被当作自传来读，也被当作关于意志软弱的论证。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Seek not proud riches, but such as thou mayest get justly, use soberly, distribute cheerfully, and leave contentedly.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Riches", advice on how to hold wealth without contempt and without greed.

interpretation.en: In Of Riches Bacon has just argued that great wealth has no real use to its owner beyond giving it away, and that its supposed security is mostly imagined. The sentence gives his positive rule: acquire honestly, spend with restraint, give gladly and part with wealth without regret. He immediately adds that riches should not be despised in a monkish way, so the essay steers between greed and contempt rather than preaching poverty.
interpretation.zh: 在《论财富》中，培根刚刚论证，巨额财富除了用于分施之外，对拥有者并无真正用处，所谓的保障多半只是想象。这句话给出了他正面的准则：正当地获取，节制地使用，乐意地分施，坦然地留下。他紧接着补充，不应像修士那样鄙弃财富，所以这篇文章是在贪婪与轻视之间寻求平衡，而不是宣扬贫穷。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Let not a man force a habit upon himself, with a perpetual continuance, but with some intermission.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Nature in Men", on changing your habits by practice with pauses rather than by unbroken strain.

interpretation.en: In Of Nature in Men Bacon is giving practical advice on changing one's natural inclinations. He argues that a new habit should be practised with breaks, because a pause gives the next attempt more force, and because someone still imperfect who practises constantly will drill in faults along with skills. He then warns that nature can lie dormant and return under temptation, so his view of self-change is cautious rather than confident.
interpretation.zh: 在《论人的天性》中，培根就如何改变天性给出实用的建议。他认为养成新习惯应当有间歇，因为停顿能使下一次尝试更有力，而且尚未完善的人若不停练习，会把错误和本领一起练成习惯。他随后警告说，天性可以长期潜伏，一遇诱惑便会复苏，所以他对自我改变的看法是谨慎的，而非乐观的。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: A wise man will make more opportunities, than he finds.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Ceremonies and Respects", on manners, timing and opportunity.

interpretation.en: In Of Ceremonies and Respects Bacon warns that being too attentive to forms and timing can hurt a person in business. He cites Solomon on the farmer who watches the wind and never sows, and then states the counter-principle: a capable person creates openings rather than waiting for them. The sentence belongs to his practical advice about not being paralysed by excessive caution and courtesy.
interpretation.zh: 在《论礼节与尊重》中，培根提醒说，过分讲究形式和时机，会在事务上吃亏。他引用所罗门关于只看风向便不撒种的农夫的话，然后提出相反的原则：能干的人自己创造机会，而不是坐等机会。这句话属于他关于不要被过度谨慎和客套束缚的实用建议。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: There is surely no greater wisdom, than well to time the beginnings, and onsets, of things.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Delays", on timing: dangers handled early are smaller.

interpretation.en: In Of Delays Bacon compares fortune to a market and to the Sibyl's shrinking offer, both images of opportunities that change in price over time. He then argues that the greatest practical wisdom lies in timing the start of things well, since dangers grow worse when they are taken lightly. He balances this immediately by warning against acting too early, so the essay is about judging ripeness, not simply about acting fast.
interpretation.zh: 在《论拖延》中，培根把命运比作市场，又比作西比尔不断减少却不降价的书卷，两者都说明机会的代价会随时间变化。他接着论证，最大的实际智慧在于把握好事情开始的时机，因为危险一旦被轻视就会变得更严重。他随即又提醒不要行动过早，所以这篇文章讲的是判断时机是否成熟，而不只是要迅速行动。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Wisdom for a man's self is, in many branches thereof, a depraved thing.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: The opening line of Bacon's essay "Of Wisdom for a Man's Self", on the kind of cleverness that serves only oneself.

interpretation.en: This opens Of Wisdom for a Man's Self, where Bacon criticises cleverness used only for one's own advantage. He illustrates it with animals that save themselves at others' cost, the rat leaving a falling house and the fox evicting the badger, and notes that those who love only themselves often end up unlucky. Bacon qualifies the claim with in many branches, so he is not condemning all self-interest, only the kind that harms others or the common good.
interpretation.zh: 这是《论利己之智》的开头，培根在这里批评只为自身利益服务的精明。他用一些牺牲他人以保全自己的动物来说明，如在房屋倒塌前逃走的老鼠、赶走獾的狐狸，并指出只爱自己的人往往结局不幸。培根用在许多方面来限定这一说法，所以他并非谴责一切自利，而只是谴责损害他人或公共利益的那种。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Anger must be limited and confined, both in race and in time.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Anger": not to abolish anger, but to limit how far it goes and how long it lasts.

interpretation.en: This opens Bacon's essay Of Anger, which rejects the Stoic aim of removing anger altogether as mere bravado. Drawing on the biblical advice to be angry without sinning and not to let the sun set on one's anger, he proposes instead to limit anger in how far it goes and how long it lasts. The essay then lays out a plan in three parts: calming the habit of anger, restraining particular fits, and raising or soothing anger in others.
interpretation.zh: 这是培根《论愤怒》的开头，他把斯多葛派要彻底消除愤怒的目标斥为一种逞强。他借用《圣经》中生气却不要犯罪、不可含怒到日落的教导，主张限制愤怒的程度和持续时间。文章随后分三部分展开：平息易怒的习性，克制具体的怒气发作，以及激起或平息他人的愤怒。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Whosoever is out of patience, is out of possession of his soul.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Anger", echoing the scriptural counsel to possess one's soul in patience.

interpretation.en: Still in Of Anger, Bacon is on the first of his three topics, how to calm the habit of anger. His method is to reflect on the damage anger does, best done once the fit has passed, and he cites Seneca and the scriptural advice to possess one's soul in patience. The sentence draws the consequence: losing patience means losing control of oneself, so anger is presented as a kind of self-dispossession.
interpretation.zh: 仍在《论愤怒》中，培根谈的是三个话题中的第一个：如何平息易怒的习性。他的方法是反思愤怒造成的危害，最好在怒气完全过去之后进行；他引用塞内卡以及《圣经》中以忍耐保守灵魂的教导。这句话得出结论：失去耐心就是失去对自己的掌控，因此愤怒被描述为一种丧失自我的状态。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: He that builds a fair house, upon an ill seat, committeth himself to prison.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Building", about the siting of actual houses; the line reads as a figure, but Bacon meant it literally.

interpretation.en: Of Building is a practical essay about real houses, and it opens by insisting that houses are for living in, not for looking at. The sentence means that a beautiful house on a bad site traps its owner, and Bacon lists what makes a site bad: unhealthy or uneven air, poor roads and markets, lack of water and wood, bad neighbours. Readers often take the line as a metaphor, but in context it is literal advice about choosing where to build.
interpretation.zh: 《论建筑》是一篇关于真实房屋的实用文章，开篇就强调房子是用来住的，不是用来看的。这句话的意思是，把漂亮的房子建在不好的地方，等于把主人关进监狱；培根列举了地段不好的种种原因：空气不洁或冷热不均、道路和集市不便、缺水缺柴、邻居不好。读者常把这句话当作比喻，但在上下文中，它是关于选址的字面建议。

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: He that is too much in anything, so that he giveth another occasion of satiety, maketh himself cheap.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Ceremonies and Respects", on keeping a little reserve in company.

interpretation.en: In Of Ceremonies and Respects Bacon is weighing how much formality to use with different people: keep a little dignity among equals, be a little familiar with inferiors. The sentence warns that anyone who overdoes anything, until others grow tired of it, loses value in their eyes. It is advice about measure in social conduct, and fits the essay's general view that manners should be natural and unforced.
interpretation.zh: 在《论礼节与尊重》中，培根在权衡对不同的人应讲究多少礼节：在同辈中稍保持体面，对下属稍显亲近。这句话提醒说，任何事做过了头，让别人感到厌腻，就会降低自己的身价。这是关于社交分寸的建议，符合这篇文章总体上主张举止应自然而不做作的看法。

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Every motive, in the final analysis, is the perspective of a pleasure to be procured, or of a pain to be avoided.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, an English version of Bentham's work edited by Dumont, arguing that motives are neither good nor bad in themselves.

interpretation.en: The Theory of Legislation reaches English through Dumont's French reworking of Bentham's manuscripts, so the wording is at two removes from Bentham. The passage argues that motives should not be labelled good or bad, since every motive comes down to seeking pleasure or avoiding pain; the same hunger can lead one person to steal and another to work. For Bentham this means the law should judge actions by their effects, not by the motive behind them.
interpretation.zh: 《立法理论》的英文版来自杜蒙对边沁手稿的法文改写，所以措辞与边沁原文隔了两层。这段话认为不应把动机分为好与坏，因为一切动机归根到底都是追求快乐或避免痛苦；同样的饥饿，可以使一个人去偷，另一个人去工作。对边沁来说，这意味着法律应根据行为的后果而不是背后的动机来评判。

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Every new and important truth must of necessity have many enemies, for the single reason that it is new and important.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, arguing against censorship of the press.

interpretation.en: Bentham is arguing against censorship of the press, and says its harm cannot be measured because it can halt progress in every field. Any important new truth will have enemies simply because it is new, and a censor is unlikely to be one of the rare people above common prejudice. Even if he were, he risks nothing by forbidding and everything by allowing, so the system itself pushes him to suppress whatever goes beyond ordinary ideas.
interpretation.zh: 边沁在反对出版审查，他说审查的危害无法衡量，因为它可能阻断人类心智在各个领域的进步。任何重要的新真理都会树敌，只因为它新而重要；而审查官不太可能属于那少数超越流行偏见的人。即使他是，禁止对他毫无风险，准许却可能招来一切风险，所以这个制度本身就会促使他压制一切超出寻常观念的东西。

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Love which descends has more force than love which ascends.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, on family duties: the love of parents for children is stronger than children's gratitude to parents.

interpretation.en: Bentham is discussing how poorly the old are provided for when they must rely on their families. He argues that the love of parents for children is stronger than the love of children for parents, because instinct and hope attach to the young, while gratitude, which is all the old can count on, is weaker. He adds that even well-cared-for old people feel the bitterness of changing from giver to receiver, which supports his case for other forms of provision.
interpretation.zh: 边沁在讨论老人依靠家庭时得到的供养如何不足。他认为父母对子女的爱比子女对父母的爱更强，因为本能和希望都附着在年轻人身上，而老人唯一能指望的感恩之情要弱得多。他还说，即使受到悉心照料，老人也会因从给予者变成接受者而感到苦涩，这支持了他主张另寻供养方式的论点。

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Nothing is more common than to authorize under one name what would be odious under another.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, on how the same act is excused when it is given a different name.

interpretation.en: Bentham is introducing examples of attacks on security, meaning the protection people need for their property and expectations. He argues that governments routinely permit, under a respectable name, acts that would be condemned under their true one. The broader claim is that what is unjust in private morals cannot become innocent just because the state does it.
interpretation.zh: 边沁在引出侵害安全的例子，这里的安全指人们对财产和预期所需要的保障。他认为，政府常常给某些行为冠以体面的名称加以准许，而这些行为若用真名就会受到谴责。更大的主张是，私人道德中不公正的事，不会因为由国家来做就变得无辜。

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: It is only in the absence of interest that experience can hope to be regarded, or reason heard.
entries.work: The Book of Fallacies
entries.context: The Book of Fallacies, Bentham's catalogue of bad political arguments, on why self-interested people cannot weigh experience fairly.

interpretation.en: The surrounding text applies this line to the English government's treatment of Ireland, arguing that officials with sinecures and inflated salaries have an interest in keeping the Irish majority down. The general claim is that when people have something to gain, they will neither heed experience nor listen to reason, so arguments addressed to them are wasted. It fits the theme of The Book of Fallacies, that many political arguments are really cover for the speaker's interest; the passage may come from an editor's arrangement of Bentham's material rather than his finished text.
interpretation.zh: 上下文把这句话用于英国政府对爱尔兰的统治，指出领取闲职和高薪的官员有压制爱尔兰多数人的利益。一般的主张是，人一旦有利可图，就既不会重视经验，也不会听从理性，向他们讲道理是徒劳的。这符合《谬误之书》的主题：许多政治论证其实是在掩护说话者的利益；这段文字可能出自编者对边沁材料的整理，而非他定稿的文本。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: All that is serious in life comes from our freedom.
entries.work: Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of the Comic
entries.locator: OF WORDS WE GENERALLY FIND TWO
entries.context: Laughter, Bergson's essay on the comic, explaining why tragedy and serious life belong to freedom while comedy belongs to automatism.

interpretation.en: Bergson's theory of the comic holds that people laugh at something mechanical laid over something living. Here he sets up the contrast: the serious, even dramatic side of life comes from what is freely matured and chosen, the feelings and decisions that are truly one's own. Comedy arises, he goes on, the moment that apparent freedom is imagined as hiding the strings of a puppet, so seriousness and laughter are defined against each other.
interpretation.zh: 柏格森的喜剧理论认为，人们笑的是覆盖在活生生的事物上的机械性。这里他设下对照：生活中严肃乃至富有戏剧性的一面，来自那些经过自由酝酿和选择、真正属于自己的情感和决定。他接着说，只要把这种表面的自由想象成掩盖着木偶的提线，喜剧就产生了；所以严肃与笑是相互界定的。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: To act is to re-adapt oneself.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, on the intellect as a tool for action: to act is to keep adjusting to a changing situation.

interpretation.en: Bergson is arguing that science, however theoretical, is ultimately shaped by practical action. Action moves in jumps from one situation to the next, so to act means constantly adjusting to a new arrangement, and knowledge that serves action must likewise move from state to state. His point is critical: science and ordinary thought grasp only separate moments, like frames of film, and miss the continuous change between them.
interpretation.zh: 柏格森在论证，科学无论多么理论化，最终都受实际行动的塑造。行动是跳跃式地从一个情境到另一个情境，所以行动就意味着不断适应新的局面，服务于行动的知识也必须从一个状态跳到另一个状态。他的观点带有批判性：科学和日常思维只把握孤立的瞬间，就像电影的一帧帧画面，而错过了其间连续的变化。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: The more we study the nature of time, the more we shall comprehend that duration means invention, the creation of forms, the continual elaboration of the absolutely new.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, Bergson's central claim that time as lived is continual invention rather than repetition.

interpretation.en: Near the start of Creative Evolution Bergson states his central thesis that the universe endures, meaning that real time is not a series of interchangeable instants but an ongoing production of novelty. He contrasts this with the systems science isolates, which last only because they are tied to the whole. He also distinguishes a descending movement that merely unwinds and an ascending one that creates, which the rest of the book develops.
interpretation.zh: 在《创造进化论》开篇不久，柏格森提出他的核心论点：宇宙是绵延的，也就是说，真实的时间不是一串可以互换的瞬间，而是不断产生新事物的过程。他把这与科学所划分出的系统作对比，后者之所以能持续，只是因为与整体相连。他还区分了只是展开既定之物的下降运动和进行创造的上升运动，全书其余部分会加以发挥。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: Our intellect has been cast in the mold of action.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, arguing that we first think in order to act, so the intellect is shaped for practical use.

interpretation.en: Bergson is criticising both radical mechanism and radical finalism, the view that everything follows a preset purpose. He argues that both stretch concepts beyond their proper range, because the intellect evolved to serve action: to act, it sets goals, plans means and relies on regular causes. This explains why the mind naturally thinks in terms of plans and mechanisms, and why, in his view, neither fits life itself.
interpretation.zh: 柏格森在同时批判彻底的机械论和彻底的目的论，后者认为一切都遵循预先设定的目的。他认为两者都把某些概念用得太远，因为理智是为行动服务而演化出来的：为了行动，它设定目标、筹划手段、依赖有规律的因果。这解释了为什么心智天然地用计划和机制来思考，也解释了为什么在他看来，两者都不适合生命本身。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: We must recognize that all is not coherent in nature.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, allowing that accident and incoherence are real in the history of life.

interpretation.en: Bergson is describing evolution as an impulse that advances along a few main lines while countless side paths stall or regress. He criticises the philosopher who assumes every detail belongs to an overall plan, since such a person ends up seeing everything as accidental. Granting from the start that much in nature is incoherent, he argues, is what allows the main directions of life to become visible.
interpretation.zh: 柏格森把进化描述为一种冲动，沿着少数几条主线前进，而无数旁支则停滞或倒退。他批评那种认定每个细节都属于某一总体计划的哲学家，因为这样的人最后会把一切都看作偶然。他认为，从一开始就承认自然中有许多不连贯之处，才能看清生命发展的主要方向。

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: Nature is more and better than a plan in course of realization.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, arguing that life is not the carrying out of a plan fixed in advance.

interpretation.en: This follows directly from Bergson's point that much in nature is incoherent. A plan, he says, fixes the form of the future in advance and so closes it off, whereas the evolution of life leaves the future open as a creation that continues from an original impulse. The line rejects both strict design and pure chance, and is central to his idea of creative evolution.
interpretation.zh: 这句话紧接着柏格森关于自然中有许多不连贯之处的论点。他说，计划预先规定了未来的形式，因而把未来封闭了；而生命的进化则让未来保持敞开，是一种源于最初冲动、持续不断的创造。这句话既拒绝严格的设计论，也拒绝纯粹的偶然论，是他创造进化思想的核心。

entries.name: George Berkeley
entries.en: The more doubt the more room there is for faith, a sceptic of all men having the least right to demand evidence.
entries.work: Alciphron; or, The Minute Philosopher
entries.context: Alciphron, Berkeley's dialogue against the freethinkers; here his spokesman argues that doubting everything is no ground for refusing faith.

interpretation.en: The line is spoken by Crito, one of the Christian speakers in Berkeley's dialogue, to a freethinker who has admitted he doubts everything. Crito turns that doubt against him: someone who doubts all opinions must doubt his own unbelief too, so he has no special right to demand proof before taking faith seriously. The argument goes on in a wager-like form, that since the stakes favour belief, a consistent sceptic should lean toward it; whether this treats faith fairly is a matter readers dispute.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自贝克莱对话中一位基督徒说话者克里托之口，对象是一位承认自己怀疑一切的自由思想者。克里托把这种怀疑反过来用于对方：怀疑一切观点的人，也必须怀疑自己的不信，因此他没有特别的权利在认真对待信仰之前要求证据。论证接着以类似赌注的方式展开：既然利害偏向信仰，一贯的怀疑者就应倾向于信；这样对待信仰是否公允，读者有争议。

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Never will fortune make thine that which the nature of things has excluded from thy ownership.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison; Philosophy tells the grieving Boethius that fortune's gifts were never his to keep.

interpretation.en: The speaker is Lady Philosophy, addressing Boethius as he laments the loss of his position and wealth. She asks whether the beauty of fields, sea and sky is in any sense his, and argues that admiring such things does not make them one's own possessions. Fortune cannot give what by nature belongs to someone else, so what Boethius has lost was never truly his, and his grief rests on a mistake about ownership.
interpretation.zh: 说话的是哲学女神，她对正为失去地位和财富而悲叹的波爱修斯说话。她问，田野、大海和天空的美在什么意义上属于他，并论证欣赏这些事物并不使它们成为自己的财产。命运不能给予本质上属于别人的东西，所以波爱修斯所失去的从来就不真正属于他，他的悲伤建立在对所有权的误解之上。

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Nature is content with few things, and with a very little of these.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy: Philosophy argues that what nature truly needs is small, and fortune's extras add nothing.

interpretation.en: Lady Philosophy is continuing her argument that fortune's gifts add nothing to a person's real good. If one supplies only what nature needs, there is no reason to depend on fortune, because nature requires very little; anything added beyond that is either unpleasant or harmful. The claim draws on older Stoic and Epicurean ideas of natural need, and it prepares her case that true happiness cannot lie in external goods.
interpretation.zh: 哲学女神继续论证，命运的馈赠对一个人真正的善毫无增益。如果只满足自然所需，就没有理由依赖命运，因为自然所需极少；超出的部分要么令人不快，要么有害。这一主张借用了斯多葛派和伊壁鸠鲁派关于自然需要的古老观念，并为她后面的论证作铺垫：真正的幸福不可能在于外在之物。

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Look upon the infinitude, the solidity, the swift motion, of the heavens, and for once cease to admire things mean and worthless.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy: Philosophy turns Boethius from bodily goods to the order of the heavens.

interpretation.en: Lady Philosophy is going through the false goods people pursue, money, office, power, glory, pleasure and bodily excellence, and showing that each brings trouble or is easily surpassed. Against bodily strength and beauty she sets the vastness and order of the heavens, then adds that the heavens deserve admiration less for their size than for the reason that governs them. The passage moves the argument from worldly goods toward the rational order she will identify with the true good.
interpretation.zh: 哲学女神在逐一审视人们追求的虚假之善：金钱、官职、权力、荣耀、享乐和身体的优越，说明每一种都带来烦恼，或很容易被超越。针对体力和美貌，她提出天体的广大与秩序，又补充说天体值得赞叹，与其说因其广大，不如说因支配它们的理性。这段话把论证从世俗之善引向她将要认定为真正之善的理性秩序。

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Love, when real, ever desires light, in order to attain its ends.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, Comte's summary of his system, arguing that true feeling helps thought rather than clouding it.

interpretation.en: Comte is defending his plan to make feeling the guiding element of human nature, with intellect as its servant but not its slave. Against the worry that this would stunt thought, he argues that genuine love wants knowledge because it needs to reach its goals, so true feeling favours sound thinking. The claim is central to his later system, and critics have questioned whether placing reason under feeling protects inquiry as well as he says.
interpretation.zh: 孔德在为他的设想辩护：让情感成为人性的主导因素，理智是情感的仆人而不是奴隶。有人担心这会妨碍思想的发展，他回应说，真正的爱需要知识，因为它要实现自己的目标，所以真实的情感有利于健全的思考。这一主张是他后期体系的核心，批评者则怀疑把理性置于情感之下，是否真能像他说的那样保护探究。

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Love cannot be deep unless it remains constant to a fixed object.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, Comte's case for constancy in love and marriage.

interpretation.en: Comte is setting out the conditions of marriage in his system, which he holds must be exclusive and indissoluble. He argues against those who think happiness lies in changeable love, claiming that love deepens only through constancy and that the mere possibility of change tempts it. He concludes that society must restrain caprice, so that love is placed under a strict and permanent discipline.
interpretation.zh: 孔德在阐述他的体系中婚姻的条件，他认为婚姻必须是排他的、不可解除的。他反驳那些认为幸福在于爱情多变的人，主张爱只有在专一中才能加深，而仅仅存在改变的可能就是一种诱惑。他由此得出结论，社会必须约束反复无常，使爱情受到严格而持久的约束。

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Our life is really destined to be a compound of resignation and action.
entries.work: The Catechism of Positive Religion
entries.context: The Catechism of Positivism, a dialogue setting out Comte's "religion of humanity"; here the priest speaks, Comte's own spokesman.

interpretation.en: The Catechism is a dialogue between a priest of Comte's religion of humanity and a woman, and this line belongs to the priest, who speaks for Comte. He argues that natural order is a necessity that still allows modification, so life combines accepting fixed laws with acting within them. Resignation is presented not as passivity but as the ground of effective action, since only knowing what cannot be changed lets one change what can.
interpretation.zh: 《实证主义教义问答》是孔德人道教的一位祭司与一位女性之间的对话，这句话出自代表孔德立场的祭司。他认为自然秩序是一种允许修正的必然性，所以人生既要接受固定的规律，又要在其范围内行动。顺从在这里不是消极，而是有效行动的基础，因为只有知道什么不能改变，才能改变可以改变的东西。

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: All practical work requires as the first condition of its success that each one who co-operates should be honest, intelligent, and courageous.
entries.work: The Catechism of Positive Religion
entries.context: The Catechism of Positivism, on the qualities any shared work depends on.

interpretation.en: The priest is defining the practical scope of Comte's religion: it aims to improve human order physically, intellectually and morally, but leaves the details of industry and politics to their own fields. Religion's part in practical work is indirect, by shaping the character of the people who do it. Honesty, intelligence and courage are named as the conditions any cooperative work needs, and beyond securing these religion does not intervene.
interpretation.zh: 祭司在界定孔德宗教的实践范围：它旨在从物质、智识和道德上改善人类秩序，但把工业和政治的具体事务留给各自的领域。宗教在实际工作中的作用是间接的，即塑造从事这些工作的人的品格。诚实、智慧和勇气被列为任何合作事业所需的条件，除了确保这些品质之外，宗教不加干预。

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: The best workmen, like the best philosophers, will soon cease to feel envy for greatness, laden, as it always must be, with heavy responsibilities.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, imagining workers in a future society freed from envy of those who hold power.

interpretation.en: Comte is describing how, in his future society, public praise and blame would make up for unavoidable inequalities of rank and wealth. He argues that workers will come to see that happiness does not depend on high position, and that power and fame bring heavy burdens. The passage is openly prospective, as Comte admits the compensation does not yet exist, and it can also be read as an argument for reconciling workers to their station.
interpretation.zh: 孔德在描述，在他设想的未来社会中，公众的褒贬将弥补等级和财富上不可避免的不平等。他认为工人将会明白，幸福并不取决于高位，而权力和名声都伴随着沉重的负担。这段话明显是展望性的，孔德自己也承认这种补偿尚未实现；这段话也可以读作一种让工人安于本分的论证。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: He who wishes truth to be generated without error wishes for the son without the father.
entries.work: What is Living and What is Dead of the Philosophy of Hegel
entries.context: What Is Living and What Is Dead of the Philosophy of Hegel, Croce's study, on error as a necessary stage on the way to truth.

interpretation.en: Croce is defending Hegel's idea that the history of philosophy moves through its mistakes. He gives examples: Schelling's error led toward a better conception of the absolute, Plato's transcendent Ideas led to Aristotle, Hume's scepticism made Kant possible. The image of father and son makes the point that error is not an accident on the way to truth but its parent, without which the truth could not have been reached. He goes on to say that despising error means despising truth itself.
interpretation.zh: 克罗齐在为黑格尔的一个观点辩护：哲学史是通过错误前进的。他举例说，谢林的错误通向对绝对者更好的理解，柏拉图超验的理念引出了亚里士多德，休谟的怀疑论使康德成为可能。父与子的比喻要说明，错误不是通往真理途中的意外，而是真理的来源，没有它就无法抵达真理。他接着说，轻视错误就是轻视真理本身。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: Hope and fear are related to action itself in its becoming, not to its result and succession.
entries.work: The Philosophy of the Practical: Economic and Ethic
entries.locator: OF VOLITION AND ACTION AND DISTINCTION
entries.context: The Philosophy of the Practical, on why the good person acts without fixing on outcomes, since there is always good still to be done.

interpretation.en: Croce is describing the inner state of the person of action, using Machiavelli's view that we control about half of what happens and fortune the rest. Between the anxious and the overconfident he places the sage, who stays calm because there will always be some good to do whatever happens. The passage then locates hope and fear in the doing of an action as it unfolds, not in its eventual outcome. The sense seems to be that the emotions belong to the effort itself, so the sage can feel them without being ruled by results; the compressed wording leaves this somewhat open.
interpretation.zh: 克罗齐在描述行动者的内心，借用马基雅维利的看法：人能掌控的约占一半，其余归于命运。在焦虑者与过度自信者之间，他安放了一位智者，智者之所以平静，是因为无论发生什么，总有善事可做。这段话随后把希望与恐惧放在行动展开的过程之中，而不是放在行动最终的结果上。大意似乎是，这些情绪属于努力本身，所以智者可以感受它们而不被结果所支配；原文措辞简练，这一点仍有解释空间。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: Love passes, but generates other beings, who will love.
entries.work: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept
entries.context: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, on how everything passes yet gives rise to more of its kind.

interpretation.en: Croce is discussing why philosophy never reaches a final state, and answering those who find this a sign that everything is vain. He argues that each new philosophy depends on the old one and carries it forward, so constant change is growth rather than waste. Love is offered as a comparison: no one gives it up because it does not last, and it continues by producing new people who love in turn. The same holds, he says, for thoughts, which give rise to further thoughts.
interpretation.zh: 克罗齐在讨论哲学为什么永远不会到达终点，并回应那些因此认为万事皆空的人。他认为每一种新哲学都依赖旧哲学并把它延续下去，所以不断变化是成长而非浪费。他拿爱作比较：没有人因为爱不长久而放弃它，而爱的延续方式，是孕育出新的、也会去爱的人。他说思想也是如此，会生出更多的思想。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: Knowledge of lesser beauties leads to loftier spiritual beauties.
entries.work: Aesthetic as Science of Expression and General Linguistic
entries.context: Croce's Aesthetic, in its history of ideas, summarising a Renaissance dialogue on love and beauty.

interpretation.en: This line is not Croce's own view. It comes from his historical survey of earlier ideas about beauty, where he summarises the Dialogues of Love by Leone, a Spanish Jewish author of the Renaissance. Croce reports the dialogue's teaching that beauty delights the soul and draws it to love, and that knowing lesser beauties leads upward to higher, spiritual ones. Croce himself places this within what he calls mystical aesthetics, a tradition his own theory of art largely sets aside.
interpretation.zh: 这句话不是克罗齐本人的观点。它出自他对前人美学思想的历史回顾，他在这里概述文艺复兴时期西班牙犹太作家莱昂内所著的《爱的对话》。克罗齐转述该书的教导：美使灵魂愉悦并引它去爱，认识较低的美会把人引向更高的、精神性的美。克罗齐把这归入他所说的神秘主义美学，而他自己的艺术理论大体上并不采纳这一传统。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: It is forgotten that man does not live by bread alone, and that bread itself is a spiritual food if it increase the force of spiritual life.
entries.work: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept
entries.context: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, rejecting the idea that only material needs are "practical".

interpretation.en: Croce is rejecting the claim, which he traces to Bacon, that natural science is uniquely practical because it serves human needs. He says all knowledge, including art, philosophy and history, is directed toward action, and that the bias toward the sciences comes from a narrow idea that only food, clothing and shelter count as practical. The line borrows the biblical phrase about bread to argue that even material goods matter because they strengthen spiritual life, so the material and the spiritual cannot be split as that view supposes.
interpretation.zh: 克罗齐在反驳一种他追溯到培根的主张：自然科学因为服务于人的需要，所以唯独它是实用的。他说一切知识，包括艺术、哲学和历史，都指向行动；偏重科学的成见，来自一种狭隘的观念，以为只有吃穿住才算实用。这句话借用了《圣经》中关于面包的说法，论证即便物质之物，其价值也在于增强精神生活，因此物质与精神不能像那种观点那样截然分开。

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: We do not know, nor do we need to know, what will happen.
entries.work: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept
entries.context: Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, arguing that we act on what has happened, not on knowledge of the future.

interpretation.en: Croce is answering the objection that ordinary life depends on predicting the future, such as knowing an egg will cook in five minutes. He replies that such predictions are only summaries of what has already happened, and that action rests on knowledge of the past, not of the future. He adds that real knowledge of the future would paralyse action rather than help it. The egg sometimes comes out wrong, yet one still cooks it, because acting is necessary regardless.
interpretation.zh: 克罗齐在回应一种反驳：日常生活依赖对未来的预测，比如知道鸡蛋煮五分钟就熟。他答道，这类预测不过是对已经发生之事的概括，行动所依据的是对过去的认识，而非对未来的认识。他还说，如果真的知道未来，非但无助于行动，反而会让人无法行动。鸡蛋有时煮得不对，人还是照样去煮，因为无论如何都必须行动。

entries.name: John Dewey
entries.en: Love of certainty is a demand for guarantees in advance of action.
entries.work: Human Nature and Conduct: An Introduction to Social Psychology
entries.context: Human Nature and Conduct, Dewey's study of habit, on dogmatism as fear of risking anything in new experience.

interpretation.en: Dewey is criticising the long tradition in science and morals that sought fixed ends and unchanging truths. He argues that behind this lies fear of the new and attachment to what one already has, and that even the classicist who appeals to tradition is moved by unadmitted impulses such as timidity. The line defines the wish for certainty as a demand to be guaranteed the result before acting. He goes on to say this turns truth into a kind of insurance, when truth can only be gained by experiment.
interpretation.zh: 杜威在批评科学与道德中一个由来已久的传统：追求固定的目的和不变的真理。他认为，其背后是对新事物的恐惧和对已有之物的依恋；即便诉诸传统的古典主义者，也受着胆怯之类未承认的冲动驱动。这句话把对确定性的渴求界定为在行动之前就要求结果得到保证。他接着说，这样就把真理变成了一种保险，而真理只能通过实验去获得。

entries.name: John Dewey
entries.en: Nothing is more tragic than failure to discover one's true business in life, or to find that one has drifted or been forced by circumstance into an uncongenial calling.
entries.work: Democracy and Education: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Education
entries.context: Democracy and Education, in its chapter on vocation: finding the work one is fitted for is the key to happiness.

interpretation.en: Dewey is discussing the place of vocation in education. He defines an occupation as what balances a person's particular abilities with service to others, and calls finding and getting the chance to do one's fitting work the key to happiness. The line names the opposite case, drifting or being pushed into unsuitable work, as the worst outcome. He then argues the loss is social as well as personal, since others receive less than the person could give, and cites slave labour as wasteful for that reason.
interpretation.zh: 杜威在讨论职业在教育中的地位。他把职业界定为使个人特殊才能与服务他人相平衡的东西，并说找到适合自己的工作并获得去做的机会，是幸福的关键。这句话指出相反的情形，即随波逐流或被环境逼入不合适的工作，是最坏的结果。他接着论证，这种损失既是个人的也是社会的，因为他人得到的少于此人本可贡献的，并以奴隶劳动的浪费为例。

entries.name: John Dewey
entries.en: Love of the pleasures of cheerfulness, of companionship is one of the steadying influences in conduct.
entries.work: Human Nature and Conduct: An Introduction to Social Psychology
entries.context: Human Nature and Conduct, defending ordinary pleasures as a source of balance rather than a moral danger.

interpretation.en: Dewey is responding to moralists who warn against love of pleasure. He separates ordinary pleasures such as cheerfulness and company, which he says help keep conduct steady, from the hunt for isolated thrills pursued for their own sake regardless of results. The second kind he links to lives cut off from normal activity, through routine or over-specialisation, which then seek artificial stimulation. The problem, on his account, is not pleasure but pleasure detached from the rest of activity.
interpretation.zh: 杜威在回应那些告诫人们不要贪图享乐的道德家。他把愉快、陪伴这类寻常乐趣，与为刺激本身而追求、不顾后果的孤立快感区分开来；前者他认为有助于稳定行为。后者他归因于被常规或过度专门化隔绝于正常活动的生活，这样的生活便去寻求人为的刺激。在他看来，问题不在快乐本身，而在于快乐脱离了其他活动。

entries.name: John Dewey
entries.en: Always our old habits and dispositions carry us into new fields.
entries.work: Human Nature and Conduct: An Introduction to Social Psychology
entries.context: Human Nature and Conduct, on why moral learning is never finished, since every choice meets new conditions.

interpretation.en: Dewey is arguing that moral deliberation is never finished. Even the most careful decision only fixes a disposition, which then has to be applied to new and unforeseen situations and adjusted again. The line makes the point that the habits formed in the past are what take a person into new circumstances, so their meaning must keep being relearned. He then raises the objection that this makes moral life a labour of Sisyphus, and answers that continual inquiry keeps activity alive and growing in meaning.
interpretation.zh: 杜威在论证道德审议永远不会结束。即便是最审慎的决定，也只是确立了一种倾向，而这种倾向还必须应用于新的、不可预见的情境，并再次调整。这句话要说明，过去形成的习惯正是把人带入新境况的东西，因此必须不断重新理解它们的意义。他随后提出一个反驳，说这让道德生活成了西西弗斯式的苦役，并回答说，持续的探究使活动保持生机，意义不断增长。

entries.name: John Dewey
entries.en: It is the very nature of life to strive to continue in being.
entries.work: Democracy and Education: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Education
entries.context: Democracy and Education, opening its account of education as the way a life renews itself.

interpretation.en: This opens the summary of Dewey's first chapter, where he builds his account of education on a biological starting point. Living things keep themselves going only by constant renewal, and he argues that education does for social life what nutrition and reproduction do for the body. The line is the premise: striving to continue is what life is. From it he moves to education as the passing on of experience through communication, which changes everyone who takes part.
interpretation.zh: 这是杜威第一章总结的开头，他在这里以生物学为起点建立对教育的论述。生物只有通过不断更新才能维持自身，他认为教育之于社会生活，正如营养与繁殖之于身体。这句话是前提：努力延续自身正是生命的本性。由此他转向把教育看作通过交流传递经验的过程，而这一过程会改变所有参与者。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Nothing will supply the want of sunshine to peaches, and, to make knowledge valuable, you must have the cheerfulness of wisdom.
entries.work: The Conduct of Life
entries.context: The Conduct of Life, in the essay "Considerations by the Way", on cheerfulness as a condition of wisdom.

interpretation.en: Emerson is arguing that good temper is more essential than talent, even for work that depends on talent. Just before, he criticises indulging the sick and the gloomy; just after, he says healthy things are sweet-tempered and that despondency shows a failure to see the law by which things are ordered. The peach image makes cheerfulness a condition for knowledge to ripen, not a decoration on it. For Emerson the cheerfulness he has in mind follows from insight into how the world works.
interpretation.zh: 爱默生在论证好的性情比才能更重要，即使在依靠才能的工作中也是如此。在此之前，他批评对病弱与消沉者的纵容；在此之后，他说健康的事物都性情温和，沮丧说明人没有看到万物运行的法则。桃子的比喻把愉悦当作知识成熟的条件，而不是知识的点缀。在爱默生看来，他所说的愉悦来自对世界运行方式的洞见。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: He who wishes to walk in the most peaceful parts of life with any serenity must screw himself up to resolution.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: From Emerson's essay "Prudence", on facing what we fear rather than escaping it.

interpretation.en: In the essay Prudence, Emerson argues that dealing wisely with frightening things means courage, not avoidance. Even a quiet life, he says, requires steeling oneself, because calm comes from facing what one dreads. He supports this with the Latin proverb that the eye is beaten first in battle, and with soldiers and sailors who endure danger better than those who only imagine it. The claim is that fear is mostly fed by distance and anticipation.
interpretation.zh: 在《审慎》一文中，爱默生主张，明智地对待可怕之事意味着勇气，而非逃避。他说即便是安宁的生活，也需要人鼓起决心，因为平静来自直面所畏惧的东西。他用拉丁谚语说战斗中眼睛最先被击败，并以士兵和水手为例，说他们比只会想象危险的人更能承受危险。其主张是，恐惧大多由距离和预想滋养。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Friendship requires more time than poor busy men can usually command.
entries.work: The Conduct of Life
entries.context: The Conduct of Life, in the essay "Behavior", on manners and the time real friendship needs.

interpretation.en: In the essay Behavior, Emerson is discussing manners, which he says require time because haste is vulgar. Friendship, he argues, deserves ceremony and space rather than being squeezed into corners, and busy people rarely have the leisure it needs. He follows this with an example of a refined friend and calls it a loss to both when such a friendship is crowded out by pressing affairs. The busy men are pitied here, not blamed.
interpretation.zh: 在《举止》一文中，爱默生讨论礼仪，说礼仪需要时间，因为匆忙是粗俗的。他认为友谊应当有礼节与空间，而不应被挤到角落里，忙碌的人很少拥有友谊所需的闲暇。他随后举了一位情感细腻的朋友为例，说这样的友谊若被紧迫的事务挤掉，对双方都是损失。这里对忙碌之人是怜惜，而非指责。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: There is no beautifier of complexion, or form, or behavior, like the wish to scatter joy and not pain around us.
entries.work: The Conduct of Life
entries.context: The Conduct of Life, closing the essay "Behavior" with the source of good manners.

interpretation.en: Emerson closes Behavior by naming what makes manners as moving as beauty. He lists fine perception and self-control, then a good heart, and ends with the desire to spread joy rather than pain. The claim is that this desire shows outwardly and improves how a person looks and acts more than anything else. Good manners, on this account, are finally an expression of goodwill rather than a learned technique.
interpretation.zh: 爱默生在《举止》的结尾指出，是什么使礼仪像美貌一样动人。他列举了敏锐的感知与自制，然后是善良的心，最后归结为希望给周围带来快乐而非痛苦的愿望。其主张是，这种愿望会显露在外，比任何东西都更能改善一个人的容貌与举止。照此看来，良好的礼仪归根到底是善意的表达，而非学来的技巧。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Friendship, like the immortality of the soul, is too good to be believed.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: From Emerson's essay "Friendship", which admits that we idealise those we love.

interpretation.en: In Friendship, Emerson admits a doubt that runs alongside love. He compares friendship to the immortality of the soul, something so good that one half suspects it is not real. He explains that we partly know we attribute to the friend virtues we ourselves supply, much as a lover knows the beloved is not quite what he worships. The essay does not abandon friendship over this; it asks whether examining its foundations will cool it, and goes on to seek a sturdier basis.
interpretation.zh: 在《友谊》中，爱默生承认与爱相伴的一种怀疑。他把友谊比作灵魂不朽，美好得让人半信半疑。他解释说，我们隐约知道，朋友身上那些美德有一部分是我们自己赋予的，就像恋人知道所爱之人并不完全是他所崇拜的样子。文章并未因此放弃友谊，而是追问审视它的根基是否会使它冷却，并继续寻找更坚实的基础。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Do your work, respecting the excellence of the work, and not its acceptableness.
entries.work: The Conduct of Life
entries.context: The Conduct of Life, in the essay "Wealth", on spending on what your talent truly needs.

interpretation.en: In the essay Wealth, Emerson's first rule of spending is that it should follow character: money spent on the tools of one's real talent is well spent. The line extends this to work itself, valuing quality over what will please others. He goes on to define waste not as spending a lot but as spending off the line of one's career, and calls taking on side jobs that pull away from one's main purpose the thing that ruins people and states. Economy, for Emerson here, means staying on one's own path.
interpretation.zh: 在《财富》一文中，爱默生关于花费的第一条准则是，花费应出自品格：花在发挥真正才能所需工具上的钱是值得的。这句话把这一点延伸到工作本身，看重品质，而非是否讨人喜欢。他接着把浪费界定为不是花得多，而是花在偏离自己事业方向的地方，并说为了一时之需而偏离主要目标的零活，才是使个人与国家破产的原因。在这里，爱默生所说的节俭，意味着坚守自己的道路。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: From Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance", on nonconformity.

interpretation.en: In Self-Reliance, Emerson argues that a person must test even accepted ideas of goodness rather than simply obey them. The line makes the integrity of one's own mind the only final authority. He illustrates it with a story from his youth: told that his inner impulses might come from below rather than above, he answered that if so he would live from the Devil. This is deliberate provocation, and the passage is often read as his most extreme statement of trust in inner conviction over tradition.
interpretation.zh: 在《自立》中，爱默生主张，人必须检验即便是公认的善的观念，而不是一味服从。这句话把自己心灵的完整视为唯一的最终权威。他用年轻时的一段往事说明：有人告诉他，他内心的冲动可能来自下界而非上天，他回答说，若真如此，那他就依魔鬼而活。这是有意的挑衅，这段话常被视为他主张内在信念高于传统的最极端表述。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Do your work, and you shall reinforce yourself.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: From Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance", on how conformity hides who a person is.

interpretation.en: Emerson is objecting to conforming to customs that have gone dead for a person, such as supporting a church or party out of habit. He argues that such conformity scatters a person's energy and hides who they are behind screens. Doing one's own work is the opposite: it makes the person known to others and strengthens them. He then gives the example of a preacher whose argument can be predicted from his church, since he speaks as a retained advocate rather than as a man.
interpretation.zh: 爱默生在反对遵从那些对自己已经失去生命的习俗，比如出于习惯支持某个教会或政党。他认为这种从众会分散人的精力，把人的真面目藏在屏风之后。做自己的工作则相反：它让别人认识这个人，也使他更有力量。他随后举了一位传教士为例，说从他的教会就能预知他的论点，因为他是以受雇辩护者的身份而非以一个人的身份说话。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: The closing line of Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance", warning against trusting good luck for peace of mind.

interpretation.en: These are the final words of Self-Reliance. Emerson has just warned against trusting fortune, listing good news such as a political win or a friend's recovery that make people think good days are coming, and tells the reader not to believe it. Against chance he sets cause and effect and the will. The closing line locates lasting peace in living by principles, which, unlike luck, do not turn with the wheel of fortune. It pairs with the sentence just before, which places peace in the self.
interpretation.zh: 这是《自立》的最后一句。爱默生刚刚告诫不要依赖运气，列举了政治胜利、朋友康复之类让人以为好日子将至的好消息，并说不要相信。他用因果与意志来对抗机运。结尾这句把持久的平静放在依原则而活上，原则不像运气那样随命运之轮转动。它与前一句相呼应，前一句把平静归于自身。

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Love, and you shall be loved.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: From Emerson's essay "Compensation", on the law that every act returns to the person who does it.

interpretation.en: In Compensation, Emerson argues that every action returns to the one who does it, by a law as exact as an equation. After describing how wrongdoing punishes itself, he turns to right action and states that love is repaid by love. He goes further, claiming that a good person cannot really be harmed, since even sickness, poverty and offence turn into benefits. The claim is meant as a moral law, not a promise about how particular people will behave.
interpretation.zh: 在《补偿》中，爱默生主张，每一个行为都会回到行为者身上，其法则像方程一样精确。在描述了恶行如何自我惩罚之后，他转向正当的行为，说爱必得爱的回报。他更进一步，认为好人实际上无法受到伤害，因为连疾病、贫穷与冒犯都会转化为益处。这一主张是作为道德法则提出的，而不是对具体某个人会如何回应的保证。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Do not admire your clothes, and then you will not be angry with the thief.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Discourses of Epictetus, as recorded by his student Arrian, on how anger at a thief begins with how much we value our things.

interpretation.en: Epictetus, as recorded by his student Arrian, is arguing against anger at wrongdoers. He says a thief is mistaken about what is truly good, thinking it lies in fine clothes, and that the angry owner shares exactly the same mistake. If the clothes were not prized so highly, their loss would not provoke rage. He goes on to a personal story about an iron lamp stolen from beside his household gods, which he uses to show that his loss was trivial compared with what the thief became.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德（由其学生阿里安记录）在反对对作恶者发怒。他说，小偷误解了什么是真正的善，以为善在于华美的衣服，而愤怒的失主恰恰犯了同样的错误。如果不那么看重衣服，失去它就不会引发怒火。他接着讲了自己的一段经历：放在家神旁边的一盏铁灯被偷了，他借此说明，自己的损失与小偷因此变成的样子相比，微不足道。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Never then look for the matter itself in one place, and progress towards it in another.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Discourses, on progress: it lies in your own will, not in reading philosophy books.

interpretation.en: Epictetus is rebuking students who think progress means having studied philosophical treatises. He compares them to an athlete who shows his weights instead of his shoulders: what counts is the result in how one desires, avoids and chooses. The line says not to look for the goal in one place and the progress toward it in another, meaning that if the goal is a well-ordered will, progress must be measured there and not in books. He then describes real progress as turning from externals to train one's own will.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德在斥责那些以为进步就是读过哲学论著的学生。他把他们比作一个只展示哑铃而不展示肩膀的运动员：重要的是在欲求、回避与选择上的成效。这句话说，不要在一处寻找目标，却在另一处寻找通往它的进步；意思是，如果目标是有序的意志，那么进步就必须在意志上衡量，而不是在书本上。他随后把真正的进步描述为从外物转向，锻炼自己的意志。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Know you not how small a part you are compared with the whole.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Discourses, on contentment with one's place in the order of things.

interpretation.en: Epictetus is addressing an imagined complainer, here someone upset about a lame leg, who blames the world for his lot. He argues that refusing what the gods and the Fates have ordered is itself a prison, and that one leg is a trivial thing to set against the whole. The line reminds the complainer how small a part of the universe he is. Epictetus immediately limits this to the body: in intelligence, he says, a human is not inferior to the gods, since mind is measured by thoughts and not size.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德在对一位想象中的抱怨者说话，此人因一条腿瘸了而怨天尤人。他认为，拒绝接受众神与命运女神所安排的事，本身就是一座监狱；一条腿与整体相比微不足道。这句话提醒抱怨者，他在宇宙中只是多么小的一部分。爱比克泰德随即把这一点限定于身体：他说就理智而言，人并不逊于众神，因为心智的大小以思想衡量，而非以尺寸衡量。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Make no tragedy show of the thing, but speak of it as it is.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Discourses, on speaking plainly about death as the body returning to its elements.

interpretation.en: Epictetus is describing how a person who has grasped what is truly his own can face poverty, power, exile and death with ease, since only his opinions belong to him and these cannot be taken. When the moment to die comes, the line tells him not to dramatise it but to describe it accurately. He then gives the plain description: the body's matter returning to the elements it came from, with nothing in the universe actually perishing. The point is that the terror lies in the theatrical framing, not in the event.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德在描述，一个明白什么才真正属于自己的人，如何能从容面对贫穷、权力、放逐与死亡，因为只有他的见解属于他，而这些无法被夺走。当死亡来临时，这句话要他不要把它渲染成悲剧，而要如实地描述它。他随后给出朴素的描述：身体的物质回归它所由构成的元素，宇宙中并没有什么真正消亡。要点在于，恐惧来自戏剧化的表述，而不是事件本身。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Make trial of your power, and you will know how far it reaches.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Discourses, the closing words of a passage on a tyrant's threats, which reach only the body and possessions.

interpretation.en: These words are addressed to an imagined tyrant. Epictetus grants that the tyrant controls his body, property, exile and chains, and says he will give all of these up whenever ordered. The closing challenge invites the tyrant to test his power and discover its limit: it reaches the body and possessions but not the person's judgments, which are the only things that are truly his. It is a dare spoken from the position of someone who has already let go of everything the tyrant can touch.
interpretation.zh: 这些话是对一位想象中的暴君说的。爱比克泰德承认暴君能掌控他的身体、财产、放逐与锁链，并说只要被命令，他随时可以放弃这一切。结尾的挑战邀请暴君试一试自己的权力，看看它到底能伸多远：它能触及身体和财物，却触及不到人的判断，而只有判断才真正属于这个人。这是一个已经放下暴君所能触及的一切的人所发出的挑战。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Let not your laughter be much, nor on many occasions, nor excessive.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Enchiridion, or Handbook, of Epictetus: short rules for everyday conduct.

interpretation.en: This is one of a run of brief rules in the Enchiridion on everyday behaviour, alongside avoiding oaths and being careful at banquets with uninstructed people. The rule does not forbid laughter but limits how often and how much. Around it, the concern is self-command in company and not slipping into the habits of those who have not studied philosophy. Like much of the Enchiridion, it reads as practical advice for students in training rather than a full argument.
interpretation.zh: 这是《手册》中一连串关于日常行为的简短规则之一，同列的还有尽量不发誓、在与未受教化者的宴席上保持警觉。这条规则并不禁止笑，而是限制笑的频率和程度。上下文关心的是在人群中的自制，以及不沾染未学哲学之人的习气。和《手册》的许多内容一样，它更像是给修习中学生的实用建议，而非完整的论证。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Practise sometimes a way of living like a person out of health that you may at some time live like a man in health.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.locator: OF PERSON A SOLITARY MAN IS
entries.context: The Discourses, on training: practise hardship sometimes, in small measure.

interpretation.en: Epictetus warns that any great power is dangerous to beginners, and that one should take on only what one can bear. The line recommends occasionally living as an invalid would, plainly and with restraint, as training so that one can later live soundly. The surrounding text is fragmentary here, with an ellipsis in the source, so the exact link to what comes before is unclear. The general sense fits his frequent advice to practise small hardships deliberately.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德告诫说，任何强大的能力对初学者都是危险的，人只应承担力所能及的事。这句话建议偶尔像病人那样生活，简朴而有节制，作为训练，以便日后能健全地生活。这里的上下文残缺，原文有省略号，因此与前文的确切联系并不清楚。总体意思与他经常给出的建议相合：有意地练习小小的艰苦。

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: Pain does not abide continuously in the flesh, but in its extremity it is present only a very short time.
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: One of Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, on why severe pain does not last.

interpretation.en: Right after defining the greatest pleasure as the removal of all pain, Epicurus turns to the fear of pain itself. He sorts pain by intensity and duration: the sharpest pain is brief, pain that barely outweighs pleasure lasts only days, and long illnesses, he claims, still hold more pleasure than pain. The point is to show that pain is not the unbounded threat it seems, so it need not dominate a life. Critics ancient and modern have found the claim about chronic illness too hopeful, and it is best read as a therapeutic argument rather than a medical observation.
interpretation.zh: 伊壁鸠鲁刚把最大的快乐界定为消除一切痛苦，随即转向对痛苦本身的恐惧。他按强度和持续时间区分痛苦：最剧烈的痛苦为时短暂，只略胜于快乐的痛苦不过持续数日，而长期的疾病据他说仍是快乐多于痛苦。其用意在于说明痛苦并非看上去那样无边无际的威胁，因而不必主宰人的一生。古今批评者都认为他对慢性病的说法过于乐观，这段话更宜读作一种疗愈性的论证，而不是医学观察。

entries.name: Sigmund Freud
entries.en: Love of comfort is really not compatible with consideration for others.
entries.work: The Interpretation of Dreams
entries.context: The Interpretation of Dreams: Freud's analysis of one of his own dreams, in which a wish to stay asleep wins out over a duty.

interpretation.en: Freud is analysing one of his own dreams: thirsty in the night, he dreams his wife gives him water rather than getting up to fetch it himself. He uses the dream to support his central claim that a dream exists to fulfil a wish, and that such wishes can be frankly selfish because the dream answers to no one. The line about comfort and consideration is a wry aside on his own behaviour in the dream, not a general moral doctrine. It shows the method of the book, in which Freud offers his own private material as evidence.
interpretation.zh: 弗洛伊德在分析自己的一个梦：夜里口渴，他梦见妻子给他递水，而不是自己起身去取。他借这个梦支持全书的核心论点：梦的存在是为了满足愿望，而且这种愿望可以毫不掩饰地自私，因为梦无须对任何人负责。关于贪图舒适与体谅他人的这句话，是他对自己在梦中行为的一句自嘲式旁白，并不是一条普遍的道德主张。它也体现了这本书的方法：弗洛伊德把自己的私人材料拿来当作证据。

entries.name: Sigmund Freud
entries.en: It is in the nature of every censorship that it permits the telling of untruth about forbidden things rather than truth.
entries.work: The Interpretation of Dreams
entries.context: The Interpretation of Dreams, on how a dream disguises what the dreamer will not openly think.

interpretation.en: Freud is working through an absurd dream about his father, and explains why the dream is allowed to mock him: in the underlying thoughts the father stands in for someone else, here the neurologist Meynert, whom Freud cannot openly criticise. The remark about censorship states his general theory of dream distortion: the mind's censor lets a forbidden thought through only in a false or displaced form, so the dream says untrue things about the father instead of true things about the real target. The wording comes from Brill's early translation, and the passage sits in Freud's discussion of absurd dreams rather than in the chapter the locator gives.
interpretation.zh: 弗洛伊德在剖析一个关于他父亲的荒谬之梦，并解释这个梦为何可以嘲弄父亲：在潜藏的梦念中，父亲是另一个人的替身，这里指神经学家迈内特，弗洛伊德无法公开批评他。关于审查的这句话陈述了他关于梦的变形的一般理论：心灵的审查者只允许被禁止的念头以虚假或移置的形式通过，于是梦对父亲说了不实之词，而不是对真正的对象说出实情。这段措辞出自布里尔的早期英译本，而且这段话位于弗洛伊德讨论荒谬之梦的部分，并不在所标注的章节中。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: To work is not only a right, it is a duty.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, Gilman's critique of the household, arguing that every adult should do productive work.

interpretation.en: Gilman is attacking the ideal of the protected, idle wife, kept at home as a sign of a husband's success. She argues that work is a condition of human development, like exercise for the body, so sparing someone from it is an injury rather than a kindness. Her image of a man putting his wife and daughters to bed like infants makes the point that comfort without activity weakens a person. The argument underpins her larger case that women should do skilled work outside the household.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼在抨击一种理想：受庇护、无所事事的妻子被留在家中，作为丈夫成功的标志。她认为工作是人得以发展的条件，就像锻炼之于身体，因此让人免于工作不是善意，而是伤害。她设想一个男人把妻女像婴儿一样安置在床上喂养，以此说明缺乏活动的舒适只会使人衰弱。这一论点支撑着她更大的主张：女性应当在家庭之外从事专业劳动。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: It is not enough to receive a new truth, you must discharge the old lie, if your mind is to work straight.
entries.work: Human Work
entries.context: Human Work, on how old beliefs about labour persist after new ideas arrive.

interpretation.en: The error Gilman has in mind is the religious teaching that labour is a curse laid on humanity, which she says has shaped attitudes toward work for centuries. Later religious writers tried to soften it by calling labour a form of prayer, but she argues that adding a kinder idea does not cancel the old one. The claim is about how beliefs change: a mind that accepts a new view while still holding the old assumption underneath will keep reasoning from the old one. She wants the idea of work as punishment rejected outright, not decorated.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼所指的错误，是认为劳动是加在人类身上的诅咒的宗教教义，她说这种观念塑造了几个世纪以来人们对工作的态度。后来的宗教作者试图把劳动说成一种祈祷来加以缓和，但她认为添上一个更温和的观念并不能抵消旧观念。这个主张关乎信念如何改变：一个人接受了新观点，底下却仍保留旧的假设，就会继续从旧假设出发进行推理。她要的是彻底抛弃劳动即惩罚的观念，而不是给它加以修饰。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: Let no one tremble in fear of losing precious things.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, reassuring readers that reforming the home will not destroy what is precious in it.

interpretation.en: Early in the book Gilman proposes that much of the strain in modern character and social life comes from outdated customs of home life. Anticipating that readers will hear this as an attack on the home itself, she separates its lasting essentials from habits that should have been outgrown. Her reassurance has a sharp edge: she suggests it is a poor view of nature's laws to think they depend on one local custom. The line is a rhetorical move to lower readers' defences before the criticism that follows.
interpretation.zh: 在书的开头，吉尔曼提出，现代人性格与社会生活中的许多紧张，源于家庭生活中过时的习俗。她预料读者会把这当作对家庭本身的攻击，于是把家庭中持久不变的本质与早该淘汰的习惯区分开来。她的安抚带着锋芒：她暗示，以为自然法则的实现要靠某一种地方习俗，其实是看低了这些法则。这句话是一种修辞手法，意在后面的批评展开之前先放下读者的戒备。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: Learn what we may of art and science, the art of living, the science of living is not yet known to us.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, on how little we know about living well, even with modern science.
