interpretation.en: Gilman asks readers to set aside the sentimental picture of home and look at it the way a health inspector or sanitary engineer would. Her claim is that despite advances in art and science, the practical knowledge of how to live well has not been worked out, and houses are built by tradition rather than by attention to what living bodies need. She treats domestic life as something that could be studied and improved like any other field. The passage reflects her wider belief that household arrangements should answer to evidence rather than custom.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼请读者放下对家的温情想象，像卫生检查员或卫生工程师那样去审视它。她的主张是：尽管艺术和科学都在进步，如何过好生活的实际知识却尚未建立起来，人们建房子依循的是传统，而不是生命体的实际需要。她把家庭生活看作可以像其他领域一样加以研究和改进的对象。这段话反映了她更广泛的信念：家务安排应当服从证据，而不是习俗。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: Love has to pass muster in results, as well as intentions.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, arguing that a mother's love should be judged by how well her children actually fare, not by her intentions alone.

interpretation.en: Gilman is arguing that the mother who does all the housework by old methods should stop and let skilled workers do it, and she answers the fear that the family will be loved less. Her reply is that love is measured by how well children actually fare, not by the feeling or effort behind it. She goes on to compare equally loving mothers from different cultures whose children fare very differently, using ethnic labels typical of her time. The passage shows her habit of judging domestic ideals by their results.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼主张，用旧方法包揽全部家务的母亲应当停下来，交给专业人员去做，并回应家人会因此少得到爱的担忧。她的回答是：爱要看孩子实际过得如何来衡量，而不是看背后的感情或辛劳。接着她比较了来自不同文化、同样慈爱的几位母亲，她们的孩子境况却大不相同，其中用了她那个时代常见的族群称呼。这段话体现了她以结果来评判家庭理想的一贯做法。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: Love never yet went with self-interest.
entries.work: Women and Economics
entries.context: Women and Economics, Gilman's argument that economic dependence corrupts marriage, on love and self-interest as opposed forces.

interpretation.en: In Women and Economics Gilman argues that because wives depend on husbands for their living, marriage forces love and economic gain together. Drawing on evolutionary language, she treats self-preservation and the self-sacrificing instincts of reproduction as opposed forces in nature. Her charge is that society has made women gain their livelihood through love, which she calls a contradiction that corrupts both. The claim is polemical and rests on the evolutionary theory of her day, but its target is the economic structure of marriage, not love itself.
interpretation.zh: 在《妇女与经济》中，吉尔曼认为，由于妻子靠丈夫维生，婚姻把爱与经济利益强行捆在一起。她借用进化论的语言，把自我保存与繁衍中自我牺牲的本能看作自然界中相互对立的力量。她的指控是：社会让女性通过爱来获得生计，她称之为一种同时败坏两者的矛盾。这个论断带有论战色彩，依据的是她那个时代的进化理论，但其矛头指向的是婚姻的经济结构，而不是爱本身。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: There is wisdom in youth, and power, if we would but let it grow.
entries.work: Concerning Children
entries.context: Concerning Children, Gilman's book on child-rearing, arguing that children should be left room to grow by their own reasoning.

interpretation.en: Gilman pictures a childhood allowed to develop steadily along reasonable lines, without needless pressure or interference. Such children, she argues, would reach adolescence with a base of real accomplishment and would turn their energy toward improving themselves and the world. She treats the years of youth as a short and decisive window for that growth. Her argument is tied to a hope, common in her time and now seen as troubling in parts, that better upbringing would improve the human race over a few generations.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼设想一种童年：沿着合理的方向稳步成长，没有不必要的压力或干涉。她认为，这样的孩子进入青春期时会拥有切实的成就作为基础，并会把精力投向改善自己和世界。她把青年时期看作这种成长短暂而关键的窗口。她的论证与当时常见的一种期望相连，即更好的养育能在几代之内改良人类，这种期望的部分内容如今被视为有问题。

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: It is not enough to keep one's self alive, it is not enough to keep one's kind alive, we must improve.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, on progress as life's third law, after self-preservation and reproduction.

interpretation.en: Gilman contrasts bees and ants, which she sees as endlessly multiplying without improving, with a third law of life she calls progress. Beyond staying alive and reproducing, a species must get better, and she presents this as the deepest law of nature. In the surrounding text she claims that this drive to vary acts mainly through males while females conserve the type, a view drawn from the biology of her time. The passage is part of her argument that a home organised only around motherhood cannot be the whole of human life.
interpretation.zh: 吉尔曼拿蜜蜂和蚂蚁作对比，认为它们只是无休止地繁衍而没有改进，并由此提出生命的第三条法则，她称之为进步。物种除了活下去和繁衍，还必须变得更好，她把这说成自然最深层的法则。在上下文中，她声称这种变异的动力主要通过雄性起作用，而雌性保存物种的原型，这一观点来自她那个时代的生物学。这段话是她论证的一部分：只围绕母职组织起来的家庭，不能构成人类生活的全部。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: He that is habitually goaded by the incentives of vice will not fail to be vicious.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, arguing that people are largely shaped by the circumstances they live in.

interpretation.en: Godwin is arguing that law as an institution is harmful, and he extends the point to those who practise it. His claim is that people are formed largely by their circumstances, so someone constantly exposed to temptations and to trickery in argument will be shaped by them. He presents the dishonesty of lawyers as a matter for regret rather than blame, since the profession, not the person, does the damage. This environmental view of character runs through the whole book and supports his hope that changed institutions would produce better people.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文在论证法律作为一种制度是有害的，并把这一点推及执业者。他的主张是：人在很大程度上由所处环境塑造，一个人如果长期面对诱惑和诡辩，就会被它们改变。他把律师的不诚实说成值得惋惜而非应受谴责的事，因为造成损害的是这个行业，而不是个人。这种环境决定品格的观点贯穿全书，也支撑着他的希望：制度改变了，人也会变得更好。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: No man can be eminently virtuous, who is not accustomed to an extensive range of reflection.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.locator: OF THE ISFLVEKCE OF CLIMATE, Book IV
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice: innocence is not virtue, since virtue takes thought and effort for the general good.

interpretation.en: Godwin is answering an objection that nations, like people, grow old and corrupt through luxury and cannot be restored to innocence. He rejects the premise that simple rustic life was ever virtuous: innocence only means doing no harm, while virtue requires actively working for the general good. That in turn requires wide reflection, since a person must understand what benefits an action will produce and how to bring them about. The passage turns against the romantic idealisation of pastoral life and places virtue in understanding rather than simplicity.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文在回应一种反对意见：国家和个人一样，会因奢侈而衰老腐化，无法恢复纯真。他否认质朴的乡野生活曾经是有德的这一前提：纯真只意味着不作恶，而德性要求积极为公共利益而努力。这又需要广泛的思考，因为人必须明白一个行动会带来什么益处，以及如何实现它们。这段话反对对田园生活的浪漫理想化，把德性置于理解而非简朴之中。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Whoever frequents the habitations of the luxurious, will speedily be infected with the vices of luxury.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on how courts and luxury corrupt those who live around them.

interpretation.en: In his chapters on monarchy, Godwin questions whether it can be right for many to labour hard so that one person may live in idleness. He then argues that the luxury of a court corrupts everyone around it: ministers and servants learn to look down on poverty and to overlook merit that comes without wealth. The claim applies his general view that character is shaped by surroundings. It forms part of his case that monarchy damages not only the ruler but the moral judgment of a whole society.
interpretation.zh: 在讨论君主制的章节中，葛德文质疑让众人辛苦劳作以供一人闲逸是否正当。接着他论证，宫廷的奢华会腐蚀周围的每一个人：大臣和仆从学会轻视贫穷，忽视没有财富相伴的才德。这一论断运用了他关于品格由环境塑造的总体观点。它是他论证的一部分：君主制损害的不只是统治者本人，还有整个社会的道德判断。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Let truth be incessantly studied, illustrated and propagated, and the effect is inevitable.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on spreading knowledge, not passing laws, as the way to reform a society.

interpretation.en: Godwin has just argued that laws and regulations cannot by themselves change how people think. Here he names the alternative: reform comes through knowledge, and if truth is studied, explained and spread, change will follow. He counsels patience, saying no new political practice should be introduced until public opinion calls for it. The confidence that truth spread freely will prevail is one of the book's defining features and one of the most debated, since critics have doubted that argument alone moves societies.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文刚刚论证，法律和规章本身无法改变人们的思想。在这里他提出了替代办法：改革要靠知识，只要真理得到研究、阐明和传播，变化就必然随之而来。他主张耐心，认为在公众舆论提出要求之前，不应推行任何新的政治做法。相信自由传播的真理终将胜出，是这本书最鲜明的特点之一，也是最受争议的一点，因为批评者怀疑仅凭论证能否推动社会。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Nothing can be more unworthy, than a propensity to take refuge in indolence and neutrality, simply because we have not the courage to encounter the consequences of ingenuousness and sincerity.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.locator: OF THE MODES OF DECIDING A QUESTION ON THE, Book VIII
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, against staying neutral out of fear of what honesty will cost.

interpretation.en: Godwin is discussing how people should act once they have formed a view, or know they ought to form one. His point is that holding back from a position one actually holds, and hiding in neutrality to avoid the cost of saying it, is cowardice. This fits his strong commitment to sincerity, which elsewhere in the book leads him to argue that people should always speak the truth as they see it. The surrounding text is brief, so the precise political question he has in view at this point is not clear from it.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文在讨论人在已经形成看法、或知道自己应当形成看法之后该如何行事。他的观点是：对自己实际持有的立场有所保留，躲进中立以逃避说出来的代价，就是怯懦。这与他对真诚的坚定主张相一致，他在书中别处据此主张人应始终说出自己所见的真相。所给的上下文很简短，因此从中看不清他此处针对的是哪个具体的政治问题。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Nothing perhaps can put a stop to the advances of mind but oppression.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on thought begetting thought when people are free and at ease.

interpretation.en: Godwin is answering the objection that a society of equality and ease would sink into idleness and ignorance. He replies that civilised people are driven by thought, and thought generates more thought, so only oppression could halt intellectual progress. In the society he imagines, everyone is equal and independent, so that obstacle would be absent. He admits that republics have lost their early enthusiasm, but argues that this is because they left deeper injustice untouched, not because freedom breeds sloth.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文在回应一种反对意见：一个平等安逸的社会会陷入懒惰与无知。他答道，文明人受思想驱动，思想会催生更多思想，因此只有压迫才能阻止心智的进步。在他设想的社会里，人人平等独立，这个障碍也就不复存在。他承认共和国曾失去最初的热情，但认为原因在于它们没有触动更深的不公，而不是自由滋生了懒惰。

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: He who has tasted the pleasures of refinement and knowledge, will not relapse into ignorance.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, arguing that the love of knowledge would outlast the end of great wealth.

interpretation.en: Godwin concedes that inequality may have been needed to start civilisation: the sight of others' wealth pushed people to work, and work produced the leisure that made art and learning possible. But he argues it is not needed to sustain civilisation, comparing it to scaffolding that can be removed once the building stands. The passage answers the worry that equality would return humanity to barbarism, on the grounds that people who have known learning will not give it up. The argument depends on his optimism about human motives, which critics have often found too hopeful.
interpretation.zh: 葛德文承认，不平等或许是开启文明所必需的：看到他人的财富促使人们劳作，劳作又带来了使艺术和学问成为可能的闲暇。但他认为维持文明并不需要不平等，并把它比作建筑落成后便可拆除的脚手架。这段话回应的是平等会让人类退回野蛮的担忧，理由是体验过学问的人不会放弃它。这一论证依赖他对人类动机的乐观看法，批评者常认为这种看法过于理想。

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entries.en: Nature in like manner is not without mind, nor mind without nature.
entries.work: The Logic of Hegel
entries.context: The Logic of Hegel, part of his Encyclopaedia, on opposites that exist only in relation to each other.

interpretation.en: Hegel is discussing opposition, and argues that a true opposite is not just some other thing but the specific other of a thing, as north and south poles or positive and negative charge belong together. Ordinary thinking treats things as separate and indifferent to one another, while philosophy, he says, looks for the necessary relations between them. Nature and mind are offered as one such pair, each defined partly by its relation to the other. The line appears in explanatory remarks attached to the main text in Wallace's translation, and what Hegel means by mind here is much debated.
interpretation.zh: 黑格尔在讨论对立，他认为真正的对立面不只是另一个东西，而是某物特定的他者，就像南北两极或正负电荷彼此相属。日常思维把事物看作各自独立、互不相干，而他认为哲学要寻找事物之间的必然联系。自然与精神被举为这样的一对，各自部分地由与对方的关系来界定。这句话出现在华莱士译本中附于正文的解说部分，至于黑格尔此处所说的精神究竟指什么，争议很大。

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entries.en: True thoughts and scientific insight can only be won by the labour of the notion.
entries.work: The Phenomenology of Mind
entries.context: The Preface to the Phenomenology of Mind, against relying on flashes of feeling instead of the slow work of thinking.

interpretation.en: In the Preface to the Phenomenology, Hegel mocks two shortcuts to philosophy: reading reviews and prefaces instead of the works, and relying on inspired flashes of insight into the infinite. Neither, he argues, reaches real understanding. Knowledge that holds for everyone has to be worked out through concepts, step by step. Baillie translates Hegel's word Begriff as notion; most recent translators render it as concept, which makes the sense plainer.
interpretation.zh: 在《精神现象学》序言中，黑格尔嘲讽了两条通往哲学的捷径：只读书评和序言而不读原著，以及依赖对无限者的灵感闪现。他认为两者都达不到真正的理解。对所有人都成立的知识，必须通过概念一步步推演出来。贝利把黑格尔的Begriff一词译作notion，近来的译者多译作concept，即概念，意思更为明白。

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Time, and industry, produce every day new knowledge.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 03 (of 11)
entries.context: Leviathan, answering those who think a lasting political order is impossible because none has yet been built.

interpretation.en: In Leviathan Hobbes answers people who say there can be no rational grounds for absolute sovereignty, since no commonwealth has ever recognised them. He compares this to people who have never seen a well-built house denying that one can be built. Knowledge grows over time through effort, he argues, and just as builders learned the principles of their craft long after people began to build, the principles of a lasting state may be discovered long after the first imperfect ones. The passage expresses his confidence that political order can be put on a scientific footing.
interpretation.zh: 在《利维坦》中，霍布斯回应那些人的说法：绝对主权不可能有理性依据，因为从来没有哪个国家承认过这些依据。他把这比作从未见过坚固房屋的人便否认房屋能够建得坚固。他认为知识随时间和努力而增长，正如人们开始建房很久以后才掌握建筑原理，持久国家的原理也可能在最初那些不完善的国家出现很久之后才被发现。这段话表达了他的信心：政治秩序可以建立在科学的基础上。

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Courage may be virtue, when the daring is extreme, if the cause be good, and extreme fear no vice when the danger is extreme.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 04 (of 11)
entries.context: Hobbes rejecting Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: courage can be a virtue even at its extreme, if the cause is good.

interpretation.en: Hobbes is rejecting the doctrine, which he attributes to Aristotle, that virtue lies in a middle point between two extremes. His examples are meant to show that what makes something a virtue is its reason or cause, not its quantity: extreme daring can be courage in a good cause, and great fear is not a vice when the danger is great. He dismisses Aristotle's view as the common opinion of unstudied people. In the following lines he gives his own account, that virtue consists in being sociable with those who will be sociable.
interpretation.zh: 霍布斯在反驳一种他归于亚里士多德的学说，即德性在于两个极端之间的中道。他举的例子意在说明，使某种品质成为德性的是它的理由或原因，而不是它的量：在正当的事业中，极度的勇敢可以是勇气；危险极大时，极度的恐惧也不是恶。他把亚里士多德的看法斥为未经研究的普通人的成见。在接下来的几行里，他给出了自己的说法：德性在于与愿意合群的人合群相处。

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Nature dictates the seeking after peace.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 02 (of 11)
entries.context: From Hobbes's list of the laws of nature, which begins with the duty to seek peace.

interpretation.en: This line is a heading from the summary at the start of the first chapter of Hobbes's Latin treatise on the citizen, in its English version, which traces how people without a common power fall into a state of war. Having argued that everyone has a right to everything and that this right only produces war, which threatens everyone's survival, Hobbes concludes that nature itself directs people to seek peace. The detailed list of the laws of nature follows in the next chapter. The step matters because it grounds the duty to seek peace in self-preservation rather than in any natural goodwill.
interpretation.zh: 这句话是霍布斯《论公民》英译本第一章开头提要中的一条标题，该章追溯了没有共同权力的人如何陷入战争状态。霍布斯先论证人人对一切都有权利，而这种权利只会导致危及每个人生存的战争，然后得出结论：自然本身指引人们寻求和平。各条自然法的详细列举在下一章才展开。这一步的重要之处在于，它把寻求和平的义务建立在自我保存之上，而不是建立在任何天然的善意之上。

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: There is nothing in learning more difficult than to determine the signification of words.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 04 (of 11)
entries.context: From Hobbes's dispute with Bishop Bramhall, on the difficulty of fixing what words mean.

interpretation.en: In his reply to Bishop Bramhall, Hobbes defends his definition of the word holy, which he had grounded in how Scripture uses it. The general remark about how hard it is to fix the meaning of words is partly sincere, since Hobbes consistently held that confused definitions cause most errors in learning. But it is also sarcastic: he uses it to excuse Bramhall's mistake before showing that the bishop's own view contradicts itself. The passage reflects both his theory of language and his combative style in these disputes.
interpretation.zh: 霍布斯在答复布拉姆霍尔主教时，为自己对神圣一词的定义辩护，他的依据是《圣经》中的用法。关于确定词义之难的这句概括，部分是真心话，因为霍布斯一贯认为，定义混乱是学问中大多数错误的根源。但它也带着讥讽：他用这句话为主教的错误开脱，随后便指出主教自己的观点自相矛盾。这段话既反映了他的语言理论，也反映了他在这些论战中好斗的文风。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Pain and pleasure, grief and joy, passions and sensations succeed each other, and never all exist at the same time.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, Hume's argument that no single feeling stays with us constantly enough to be the self.

interpretation.en: Hume is responding to philosophers who claim we are constantly and intimately aware of a simple, unchanging self. He argues that every genuine idea must come from some impression, and an idea of an unchanging self would need an impression that stays the same throughout life. No such impression exists, since feelings and sensations keep replacing one another. So he concludes we have no idea of a self in the sense those philosophers mean, which leads to his account of the mind as a bundle of perceptions. Hume later admitted in an appendix that he was dissatisfied with parts of this account.
interpretation.zh: 休谟在回应一些哲学家，他们声称我们始终亲切地意识到一个单纯、不变的自我。他论证说，每个真实的观念都必须来自某个印象，而一个不变自我的观念就需要一个终生保持不变的印象。这样的印象并不存在，因为感受和感觉不断相互更替。所以他断定，我们并没有那些哲学家所说的自我观念，并由此提出心灵是一束知觉的说法。休谟后来在附录中承认，他对这一说法的某些部分并不满意。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: No man is absolutely indifferent to the happiness and misery of others.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, on sympathy as a basic and universal principle.

interpretation.en: In a footnote, Hume declines to explain why humans have fellow-feeling at all. Every science has to stop at some general principles, he says, and the fact that others' happiness pleases us and their misery pains us is one of them, something anyone can observe in himself. The point is aimed at theories that try to reduce all benevolence to disguised self-interest. Hume does not claim that sympathy is strong, only that it is never wholly absent, and that is enough for his account of morals.
interpretation.zh: 休谟在一个脚注中拒绝解释人为什么会有同情心。他说，每门科学都必须止步于某些一般原理，而他人的幸福使我们愉快、他人的痛苦使我们难受，就是这样一条原理，任何人都能在自己身上观察到。这一点针对的是那些试图把一切仁爱归结为变相自利的理论。休谟并不声称同情很强烈，只是说它从不完全缺席，而这对他的道德理论来说已经足够。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Every pleasure languishes when enjoyed a-part from company, and every pain becomes more cruel and intolerable.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.locator: OF THE LATTER A SEPARATE UNEASINESS
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on how much our feelings depend on the company of others.

interpretation.en: Hume is building his case that sympathy, the passing of feelings from one person to another, runs through nearly all human passions. He points to the general desire for company among animals and especially humans, and claims that complete solitude may be the worst punishment there is. Pleasures fade and pains sharpen without others to share them, and even pride, ambition or revenge would lose their force without reference to other people's thoughts. The passage illustrates how social Hume takes human nature to be, against views that start from isolated self-interested individuals.
interpretation.zh: 休谟在论证同情，即情感在人与人之间的传递，几乎贯穿人类所有的激情。他指出动物尤其是人类普遍渴望陪伴，并认为彻底的孤独也许是最重的惩罚。没有他人分享，快乐会消退，痛苦会加剧；甚至骄傲、野心或复仇，若完全不涉及他人的想法，也会失去力量。这段话说明休谟把人性看得多么社会化，与那些从孤立的自利个体出发的观点相对立。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Courage and ambition, when not regulated by benevolence, are fit only to make a tyrant and public robber.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.locator: OF OUR OWN HAPPINESS, AND GIVES US PLEASURE
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on benevolence as the virtue that steers all the others.

interpretation.en: Hume is explaining why qualities like generosity, compassion and fidelity are counted as virtues. His answer is that tender, benevolent feelings point a person's other abilities in a direction useful to society. Courage, ambition, judgment and skill are neutral in themselves and can serve good or harm depending on what guides them. Without benevolence, he argues, such strengths simply make a person more dangerous. This fits his broader view that virtues are qualities useful or agreeable to people.
interpretation.zh: 休谟在解释为什么慷慨、同情、忠诚这类品质被视为美德。他的回答是：温和仁爱的情感会把一个人的其他能力引向有益于社会的方向。勇气、野心、判断力和才干本身是中性的，取决于受什么引导，可以造福也可以为害。他认为若没有仁爱，这些长处只会让人更加危险。这与他更广泛的观点相符：美德就是对人有用或令人愉快的品质。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing is more dangerous to reason than the flights of the imagination, and nothing has been the occasion of more mistakes among philosophers.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, near the end of Book I, on imagination as the source of philosophers' errors.

interpretation.en: In the conclusion to Book I, Hume faces a dilemma his own philosophy has created: much of what we believe, including the link between cause and effect, rests on the imagination. If we accept every suggestion of the imagination we fall into contradiction and absurdity, yet rejecting it altogether would undermine reason itself. This sentence states the first horn, that fanciful leaps of imagination have misled philosophers more than anything else. It belongs to a famously troubled passage in which Hume does not fully resolve the dilemma.
interpretation.zh: 在第一卷的结论中，休谟面对一个由他自己的哲学造成的两难：我们相信的许多东西，包括因果之间的联系，都建立在想象之上。如果接受想象的每一个提示，我们就会陷入矛盾和荒谬；可若完全拒斥想象，又会动摇理性本身。这句话陈述的是两难的第一面：想象的奇思飞跃比任何东西都更多地误导了哲学家。这段话属于一个出了名充满困惑的段落，休谟在其中并未完全解决这一两难。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing causes any sentiment to have a greater influence upon us than custom, or turns our imagination more strongly to any object.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on how long habit makes a government seem legitimate.

interpretation.en: Hume is asking what gives a government its authority, and his first answer is long possession. He observes that almost every dynasty or state began in usurpation or rebellion, and that time alone makes its rule seem rightful. Custom, he argues, has unmatched power to direct feeling: people's general sense that obedience is owed attaches to whoever they have long obeyed. The point is deliberately unsentimental, treating legitimacy as largely a product of habit rather than original consent or divine right.
interpretation.zh: 休谟在探讨是什么赋予政府权威，他的第一个回答是长期占有。他指出，几乎每个王朝或国家都始于篡夺或叛乱，只有时间使其统治显得正当。他认为习惯具有无可比拟的力量来引导情感：人们普遍觉得应当服从，这种感觉会附着在他们长期服从的人身上。这一观点刻意不带温情，把合法性主要看作习惯的产物，而不是源于最初的同意或君权神授。

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing is pure and entirely of a piece.
entries.work: The Natural History of Religion
entries.context: The Natural History of Religion, near its close: good and ill are mixed in every human condition.

interpretation.en: Near the end of The Natural History of Religion, Hume steps back to a general observation: good and ill, wisdom and folly, virtue and vice are always mixed together. Every advantage brings a matching disadvantage, and he doubts anyone can even imagine a wholly desirable situation. He recalls Homer's image of Jupiter's two jars, from which life's portions are drawn mixed. The text goes on to say that the finer a good is, the sharper the evil tied to it, so the observation is meant as a general law of human life rather than a passing complaint.
interpretation.zh: 在《宗教的自然史》接近结尾处，休谟退一步提出一个普遍的观察：善与恶、智慧与愚蠢、美德与恶行总是混杂在一起。每一种好处都伴随着相应的坏处，他甚至怀疑人能否设想出一种完全令人满意的处境。他援引荷马笔下朱庇特两只酒瓮的意象，人生的份额是从中混合取出的。原文接着说，好处越精美，与之相连的坏处就越尖锐，可见这一观察是作为人生的普遍规律提出的，而不是随口的抱怨。

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: Happiness alone is, in the view of reason, far from being the complete good.
entries.work: Critique of Pure Reason (Meiklejohn)
entries.translator: Meiklejohn, J. M. D. (John Miller Dow) (d. 1902)
entries.context: The Critique of Pure Reason, in its discussion of the highest good: happiness counts only when it is joined with deserving it.

interpretation.en: In the part of the Critique on the highest good, Kant argues that reason does not accept happiness on its own as the complete good; it approves of happiness only when it is deserved. But morality alone is not complete either, since someone who has made himself worthy of happiness must be able to hope to receive it. He supports this by imagining an impartial being whose task is to distribute happiness to others. This need to join virtue and happiness becomes his ground for the moral hope in God and a future life.
interpretation.zh: 在《纯粹理性批判》讨论至善的部分，康德认为，理性并不把单纯的幸福当作完整的善；只有当幸福是应得的，理性才认可它。但单有道德也不完整，因为一个使自己配得上幸福的人，必须能够希望得到幸福。他以设想一个负责向他人分配幸福的公正存在者来支持这一点。把德性与幸福结合起来的这一要求，成为他对上帝和来世抱持道德希望的根据。

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: We must be able to will that a maxim of our action should be a universal law.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, stating Kant's test for any moral rule.

interpretation.en: Kant has just worked through examples of duties, such as keeping promises and helping others, and here states the principle behind them: an action is permissible only if one could will its underlying rule to hold for everyone. He then distinguishes two ways of failing the test. Some rules cannot even be thought of as universal without contradiction, which marks strict duties; others can be thought of but not consistently willed, which marks looser duties. Whether this test really yields the results Kant claims has been debated ever since.
interpretation.zh: 康德刚刚分析了几个义务的例子，比如守诺和帮助他人，在这里陈述了它们背后的原则：只有当一个人能够意愿其行动所依据的准则对所有人都成立时，这个行动才是允许的。接着他区分了两种不能通过检验的方式：有些准则一旦设想为普遍法则就自相矛盾，这对应严格的义务；另一些可以设想却无法一贯地意愿，这对应较宽松的义务。这一检验是否真能得出康德所声称的结论，从那时起就一直存在争论。

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: All men attribute to themselves freedom of will.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, in its closing discussion of the limits of practical philosophy.

interpretation.en: In the closing section of the Groundwork, Kant sets out a tension he cannot fully dissolve. Everyone takes themselves to be free, which is why they judge actions as things that ought or ought not to have been done. Yet it is equally necessary to think that everything happens according to the laws of nature. Neither freedom nor natural necessity comes from experience, and Kant's answer is that both can hold from different standpoints, while admitting that how freedom is possible cannot be explained.
interpretation.zh: 在《道德形而上学奠基》的最后一节，康德提出了一个他无法完全化解的张力。每个人都认为自己是自由的，所以才会把行为评判为应当做或不应当做的事。然而同样必要的是，要认为一切都按自然法则发生。自由和自然必然性都不来自经验；康德的回答是，两者可以从不同的立场同时成立，同时他承认，自由如何可能是无法解释的。

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: All ignorance is either ignorance of things or of the limits of knowledge.
entries.work: Critique of Pure Reason (Meiklejohn)
entries.translator: Meiklejohn, J. M. D. (John Miller Dow) (d. 1902)
entries.context: The Critique of Pure Reason, on two kinds of ignorance and why knowing the limits of knowledge matters.

interpretation.en: Kant distinguishes two kinds of ignorance: not knowing particular things, and not knowing where the boundaries of knowledge lie. Ignorance of things calls for further investigation of objects, while ignorance of limits calls for a critical inquiry into what can be known at all. He argues that the claim that some ignorance is unavoidable, and so excuses us from inquiry, cannot be settled by observation; it needs exactly that critical examination. The passage sits in his discussion of sceptical method, where he treats Hume's scepticism as a necessary but incomplete step.
interpretation.zh: 康德区分了两种无知：不了解具体事物，和不了解知识的边界在哪里。对事物的无知要求进一步研究对象，对边界的无知则要求对究竟什么能被认识进行批判性考察。他认为，主张某种无知不可避免、因而可以免于探究，这一点无法靠观察来确定，恰恰需要这种批判性考察。这段话位于他对怀疑论方法的讨论中，在那里他把休谟的怀疑论看作必要却不完整的一步。

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The first line of the first section of Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals.

interpretation.en: Kant opens the Groundwork by claiming that a good will is the only thing good without qualification. Talents of mind, strengths of temperament, and gifts of fortune such as wealth, power and even happiness can all become harmful if the will directing them is bad. The good will, by contrast, is good in itself, not because of what it achieves. This sets up his argument that moral worth lies in acting from duty, and it is the starting point of his break with ethics based on consequences or happiness.
interpretation.zh: 康德在《道德形而上学奠基》开篇提出，善良意志是唯一无条件善的东西。心智的才能、性情的长处，以及财富、权力乃至幸福这类运气的赐予，如果支配它们的意志是坏的，都可能变得有害。相反，善良意志本身就是善的，不是因为它成就了什么。这为他后面的论证奠定了基础：道德价值在于出于义务而行动；这也是他与基于后果或幸福的伦理学决裂的起点。

entries.name: Peter Kropotkin
entries.en: There are not many joys in human life equal to the joy of the sudden birth of a generalization, illuminating the mind after a long period of patient research.
entries.work: Memoirs of a Revolutionist
entries.context: Memoirs of a Revolutionist, Kropotkin recalling the years of his geographical research.

interpretation.en: Kropotkin is recalling his years of scientific work as a geographer. He describes the moment when a long mass of confusing and contradictory facts suddenly falls into a coherent picture, likening it to a mountain range emerging from mist. He stresses that this joy comes only after long and patient research, and that the generalisation must then be tested against many particular facts. The passage presents scientific discovery as a pleasure earned by slow work rather than a sudden gift.
interpretation.zh: 克鲁泡特金在回忆他作为地理学家从事科学研究的岁月。他描述了长期以来混乱矛盾的大量事实突然汇成一幅连贯图景的时刻，把它比作山脉从雾中显现。他强调，这种喜悦只在长期耐心的研究之后才会到来，而且这种概括随后必须用大量具体事实来检验。这段话把科学发现描绘成靠缓慢工作换来的快乐，而不是突如其来的馈赠。

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: No man can be wholly ignorant of what he does when he thinks.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THE BODY, AS MAKES IT BE TAKEN NOTICE OF, CHAPTER IV
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on how the mind cannot help having some notion of its own workings.

interpretation.en: Locke is arguing that in receiving simple ideas the understanding is passive: sense objects force their ideas on the mind whether it wants them or not. This sentence extends the point to the mind itself, saying its own operations also leave at least some dim notion of themselves, which is what Locke elsewhere calls ideas of reflection. He then compares the mind to a mirror that cannot refuse or alter what is placed before it. The claim is that self-awareness of thinking is unavoidable, though Locke allows it may be obscure. The locator given in the input does not look like a heading from this part of the Essay.
interpretation.zh: 洛克在论证，理智在接受简单观念时是被动的：感官对象不论我们愿不愿意，都会把它们的观念强加于心灵。这句话把这一点推广到心灵自身，说心灵自己的活动也至少会留下某种模糊的观念，也就是洛克在别处所说的反省观念。他接着把心灵比作一面镜子，不能拒绝也不能改变摆在面前的影像。其主张是，对自身思维的觉察是无法避免的，不过洛克承认这种觉察可能是模糊的。输入给出的位置标注看起来不像《人类理解论》这一部分的标题。

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that hath names without ideas, wants meaning in his words, and speaks only empty sounds.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THINGS WHICH THEY DO OR CAN BY NO MEANS, BOOK III
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book III, on the abuse of words.

interpretation.en: This sentence opens a summary at the end of the Third Book of the Essay, where Locke lists the faults that follow from mismatches between words and ideas. The first fault is using words with no idea behind them, which leaves only sound. The list continues through lacking words for ideas one has, using words unsteadily, using them against common usage, and holding ideas of things that do not match reality. For Locke a word means something only by standing for an idea in the mind of the speaker, so a name with no idea attached is literally meaningless.
interpretation.zh: 这句话是《人类理解论》第三卷末尾一段总结的开头，洛克在那里列举了词语与观念不相匹配所造成的种种毛病。第一种毛病是使用背后没有观念的词，剩下的只是声音。这份清单接着列出：有观念却没有相应的词、用词不稳定、违背通常用法用词，以及所持有的实体观念与事物的真实存在不符。在洛克看来，一个词只有代表说话者心中的某个观念才有意义，所以没有观念相连的名称在字面上就是无意义的。

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that uses his words loosely and unsteadily will either be not minded or not understood.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THINGS WHICH THEY DO OR CAN BY NO MEANS, BOOK III
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book III, on careless use of words.

interpretation.en: This is the third item in a summary list near the end of the Third Book of the Essay, where Locke catalogues the ways language fails. Here the fault is inconsistency: someone who shifts the sense of words from one use to the next will either be ignored or misunderstood. It belongs to a wider argument in the Third Book that many disputes come from unclear and unstable use of terms rather than from real disagreement about things. Locke treats fixing the meaning of words as a precondition for knowledge, not a matter of style.
interpretation.zh: 这是《人类理解论》第三卷末尾一份总结清单中的第三项，洛克在那里列举了语言出错的各种方式。这里的毛病是前后不一致：一个人如果随用随变地改动词义，别人要么不理会他，要么误解他。这属于第三卷的一个更大论证：许多争论源于用语不清、不稳定，而不是对事物本身真有分歧。洛克把确定词义看作获得知识的前提，而不只是文风问题。

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that knows anything, knows this, in the first place, that he need not seek long for instances of his ignorance.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on how quickly anyone runs into the limits of what they know.

interpretation.en: In the Fourth Book Locke has just argued that human knowledge is narrow, and here he turns to its dark side, ignorance, which he says is far larger. His reason for dwelling on it is practical: recognizing the limits of the understanding can quiet disputes and keep inquiry focused on what is within reach. This sentence makes the point that anyone who knows anything at all quickly meets examples of what they do not know, since even the most ordinary things have aspects no one can see into. He then sets out to list the causes of this ignorance.
interpretation.zh: 在第四卷中，洛克刚刚论证了人类知识的狭窄，这里转向它的阴暗面，即无知，他说无知要大得多。他之所以细谈无知，是出于实际考虑：认清理智的界限，可以平息争论，并使探究集中于力所能及的事物。这句话指出，凡是知道一点东西的人，很快就会碰到自己不知道的例子，因为即便最平常的事物也有无人能看透的方面。随后他着手列举这种无知的原因。

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: The mind thinks in proportion to the matter it gets from experience to think about.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, arguing that thinking grows with experience, as you can see in a child.

interpretation.en: This is a section heading in the Second Book, where Locke argues against innate ideas and in favour of experience as the source of all the materials of thought. His evidence is the growth of a child, whose mind becomes more awake and thinks more as the senses supply it with more ideas, and who learns gradually to tell familiar faces from strangers. The claim is that thinking is not fully formed at birth but expands with what experience provides. It is a core step in the case for which the Essay is best known.
interpretation.zh: 这是第二卷中的一个小节标题，洛克在这里反对天赋观念，主张一切思想材料都来自经验。他的证据是儿童的成长：随着感官提供越来越多的观念，儿童的心灵越来越清醒，思考越来越多，并逐渐学会区分熟悉的人和陌生人。其主张是，思维并非生来完备，而是随着经验所提供的东西而扩展。这是《人类理解论》最为人所知的那个论证中的关键一步。

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Every one admits how praiseworthy it is in a prince to keep faith, and to live with integrity and not with craft.
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF THE ART OF WAR, CHAPTER XVIII
entries.context: The opening of chapter XVIII of The Prince, on whether a ruler should keep his word; the chapter goes on to argue that successful princes often have not.

interpretation.en: This sentence opens the chapter of The Prince that has caused the most offence, as the footnote in this edition notes. Machiavelli grants the conventional view that keeping faith is admirable only to set it against experience: the princes who achieved great things paid little attention to their word and outmanoeuvred those who relied on theirs. He goes on to say that a ruler must know how to fight both by law, as men do, and by force, as beasts do. The opening concession is therefore a setup, not his conclusion, and how far Machiavelli endorses this or is describing politics coldly is long debated.
interpretation.zh: 这句话是《君主论》中最招非议的一章的开头，本版的脚注也指出了这一点。马基雅维利承认守信值得称赞这一通常看法，只是为了把它与经验对照：成就大事的君主很少看重信义，并以权谋胜过了那些依赖信义的人。他接着说，君主必须懂得两种斗争方式：像人一样依靠法律，像野兽一样依靠武力。所以开头的让步只是铺垫，而不是他的结论；至于马基雅维利是在赞同这种做法，还是在冷静地描述政治，历来争论不休。

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: He who believes that new benefits will cause great personages to forget old injuries is deceived.
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF OTHERS OR BY GOOD FORTUNE, CHAPTER VII
entries.context: The Prince, on Cesare Borgia's fatal mistake of trusting an old enemy he had newly favoured.

interpretation.en: In chapter VII Machiavelli praises Cesare Borgia almost without reserve, and this is the one mistake he holds against him: allowing the election of a pope, Julius II, whom Borgia had injured in the past. The general rule is that people in power do not forget old wrongs because of new favours, since men harm others out of fear or hatred. Machiavelli concludes that this misjudgement caused Borgia's ruin. The maxim is drawn from a specific episode of papal politics rather than offered as abstract psychology.
interpretation.zh: 在第七章中，马基雅维利几乎毫无保留地称赞切萨雷·博尔贾，而这是他唯一归咎于博尔贾的错误：容许一位他过去伤害过的人当选教皇，即尤利乌斯二世。其中的一般规则是，有权势的人不会因为新的恩惠而忘记旧的伤害，因为人们出于恐惧或仇恨而伤害别人。马基雅维利的结论是，这一误判导致了博尔贾的覆灭。这条格言来自教廷政治中的一个具体事件，而不是抽象的心理学论断。

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Nature breedeth few stronge menne, the industrie and the exercise maketh manie.
entries.work: The Art of War
entries.context: The Art of War, in its 1560 English translation, from a list of military maxims on training.

interpretation.en: This comes from a series of short military rules in The Art of War, set alongside maxims on secrecy, seizing opportunity and the value of deserters. The claim is that few soldiers are naturally strong, but training and practice make many of them so. It fits the wider argument of the book that a state should build disciplined, drilled troops of its own rather than rely on chance or on hired soldiers. The archaic spelling is that of the 1560 English translation.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自《战争的艺术》中一组简短的军事准则，与之并列的是关于保密、把握时机和逃兵价值的格言。其主张是，天生强壮的人很少，但训练和操练能使许多人变得强壮。这与本书更大的论点相符：一个国家应当建立自己经过训练、纪律严明的军队，而不是依靠运气或雇佣兵。英文原文的古旧拼写来自1560年的英译本。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, private notes to himself written in Greek, here in Casaubon's seventeenth-century English.

interpretation.en: This is one of the short notes Marcus wrote to himself. It pairs two Stoic claims: no one else can stop a person from living according to his own rational nature, and nothing happens except what the order of the whole requires. The first locates freedom in one's own choices rather than in circumstances; the second asks for acceptance of events as part of a larger providential order. The note that follows turns to how quickly time buries the people one tries to please.
interpretation.zh: 这是马可·奥勒留写给自己的简短笔记之一。它把两个斯多葛派主张并列：别人无法阻止一个人按照自己的理性本性生活；而发生的一切，无不是整体秩序所要求的。前者把自由放在自己的选择上，而不是外在处境上；后者要求把发生的事接受为更大的天意秩序的一部分。接下来的一条笔记转而谈到，时间多么快地埋没了人们想要讨好的那些人。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on answering people who wrong you.

interpretation.en: This one-line note concerns people who do wrong. Marcus redefines revenge so that the only worthwhile response is to refuse to take on the faults of the wrongdoer. It reflects the Stoic view that the real harm in an injury would be to let it corrupt one's own character, which is the only thing truly in one's power. The surrounding notes turn to kind actions toward others and to the ruling part of the mind shaping how events appear.
interpretation.zh: 这条一句话的笔记讲的是做错事的人。马可·奥勒留重新定义了报复：唯一值得的回应，是拒绝染上作恶者的毛病。这反映了斯多葛派的观点：伤害中真正的害处，在于让它败坏自己的品格，而品格才是真正操之在己的东西。周围的笔记转而谈到对他人的善行，以及心灵的主导部分如何决定事情在自己眼中的样子。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, from a run of short reminders to himself.

interpretation.en: This sentence sits in a compressed list of mental exercises: wipe out opinion, check passions, confine attention to the present, analyse events into matter and form, think of the last hour. Here Marcus tells himself to examine what is said and to trace things through to both their causes and their effects. The aim, typical of Stoic practice, is to see events as they are rather than through the feelings they provoke. The list ends with the injunction to love humankind and obey God.
interpretation.zh: 这句话处在一份浓缩的心智练习清单中：抹去意见，遏制激情，把注意力限定在当下，把事物分析为质料与形式，想想最后的时刻。在这里，马可·奥勒留要求自己审视别人所说的话，并把事情追溯到它的原因和结果。这是典型的斯多葛派修习，目的是看清事物本来的样子，而不是透过它引起的情绪去看。清单最后以爱人类、顺从神作结。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let not thy mind wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on not letting imagined future troubles crowd in at once.

interpretation.en: Marcus warns himself against piling up in imagination all the hardships that a human life is exposed to. Instead, he says, each trouble should be met as it comes, with the question of what exactly in it is unbearable. He adds that neither past nor future can harm, only the present, and the present shrinks when it is clearly marked off. The method is to break a vague dread into single, present moments, each of which can be borne.
interpretation.zh: 马可·奥勒留告诫自己，不要在想象中把人生可能遭遇的种种苦难堆积在一起。他说，应当在每件事发生时去面对它，并问自己其中究竟有什么是无法忍受的。他补充说，过去和未来都不能伤害人，能伤害人的只有当下，而当下一旦被清楚地划定，就会变小。这种方法是把模糊的恐惧拆分成一个个当下的时刻，每一个时刻都是可以承受的。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, a rule for acting.

interpretation.en: This opens a note in which Marcus sets out the conduct he expects of himself. Four conditions are named: act willingly, in keeping with the common good, after due thought, and without grudging. The note goes on to reject fancy language and excessive talk, and ends with the picture of a man ready to leave life at the signal, whose word needs no oath. The rule combines the Stoic ideal of acting from settled judgment with the duties Marcus felt as a Roman and a ruler.
interpretation.zh: 这是一条笔记的开头，马可·奥勒留在其中写下他对自己行为的要求。他列出四个条件：出于自愿，合乎公共利益，经过审慎考虑，毫不勉强。这条笔记接着拒绝华丽的辞藻和过多的言谈，最后描绘了一个随时准备听号令离开人世、说话无需发誓作保的人。这条准则把斯多葛派依据稳定判断行事的理想，与马可·奥勒留作为罗马人和统治者所感到的责任结合在了一起。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Be neither a great talker, nor a great undertaker.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, from a passage on plain speech and steady conduct.

interpretation.en: In the same note where Marcus rejects ornate expression, he warns himself against both talking too much and taking on too many projects. The two go together: each is a way of spreading oneself thin and acting for show rather than from judgment. The note then describes the kind of man he wants to be, steady, sociable and ready to depart life at any moment. The word undertaker in this 1634 English means someone who takes on many enterprises, not a funeral director.
interpretation.zh: 在同一条拒绝雕琢辞藻的笔记中，马可·奥勒留告诫自己既不要多言，也不要揽下太多事务。两者是相关的：都是把自己分散开来、为了表现而不是出于判断去行事的方式。这条笔记接着描述了他想成为的那种人：稳重、合群、随时准备离开人世。1634年英译中的undertaker一词指的是揽事很多的人，而不是殡葬业者。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on how much of being wronged lies in our opinion of it.

interpretation.en: Marcus argues in a chain: remove the opinion that one has been wronged, and the sense of being wronged disappears, and with it the wrong itself. The basis is the Stoic claim that what does not make a person worse in character cannot make his life worse or truly harm him. The point is not that others never act badly but that the harm lies in one's own judgment about it, which is within one's control. Readers have long found this both consoling and demanding, since it asks for a great deal of self-command.
interpretation.zh: 马可·奥勒留的论证环环相扣：去掉自己受了伤害的看法，受伤害的感觉就会消失，伤害本身也随之不存在。其依据是斯多葛派的主张：不使一个人在品格上变坏的东西，就不能使他的生活变坏，也不能真正伤害他。重点不在于别人从不作恶，而在于伤害存在于自己对它的判断中，而判断是自己能够掌控的。读者历来觉得这既令人宽慰又要求很高，因为它需要极强的自制。

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on taking the shortest way, which is the way of nature.

interpretation.en: Compendious here means the shortest, most direct way. Marcus at once explains that the shortest way is the one according to nature, which means always following what is sound in both word and deed. He claims this resolve frees a person from trouble, quarrels, pretence and display. The idea is that crooked or showy conduct adds needless complications, while acting rightly and plainly is also the simplest course.
interpretation.zh: 这里的compendious意为最短、最直接的路。马可·奥勒留随即解释说，最短的路就是合乎自然的路，也就是在言行上始终遵循健全正当的东西。他认为这样的决心能使人摆脱烦恼、争执、虚伪和炫耀。其思想是，曲折或张扬的行为会增添不必要的麻烦，而正当、朴素地行事同时也是最简单的路。

entries.name: Karl Marx
entries.en: The more or less extensive application of division of labour depends on length of purse, not on greatness of genius.
entries.work: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Volume I
entries.context: Capital, Volume I, in a footnote mocking the idea that the division of labour was a capitalist's stroke of genius.

interpretation.en: This is a footnote in the part of Capital on the division of labour in manufacture. Marx mocks the belief, which he attributes to German professors such as Roscher, that the division of labour sprang from the inventive genius of individual capitalists. His counterclaim is that how far labour is divided depends on how much capital an owner has, since more capital pays for more workers and a finer split of tasks. The remark fits his wider argument that economic forms arise from material conditions rather than from the talent of individuals.
interpretation.zh: 这是《资本论》讨论工场手工业分工那一部分中的一个脚注。马克思嘲讽了一种看法，他把它归于罗雪尔等德国教授：分工源于个别资本家的发明天才。他的反驳是，分工实行到什么程度，取决于资本家钱袋的大小，因为更多的资本能雇用更多的工人，把工序分得更细。这句话符合他更大的论点：经济形式产生于物质条件，而不是个人的才能。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: It is not necessary for keeping up our conviction that we must die, that we should be always brooding over death.
entries.work: Three Essays on Religion: Nature, The Utility of Religion, and Theism
entries.context: Three Essays on Religion, in the essay "Theism", on thinking about death no more than we need to.

interpretation.en: Near the end of the essay Theism, Mill discusses how imagination and hope should relate to reason. In this passage he argues that knowing we must die does not require constantly dwelling on death. It is better, he says, to think about it only as far as prudence and duty require, and to keep one's attention on one's duties and the rule of life instead. The wider point is that practical wisdom means giving prominence to the aspects of things that help one live well, not attending equally to everything that is true.
interpretation.zh: 在《有神论》一文接近结尾处，密尔讨论了想象和希望应当如何与理性相处。在这段话中他论证说，知道人必有一死，并不需要时时沉思死亡。他说，更好的做法是只在审慎和尽责所需的范围内想到它，而把注意力放在自己的责任和生活准则上。更大的论点是，实践智慧意味着突出那些有助于好好生活的方面，而不是对一切真实的东西都给予同等的关注。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: He who does anything because it is the custom, makes no choice.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, on individuality: our faculties grow only when we use them to choose.

interpretation.en: In the chapter on individuality, Mill grants that custom carries some evidence of what others have learned from experience, but gives three reasons it should not simply be followed: the experience may be narrow or misread, it may not fit the individual, and even good customs followed only as customs do not develop human faculties. This sentence makes the third point. Perception, judgment and moral preference are exercised only in choosing, and like muscles they grow only through use. Doing something merely because others do it gives them no exercise.
interpretation.zh: 在论个性的那一章中，密尔承认习俗在某种程度上体现了别人从经验中学到的东西，但给出三个理由说明不应简单地遵从习俗：那种经验可能狭隘或被误解；它可能不适合这个人；即便是好的习俗，如果只是作为习俗来遵从，也不能培养人的能力。这句话讲的是第三点。感知、判断和道德偏好只有在做选择时才得到运用，而且像肌肉一样，只有通过使用才会增强。仅仅因为别人这样做就去做，这些能力就得不到任何锻炼。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: Nothing has so steadying an influence as working against pressure.
entries.work: Considerations on Representative Government
entries.context: Considerations on Representative Government, on the value of having to defend one's views against opposition.

interpretation.en: Mill is arguing that having to defend one's conduct in front of others is valuable, especially for those who go against prevailing opinion, because it forces them to find solid ground of their own. This sentence sums up the point: resistance steadies a person. He adds that few people do what they expect to be strongly blamed for unless they have a fixed and considered purpose, and that merely having to give an account of one's actions encourages conduct that can be defended. The claim treats public accountability as a support for character rather than only a check on it.
interpretation.zh: 密尔在论证，必须在别人面前为自己的行为辩护是有价值的，对那些与主流意见相左的人尤其如此，因为这迫使他们找到自己的坚实立足点。这句话概括了这一点：阻力使人稳定。他补充说，很少有人会去做预料会受到严厉指责的事，除非他有坚定而深思熟虑的目的；而仅仅是必须对自己的行为作出交代，就能促使人做出可以辩护的行为。这一主张把公开问责看作对品格的支撑，而不只是对它的约束。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: Whoever is anxious that a discussion should go to the bottom of the subject, must rejoice to see the opposite side of the question worthily represented.
entries.work: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
entries.context: A System of Logic, welcoming the strongest statement of the view Mill was arguing against.

interpretation.en: Mill has just stated an unpopular view about the axioms of mathematics, namely that they rest on experience rather than being necessary truths known independently of it. William Whewell had built a whole philosophy of science on the opposite doctrine, and Mill says he is glad of it. His reason is that a dispute is only settled when the opposing case has been put at its strongest; if he can show that Whewell's arguments fail, he need not look for a better opponent. The passage is often cited as an example of engaging the strongest version of a rival view.
interpretation.zh: 密尔刚刚提出一个不受欢迎的观点，即数学公理建立在经验之上，而不是独立于经验而被认识的必然真理。威廉·休厄尔以相反的学说为基础建立了一整套科学哲学，而密尔说他为此感到庆幸。他的理由是，只有当对立的一方得到最有力的表述时，争论才能被彻底解决；如果他能证明休厄尔的论证不成立，就无需再去寻找更强的对手。这段话常被引为面对对立观点最强版本的例子。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: No one pretends that actions should be as free as opinions.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, which opens by limiting liberty of action more than liberty of opinion.

interpretation.en: Having argued for nearly complete freedom of opinion and expression, Mill turns in chapter III to freedom of action, and starts with a limit. Actions cannot be as free as opinions, and even an opinion loses its protection when expressed in circumstances that make it a direct incitement to harm. His example is the claim that corn-dealers starve the poor: acceptable in print, punishable when shouted at an angry mob outside a corn-dealer's house. The passage marks the line Mill draws between expression and harmful conduct, and the example is often used to discuss where incitement begins.
interpretation.zh: 在论证了几乎完全的意见与表达自由之后，密尔在第三章转向行动自由，并且首先划定一个限度。行动不能像意见那样自由；即便是意见，如果在构成直接煽动伤害的情境中表达，也会失去保护。他的例子是粮商让穷人挨饿这一说法：刊登在报刊上可以容许，但对着聚集在粮商家门口的激愤人群高喊时就可以受罚。这段话标出了密尔在表达与有害行为之间划的界线，这个例子也常被用来讨论煽动从何处开始。

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: There is no natural connection between strong impulses and a weak conscience.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, arguing that people go wrong not because their desires are strong but because their consciences are weak.

interpretation.en: Mill is pushing back against the common assumption that strong desires and impulses are dangerous in themselves. He argues that wrongdoing comes from a weak conscience, not from strong desire, and that the two have no natural link; if anything, strong feeling tends to go with strong conscience. A person with stronger and more varied desires simply has more of the raw material of human nature, and so is capable of more good as well as more evil. The passage belongs to his defence of individuality and energy against a society that prefers people to be tame.
interpretation.zh: 密尔在反驳一种常见的假设，即强烈的欲望和冲动本身就是危险的。他论证说，作恶源于良心软弱，而不是欲望强烈，两者之间并没有天然的联系；如果说有，强烈的情感倒往往与强烈的良心相伴。一个欲望更强烈、更多样的人，只是拥有更多人性的原材料，因此既可能做出更多的恶，也一定能做出更多的善。这段话属于他为个性和活力所作的辩护，针对的是一个更希望人们驯顺的社会。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Men of principle are sure to be bold, but those who are bold may not always be men of principle.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects of Confucius, sayings recorded by his followers, here in James Legge's translation; this is from Book XIV.

interpretation.en: This is the second half of a paired saying in which Confucius sets inner quality against its outward signs. Just before it he makes the same point about speech: a good person will speak well, but fine speech does not prove goodness. Courage works the same way here. Real moral commitment produces courage, but courage alone can belong to someone with no principles at all, so it cannot be taken as evidence of character. Legge's men of principle stands for a Chinese term usually rendered as humane or benevolent, so the English sounds more like firm conviction than the original may intend.
interpretation.zh: 这是一组对句的后半句，孔子在其中把内在品质与外在表现对照来看。紧挨着的前半句讲言语：有德之人必然言语得当，但言语动听并不证明有德。这里讲勇敢，道理相同：真正的仁德会生出勇气，但勇气本身也可能属于毫无原则的人，因此不能拿勇敢来证明品格。理雅各译作有原则的人，原文的词通常理解为仁者，英文读起来更像坚定的信念，未必贴合原意。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, attributed to Laozi, here in James Legge's translation; chapter 9.

interpretation.en: This line opens a chapter about the danger of pushing anything to its limit: the next image is a blade honed so often that it soon loses its edge. The point is that fullness and sharpness cannot be held for long, so stopping short of the maximum is the safer course. Legge renders the image as a vessel that is better left unfilled; the original is terser and can also be read as a warning against grasping and filling something to the brim, so the exact picture depends on the translation.
interpretation.zh: 这一句是一章的开头，该章讲的是把事情推到极致的危险：紧接着的比喻是一把反复磨砺的刀刃，很快就会失去锋利。其意思是，满与锐都不能长久保持，因此在达到顶点之前停下来更为稳妥。理雅各把这个意象译为宁可不把器皿装满；原文更为简省，也可以理解为告诫人不要执持而求盈满，所以具体画面取决于译法。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: There is no calamity greater than lightly engaging in war.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 69, on the conduct of war.

interpretation.en: Chapter 69 treats war as something the sage enters only reluctantly and defensively. Here the text says the worst disaster is to go to war carelessly, because doing so throws away the gentleness the book prizes, and it closes by saying that when armies actually meet, the side that grieves over the fighting wins. Legge reads the key phrase as lightly engaging in war; many other translators read it as underestimating the enemy, which shifts the warning from starting wars to fighting them carelessly.
interpretation.zh: 第六十九章把战争视为圣人只会勉强、以守势进入的事。这里说，最大的祸患是轻率用兵，因为这样会丧失本书所珍视的慈柔；章末又说，两军真正交锋时，哀痛战事的一方会取胜。理雅各把关键一语理解为轻易开战；许多其他译者则理解为轻视敌人，这样告诫的重点就从发动战争转到了作战时的轻忽。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: It is the Way of Heaven to diminish superabundance, and to supplement deficiency.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 77, comparing the Way of Heaven with the way of man.

interpretation.en: The chapter compares the Way of Heaven to stringing a bow, where the high part is pulled down and the low part raised. The passage draws the moral: nature evens things out, taking from excess and adding to lack. The sentence that follows turns it into a criticism of human conduct, which does the reverse by taking from those who have too little to add to those who already have too much. It is one of the passages in the book most often read as social and political criticism, though it is framed as a contrast between nature and human ways rather than as a programme.
interpretation.zh: 这一章把天道比作张弓：高的一端被压低，低的一端被抬高。这段话点出寓意：自然会使万物趋于均平，减损有余，补益不足。紧接着的一句把它变成对人事的批评：人道恰恰相反，从不足者那里拿走，去增添已经有余者。这是全书中最常被当作社会和政治批评来读的段落之一，不过它是以自然与人道的对照来表述的，并不是一套具体主张。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 78, on water, softness and strength.

interpretation.en: Chapter 78 begins with water, the softest thing, which nonetheless wears away the hardest. Here the text notes a gap between knowing and doing: everyone grants that softness beats hardness, yet no one acts on it. The lines that follow, presented as the words of an earlier sage, apply this to rulers, saying that the one who takes on the disgrace and misfortune of the state is the one fit to lead it. The softness meant here is usually read as yielding and bearing burdens, not as passivity, though how far it is political advice and how far personal conduct is open to reading.
interpretation.zh: 第七十八章以水开头：水是最柔弱的，却能攻克最坚硬的东西。这里指出知与行之间的落差：人人都承认柔能胜刚，却没有人照着去做。随后几句被引为一位古圣人的话，把这个道理用于君主，说能承受国家的屈辱和灾祸的人，才配做一国之主。这里的柔通常被理解为退让和承担，而不是消极；至于它多大程度上是政治建议、多大程度上是个人修养，则可以有不同读法。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 15, on the old masters of the Way and muddy water settling.

interpretation.en: This line comes from the chapter describing the ancient masters of the Way, who are pictured as cautious, reserved and murky like unsettled water. The text asks who can make muddy water clear and answers that it clears by itself if left still. The image supports the book's preference for not forcing things: clarity comes from letting agitation settle rather than from stirring. The passage pairs it at once with the opposite movement, so it is usually read as a point about timing and balance, not as a call to do nothing. The input lists this as chapter 10; the surrounding text matches chapter 15.
interpretation.zh: 这句出自描写古代善为道者的一章，书中把他们描绘得谨慎、含蓄，像未澄清的水一样浑然。文中问谁能使浊水变清，回答是让它静下来，它自己就会慢慢澄清。这个意象支持全书不强求的主张：清明来自让扰动沉淀，而不是继续搅动。这段话紧接着就配上了相反方向的运动，所以通常被理解为关于时机与平衡的道理，而不是号召什么都不做。输入标注为第十章，但上下文与第十五章相符。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 63, on attending to things while they are still small.

interpretation.en: Chapter 63 advises dealing with hard things while they are still easy and with great things while they are still small. This sentence gives the reason: every difficulty and every large matter begins in an easy or small form. The chapter then draws a paradox, that the sage never attempts anything great and for that very reason achieves great things. The claim is less about modesty than about attention: problems are handled best before they have grown.
interpretation.zh: 第六十三章主张在难事尚易时着手，在大事尚小时去做。这一句给出理由：一切难事都起于容易的状态，一切大事都起于微小的状态。这一章随后得出一个悖论：圣人从不去做大事，正因如此才能成就大事。这个主张与其说是讲谦虚，不如说是讲留意：问题在长大之前最好处理。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: He who loves others is always loved by them, and he who respects others is always respected by them.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF BEING CAREFUL WHOM WE MAKE FRIENDS OF, chapter XXIII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, in James Legge's translation, on benevolence and propriety.

interpretation.en: Mencius begins this chapter by saying that what sets the superior person apart is what he keeps in his heart, namely benevolence and propriety. Here he states the result: love and respect given to others tend to come back. The chapter goes on to ask what to do when someone responds badly anyway, and answers that one should first examine oneself for a failure of benevolence or propriety. So the line is less a promise of reciprocity than the starting point for self-scrutiny. The locator in the input names chapter XXIII; the surrounding text is chapter XXVIII.
interpretation.zh: 孟子在这一章开头说，君子与常人的不同，在于他心中所存的东西，即仁和礼。这里他说出结果：给予别人的爱与敬，往往会得到回报。这一章接着问，如果有人仍以恶意相待该怎么办，回答是应当先反省自己在仁或礼上是否有所欠缺。所以这句话与其说是承诺必有回报，不如说是自我省察的起点。输入的位置标注为第二十三章，上下文实为第二十八章。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: There is no greater delight than to be conscious of sincerity on self-examination.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VII, on looking within: "All things are already complete in us."

interpretation.en: This follows directly from the statement that all things are already complete in the self, and the previous chapter had contrasted seeking things within oneself with seeking things outside, which depends on fate. Mencius says the greatest joy is to examine oneself and find one has been sincere, true to what is within. The opening claim that all things are complete in us is one of the most debated lines in the book, read by some as a statement about moral potential and by others in a more mystical sense. Legge's sincerity renders a Confucian term that also carries the sense of being genuine or whole.
interpretation.zh: 这句话紧接在万物皆备于我之后，而前一章对比了求之在我与求之在外，后者取决于命运。孟子说，最大的快乐是反省自身，发现自己是真诚的，忠于内在之所有。开头万物皆备于我这一说法是全书最受争议的句子之一，有人理解为关于道德潜能的陈述，也有人从更神秘的意义上去理解。理雅各所译的sincerity对应的儒家概念，同时含有真实、完整的意思。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: Never has a man who has bent himself been able to make others straight.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book III, on refusing to bend one's principles to win a ruler's favour.

interpretation.en: Mencius is answering a disciple who has urged him to compromise a little in order to gain an audience with the rulers of the day, on the grounds that a small concession could bring large results. He replies with the story of a charioteer who refused to drive improperly even when doing so would have brought in a great catch of game. This line is his conclusion: a person who bends his own principles cannot set anyone else right. The underlying view is that moral influence depends on personal integrity, so compromise defeats the very goal it is meant to serve.
interpretation.zh: 孟子是在回答一位弟子，这位弟子劝他稍作妥协以求得当时诸侯的接见，理由是小小的让步可能换来大的成果。孟子用一位御者的故事作答：即使不按规矩驾车能猎获堆积如山的禽兽，这位御者也拒绝那样做。这一句是他的结论：自己枉曲原则的人，不可能使别人正直。其背后的观点是，道德影响力取决于自身的正直，所以妥协恰恰会破坏它想要达到的目的。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: He who behaves shabbily to those whom he ought to treat well will behave shabbily to all.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF TRUTH IN THOSE WHOM HE TAUGHT, Book IX
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VII, from a chapter of short sayings on character.

interpretation.en: This comes from a short chapter of sayings about character, where Mencius pairs it with the observation that a person who stops where he should not will stop short in everything. The point is that how someone treats those who have the strongest claim on his kindness, such as family or close associates, shows how he will treat everyone; if he is mean there, he will be mean everywhere. The chapter as a whole argues that failures in basic relationships cannot be compartmentalised. The surrounding text in the input is fragmentary, and its locator does not match the book named in the context note.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自一个谈论品格的短章，孟子把它与另一句并列：在不该停止的地方停止的人，做什么都会半途而废。其要点是，一个人怎样对待那些最应当受他厚待的人，比如家人或亲近的人，就显示了他会怎样对待所有人；如果他在那里刻薄，就会处处刻薄。整章论证的是，基本人伦关系上的缺失无法被隔离开来。输入中的上下文残缺不全，位置标注也与背景说明中的卷次不符。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: It is only the great man who can correct what is wrong in the ruler's mind.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book IV, on the counsellor's real task.

interpretation.en: Mencius says that it is not enough for a counsellor to criticise the officials a ruler appoints or the faults of his government. The real task is to correct the ruler himself, because once the ruler is benevolent, righteous and correct, everything that flows from him will be too, and the state will be settled. The passage expresses a recurring Confucian view that good order flows from the moral character of those at the top. The surrounding text in the input is fragmentary, so the opening of the chapter is only partly visible.
interpretation.zh: 孟子说，一个辅臣仅仅指责君主任用的人或政事的过失是不够的。真正的任务是纠正君主本人，因为君主一旦仁、义、正，从他那里出来的一切也会如此，国家就会安定。这段话体现了儒家一再出现的观点：良好的秩序来自在上者的道德品格。输入中的上下文残缺，所以这一章的开头只能看到一部分。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: Men constantly err, but are afterwards able to reform.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF SEVERAL EMINENT WORTHIES OF FORMER TIMES, Book VII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VI, on how hardship and mistakes lead people to change.

interpretation.en: This sentence belongs to the chapter on the hardships endured by great figures before they rose to office. Mencius generalises: people regularly make mistakes and only afterwards correct them, and they rouse themselves to effort only after being troubled and perplexed. He then applies the same logic to states, saying that a state with no strict ministers at home and no threats abroad tends toward ruin. The chapter concludes that people live through difficulty and perish through ease, so error and pressure are treated as necessary conditions of growth rather than mere misfortunes.
interpretation.zh: 这句话属于讲述伟大人物在出任要职之前所经历苦难的那一章。孟子加以概括：人常常犯错，然后才能改正；内心困苦、思虑阻塞，然后才能奋发有为。他接着把同样的道理用于国家：国内没有守法度的世家和辅佐的贤士，国外没有敌国外患，这样的国家往往会灭亡。这一章的结论是人在忧患中得以生存，在安乐中走向灭亡，所以错误和压力被视为成长的必要条件，而不只是不幸。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: He who will not give himself leisure to be thirsty can never find the true pleasure of drinking.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, in Charles Cotton's translation, on how pleasure dulls with constant use.

interpretation.en: Montaigne is arguing that great people are worse off than they seem, because whatever is always available stops giving pleasure. He lines up examples: choirboys bored by music, regular guests at feasts who find them flat, performers who toil at what spectators enjoy. The line about thirst states the general rule behind them: enjoyment needs a gap of want before it, so a life with every wish met at once loses the pleasures it is supposed to have in abundance.
interpretation.zh: 蒙田在论证：位高权重的人并不像看上去那样幸福，因为随时可得的东西会失去乐趣。他列举了一串例子：唱诗班的男孩对音乐感到厌倦，常赴宴会的人觉得宴会索然无味，表演者辛苦劳作，观众却从中取乐。关于口渴的这句话，是这些例子背后的通则：享受之前需要有一段匮乏，一个愿望总是立刻被满足的生活，反而失去了它本该充裕拥有的快乐。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Fear springs sometimes as much from want of judgment as from want of courage.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, Montaigne recalling that he never lost his judgment in danger.

interpretation.en: Montaigne is describing his own conduct in danger: he says he was never so frightened that he lost his judgment, and that he faced each peril with clear sight. The claim is that much panic is a failure to see the situation accurately rather than a lack of nerve. He adds the paradox that it takes courage to fear, meaning that a person must be steady enough to look at the danger to fear it in proportion, and he goes on to Socrates in retreat as the higher example.
interpretation.zh: 蒙田在描述自己身处险境时的表现：他说自己从未害怕到失去判断，每次危险都看得清清楚楚。他的意思是，许多惊慌并非出于胆量不足，而是没能准确看清处境。他还补了一个悖论：害怕也需要勇气，即一个人必须足够镇定，敢于正视危险，才能怕得恰如其分。随后他举苏格拉底撤退时的表现，作为更高的范例。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: There is no desire more natural than that of knowledge.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: The opening line of Montaigne's final essay, "Of Experience".

interpretation.en: This sentence opens Montaigne's last essay and sets up its whole argument. He grants that the wish to know is natural, then turns at once to the means: where reason falls short, people fall back on experience. The rest of the essay presses the point that reason and general rules fail before the endless variety of particular cases, and that close attention to one's own experience, especially of one's own body and life, teaches more than learned systems do.
interpretation.zh: 这句话是蒙田最后一篇随笔的开头，为全文铺开论证。他先承认求知的欲望出于天性，随即转向求知的途径：理性不够用的地方，人就只能借助经验。这篇随笔接下来反复强调，面对千差万别的具体情形，理性和普遍规则都会失灵，而细心体察自己的经验，尤其是对自身身体与生活的经验，比学问体系教给人的更多。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Nothing can be a grievance that is but once.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.locator: OF OUR HAPPINESS TILL AFTER DEATH
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on not fearing death too long, since it happens only once.

interpretation.en: Montaigne is gathering arguments, many drawn from ancient Stoic and Epicurean writers, against the dread of death. This one says that an event which happens only once and is over quickly cannot reasonably be suffered over for a lifetime; the long fear is worse than the thing feared. Around it he adds that not being alive in a hundred years is no more to be lamented than not having been alive a hundred years ago. These are borrowed consolations he is trying out, and the essay as a whole is about learning to think of death often so as to fear it less.
interpretation.zh: 蒙田在汇集反对畏惧死亡的论据，其中许多取自古代斯多亚派和伊壁鸠鲁派的作家。这一条说：一件只发生一次、转瞬即逝的事，没有理由让人一辈子为之受苦，长久的恐惧比所怕之事本身更糟。在它周围，他还说，为一百年后自己不在人世而悲伤，和为一百年前自己尚未出生而难过一样愚蠢。这些是他借来试用的慰藉，整篇随笔讲的是常常想到死，从而少怕一些。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Nothing is so distasteful and clogging as abundance.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on how excess kills appetite and restraint sharpens pleasure.

interpretation.en: Montaigne continues his case that the powerful are poorly placed to enjoy life. His examples are a sultan with hundreds of women at his disposal and a ruler who never hunted without thousands of falconers: so much supply leaves no room for appetite. He then adds a second disadvantage, that the great live in full view, so even their pleasures come with unease. The point is about the conditions of pleasure, not a moral sermon against luxury.
interpretation.zh: 蒙田继续论证：有权势的人其实难以享受生活。他举的例子是坐拥数百名女子的苏丹，以及每次打猎都带着数千名驯鹰人的君主：供给如此之多，欲望便无处容身。接着他补充第二个不利之处：大人物活在众目睽睽之下，连快乐也伴着不安。他讲的是快乐得以成立的条件，而不是一篇反对奢侈的道德说教。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Whoever will be cured of ignorance must confess it.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on scholars who would rather appear learned than admit what they do not understand.

interpretation.en: The surrounding text is Montaigne's complaint against people who speak of everything with assurance and treat the merely likely as certain. He praises hedging words such as perhaps and it seems, notes that Roman courts phrased even eyewitness testimony as an impression, and says he would teach children to ask and doubt rather than to pronounce. The sentence draws the conclusion: ignorance is cured only by first admitting it, which is the starting point of his scepticism.
interpretation.zh: 这段上下文是蒙田在抱怨那些对一切都言之凿凿、把可能当作确定的人。他称赞或许、似乎之类留有余地的说法，指出罗马法庭连目击证词也以我看来的形式表述，并说如果由他教孩子，他会教他们发问和存疑，而不是下结论。这句话是他得出的结论：无知只有先被承认才能被治好，这正是他怀疑主义的出发点。

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: We should rather examine, who is better learned, than who is more learned.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.locator: OF CUSTOM, AND THAT WE SHOULD NOT EASILY
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, in "Of Pedantry", criticising education that fills the memory but does not improve the person.

interpretation.en: Montaigne is attacking the education of his day for stuffing heads with knowledge while saying nothing of judgment and virtue. He notes that crowds turn to admire the learned man before the good man, and that people ask whether someone knows Greek or Latin, never whether he has become better or wiser. His distinction between better learned and more learned is between learning that has changed the person and learning that has only been stored.
interpretation.zh: 蒙田在抨击当时的教育只往脑袋里塞知识，却只字不提判断力和德行。他指出，人群总是先去仰慕有学问的人，而不是好人；人们会问某人懂不懂希腊文、拉丁文，却从不问他是否变得更好、更明智。他所区分的学得更好与学得更多，是改变了一个人的学问与仅仅被储存起来的学问之间的区别。

entries.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
entries.en: All great noise causes one to place happiness in the calm and the distance.
entries.work: The Joyful Wisdom ("La Gaya Scienza")
entries.translator: Thomas Common (prose; verse by Paul V. Cohn)
entries.context: The Joyful Wisdom (The Gay Science), on longing for calm in the middle of noise.

interpretation.en: The sentence closes a vivid scene: Nietzsche describes standing amid the roar of surf on rocks when a sailing ship glides silently past, and he imagines his own happiness aboard it, passing over existence without living it. Then he catches himself, suspecting the noise has made him a dreamer. The line is a diagnosis of that fantasy, not an endorsement of it: loud surroundings breed the wish for a distant calm, and the calm imagined is partly an illusion produced by the noise. The tone is ironic, and the section goes on to apply the same pattern to other ideals seen from afar.
interpretation.zh: 这句话收束了一个生动的场景：尼采描写自己站在拍打礁石的轰鸣浪涛中，一艘帆船静静驶过，他想象自己的幸福就在船上，掠过人生而不去活它。随后他察觉到自己，怀疑是噪音让他成了幻想家。这句话是在诊断这种幻想，而不是赞同它：喧闹的环境催生对远方宁静的渴望，而想象中的宁静部分正是噪音造成的错觉。语气带有反讽，这一节接着把同样的模式用到其他远望中的理想上。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: He who should find the secret of rejoicing in good without being troubled at its contrary evil, would have hit the mark.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts (Pensées), notes for an unfinished defence of Christianity, on why we cannot enjoy any good without fearing its loss.

interpretation.en: Pascal begins from human unhappiness: any pleasure comes bound to the worry that it may go wrong, which it often does. Whoever could enjoy the good without dreading its opposite would have found the secret. But the fragment ends by calling this perpetual motion, that is, something people keep trying to build and never can. Read that way, the line is not advice but a statement of impossibility, part of Pascal's case that human beings cannot reach stable happiness on their own.
interpretation.zh: 帕斯卡尔从人的不幸说起：任何快乐都捆绑着对它可能出岔子的担忧，而它也确实常常出岔子。谁能享受好事而不惧怕它的反面，谁就找到了诀窍。但这段残篇最后把这比作永动机，也就是人们不断尝试制造却永远造不出的东西。这样读来，这句话不是劝告，而是在陈述一种不可能，是帕斯卡尔论证人凭自己无法获得稳定幸福的一部分。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Time heals all pain and misunderstanding, because we change and are no longer the same persons.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on time changing both the person who gave offence and the person who took it.

interpretation.en: Pascal explains why old grievances fade: not because the wrong is forgiven or understood, but because both parties have changed. Neither the one who gave offence nor the one who took it is the same person any more, like a nation met again two generations after a quarrel, still French but not the same. The observation belongs to his larger theme of human inconstancy, and it is less a comfort than a sobering remark on how little of the self persists.
interpretation.zh: 帕斯卡尔解释旧怨为何会淡去：不是因为过错得到宽恕或理解，而是因为双方都变了。冒犯者和被冒犯者都不再是原来的人，就像两代人之后再遇见一个曾经结怨的民族，仍是法国人，却已不是同一批人。这一观察属于他关于人之无常的更大主题，与其说是安慰，不如说是一句清醒的提醒：自我之中能延续下来的东西少得可怜。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: All the efforts of violence cannot weaken truth, and only serve to give it fresh vigor.
entries.work: The Provincial Letters
entries.context: The Provincial Letters, Pascal's satirical letters against the Jesuits; from the twelfth, on the war between violence and truth.
