interpretation.en: Writing near the end of a letter, Pascal answers the Jesuits' abuse and threats against him. He sets out a symmetry: violence cannot weaken truth, and truth cannot stop violence; each only provokes the other. He then denies that this makes them equal, arguing that violence runs a limited course under divine providence while truth endures. The claim is polemical and theological, made by an embattled writer about his own dispute, not a neutral observation about power.
interpretation.zh: 帕斯卡尔在一封信的末尾回应耶稣会士对他的谩骂和威胁。他提出一种对称：暴力削弱不了真理，真理也阻止不了暴力，双方只会互相激化。随后他否认二者因此平起平坐，认为暴力在神意的限定下只能走完有限的路程，而真理长存。这是一个身陷论战的作者就自己的争端所作的论辩性、神学性的主张，而不是关于权力的中立观察。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: It is not shameful to man to yield to pain, and it is shameful to yield to pleasure.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on the difference between yielding to pain and yielding to pleasure.

interpretation.en: Pascal asks why reason counts it honourable to give way under pain but shameful to give way to pleasure. He rejects the obvious answer that pain comes from outside, and offers another: pain does not tempt, so whoever endures it does so by choice and remains master, whereas yielding to pleasure is being mastered by it. The underlying point is that glory belongs only to self-command and shame to servitude. The reasoning is compressed and somewhat paradoxical, as many of these unfinished notes are.
interpretation.zh: 帕斯卡尔追问：为什么理性认为在痛苦面前屈服是光荣的，而向快乐屈服却是可耻的？他否定了痛苦来自外部这个显而易见的答案，给出另一个解释：痛苦不诱惑人，所以忍受痛苦是出于自己的选择，人仍是主人；而向快乐屈服，则是被快乐所支配。其根本意思是，荣耀只属于自我主宰，耻辱属于受奴役。和这些未完成的笔记中的许多条一样，这里的推理简省且带有悖论色彩。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: It is false piety to keep peace to the prejudice of the truth.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on the balance between loving truth and keeping charity.

interpretation.en: These lines read like notes for a defence of how Pascal's side had treated its opponents, keeping a middle path between love of truth and the duty of charity. He names two opposite faults: keeping the peace at the cost of truth is false piety, and defending truth while wounding charity is false zeal. The exact dispute the notes refer to is not clear from the fragment itself, so the general principle is what can be read with confidence.
interpretation.zh: 这几行读起来像是一份辩护笔记，为帕斯卡尔一方对待论敌的方式辩护，说他们在热爱真理与恪守仁爱之间保持了中道。他点出两种相反的错误：以牺牲真理为代价维持和平，是虚假的虔诚；捍卫真理却伤害仁爱，是虚假的热忱。残篇本身没有说明这些笔记指向哪一场具体争论，能够确定读出的是其中的一般原则。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Nothing fortifies scepticism more than that there are some who are not sceptics.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, a fragment on scepticism.

interpretation.en: A deliberately paradoxical fragment. Pascal seems to mean that the sceptic's case is strengthened by disagreement itself: because some people are confident and others doubt, no position is secure, which is just what the sceptic claims. If everyone were a sceptic, the universal agreement would itself count against scepticism. The note is very short and its exact force is debated; it belongs to Pascal's wider view that neither dogmatists nor sceptics can win outright.
interpretation.zh: 这是一条刻意制造悖论的残篇。帕斯卡尔的意思似乎是：分歧本身就加强了怀疑论，因为有人笃定、有人怀疑，任何立场都不稳固，这恰恰是怀疑论者的主张。假如人人都是怀疑论者，这种普遍一致反倒会成为反对怀疑论的理由。这条笔记极短，确切含义有争议；它属于帕斯卡尔更大的看法：独断论者和怀疑论者都无法彻底取胜。

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Whoever stops draws attention to the onward movement of others, as does a fixed point.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on how we notice that others are moving only when someone stands still.

interpretation.en: Pascal uses the image of passengers on a ship, who feel no motion when everything moves together. In the same way, when everyone drifts toward vice, no one appears to; only someone who stops serves as a fixed point that reveals how far the rest have moved. The note is about moral perception: standards are judged against the surrounding crowd, so shared faults become invisible. The next fragment, on laws being held just simply because they are established, continues the same theme.
interpretation.zh: 帕斯卡尔用船上乘客作比：当一切一同移动时，人感觉不到移动。同样，人人都趋向恶行时，就没有人显得如此；只有停下来的人才成为一个参照点，显出其他人已走出多远。这条笔记讲的是道德感知：人以周围的人群为标准来衡量，于是共同的过错变得看不见。紧接着的一条说法律仅因已经确立就被认为正当，延续的也是这个主题。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Let every man, then, freely strive for the prize of virtue, and let there be no envy.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws, his longest dialogue; the Athenian Stranger speaks, on rivalry in virtue without envy.

interpretation.en: In the Laws the speaker is an unnamed Athenian Stranger, not Plato in his own voice. Here he ranks citizens by how they share goods like justice and wisdom: the highest is one who helps others become good, and the one who grudgingly keeps such goods to himself is blamed. He then urges open rivalry in virtue without envy, arguing that the envious man, who tries to win by slandering rivals, slackens in virtue himself and discourages others, so the whole city enters the contest untrained.
interpretation.zh: 在《法律篇》中说话的是一位无名的雅典客人，而非柏拉图本人。这里他按公民如何分享正义、智慧这类善来排序：最高的是帮助他人变好的人，而吝于与人分享这些善的人应受责备。接着他主张在德行上公开竞争而不怀嫉妒，理由是嫉妒者靠诋毁对手取胜，自己在德行上松懈，又使对手灰心，于是整个城邦都未经训练就走进了竞技场。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Let parents, then, bequeath to their children not a heap of riches, but the spirit of reverence.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws: the Athenian Stranger on what parents should leave their children.

interpretation.en: The Athenian Stranger, speaking for the lawgiver, warns against piling up wealth for one's children: great riches help neither them nor the city, and the best condition for the young is to be free of flattery but not in want. Instead parents should leave a sense of reverence, or shame before wrongdoing. He adds that scolding the young does not teach it; elders teach it by showing reverence themselves and never letting the young see them act disgracefully. The argument is about example over admonition.
interpretation.zh: 雅典客人代立法者发言，告诫人们不要为子女积攒财富：巨富对子女和城邦都无益，对年轻人最好的处境是不受奉承、又不缺衣食。父母应当留下的是敬畏之心，即对恶行的羞耻感。他补充说，训斥年轻人教不会这一点；长者要靠自己心存敬畏、绝不让年轻人看见自己做可耻之事来教。这个论证强调以身作则胜于说教。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: It is an intimation that what has happened to me is a good, and that those of us who think that death is an evil are in error.
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates' defence speech at his trial, after the verdict of death.

interpretation.en: After the death sentence, Socrates speaks to the jurors who voted to acquit him. He explains that his inner divine sign, which usually stopped him even over small mistakes, gave no warning at any point that day. He takes its silence as evidence that what is happening to him is good, and so that fearing death as an evil is a mistake. This is Plato's portrait of Socrates; the argument rests on Socrates' trust in his sign rather than on a proof, and he goes on to give further reasons immediately afterward.
interpretation.zh: 被判死刑之后，苏格拉底对投票判他无罪的陪审员讲话。他说，他内心的神圣征兆平时连小错都会阻止他，那天却始终没有发出警告。他把这种沉默当作证据，说明发生在他身上的事是好的，因此把死亡当作恶来害怕是错的。这是柏拉图笔下的苏格拉底；这个论证依靠的是苏格拉底对征兆的信任，而不是证明，他随后又给出了进一步的理由。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Our statement, then, is true, that the very rich are not good, and, if they are not good, they are not happy.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws: the Athenian Stranger on why great wealth and goodness rarely go together.

interpretation.en: In the Laws the speaker is the Athenian Stranger, not Plato in his own voice, and the line closes a piece of arithmetic. Someone who takes money by any means and spends little will pile up far more than someone who earns only justly and spends on noble things, so great fortunes tend to go to people who are not good. Since the dialogue holds that only the good are happy, the very rich cannot be happy either. The argument is offered as grounds for the city's laws, which go on to ban gold and silver and limit money-lending; it concerns the design of an ideal city, and readers differ on how far it describes wealth in general.
interpretation.zh: 在《法律篇》中，说话的是雅典客人，而非柏拉图本人，这句话是一段算账式推理的结论。不择手段赚钱而花得少的人，积攒的财富远多于只靠正当途径赚钱、又把钱花在高尚之事上的人，所以巨富往往落到不善的人手里。对话认定唯有善人才幸福，因此极富之人也不可能幸福。这个论证是为城邦立法提供依据的，接下来便是禁止金银、限制放贷；它针对的是一座理想城邦的设计，至于能否推及一般意义上的财富，读者看法不一。

entries.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
entries.en: He who prefers truth to fame, may hope to prefer it to life itself.
entries.work: Eloisa
entries.context: From Rousseau's preface to Julie, or the New Eloisa, his novel in letters, defending its publication.

interpretation.en: This comes from a preface written as a dialogue between R., Rousseau's own persona, and a critic N. who thinks publishing the love letters will damage his name, especially after his attack on the theatre. R. answers that he has not disguised the truth to excuse himself and has accused himself in advance more harshly than anyone else will. The line connects truthfulness to courage: someone who will risk reputation for the truth may hope to be ready to risk more. It is a self-justification inside a staged exchange, made by an author defending his own book.
interpretation.zh: 这段出自一篇以对话体写成的序言，对话双方是代表卢梭本人的R和批评者N；N认为出版这些情书会损害卢梭的名声，尤其在他抨击过戏剧之后。R回答说，他没有为替自己开脱而掩饰真相，而且事先对自己的指责比任何人都严厉。这句话把诚实与勇气联系起来：肯为真理冒名誉之险的人，或许也能准备好为它冒更大的险。这是作者在一场设计好的对话中为自己的书所作的辩解。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: The best part of wealth is to have worthy heirs, and mind can be transmitted only to a kindred mind.
entries.work: The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense
entries.context: The Life of Reason, Volume One, on why we want others to share and carry on what we care about.

interpretation.en: Santayana is discussing why a rational person cares how widely reason, and ideals like his own, are shared by others. Because humans are social, even a person's moral ideals need support from like-minded people, at least for warmth and courage. The line says that what one values most can only be passed on to people of similar nature; it cannot be forced on hostile minds. He goes on to say that opposed natures are not reconciled by argument or by destroying each other, only replaced over time by natures already in sympathy.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那在讨论：一个理性的人为什么在意理性以及与自己相近的理想在他人中分布得有多广。人是群居的，所以即便是个人的道德理想，也需要志同道合者的支持，至少给它温暖与勇气。这句话是说，人最珍视的东西只能传给性情相近的人，无法强加给敌对的心灵。他接着说，相互敌对的天性不会因争论或彼此毁灭而和解，只会随时间被本就相通的天性所取代。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Love makes us poets, and the approach of death should make us philosophers.
entries.work: The Sense of Beauty: Being the Outlines of Aesthetic Theory
entries.context: The Sense of Beauty, on the eloquence of the dying in tragedy.

interpretation.en: Santayana is defending the long, rhetorical speech Othello makes before killing himself against critics who call it unrealistic. He argues that the stage can be truer to the mind than ordinary life, and that intense passion naturally becomes complex and eloquent. The line pairs two such states: love produces poetry, and facing death invites a philosophical view, because a man whose life is over can look back on it from a universal standpoint and sum himself up. The claim is about dramatic and psychological truth, not a general prescription.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那在为奥赛罗自杀前那段冗长而修辞化的独白辩护，反驳认为它不真实的批评者。他认为舞台可能比日常生活更忠实于心灵，强烈的激情自然会变得复杂而雄辩。这句话把两种状态并列：爱情催生诗意，面对死亡则引出哲学的眼光，因为生命已到尽头的人可以从普遍的角度回顾一生、总结自己。这一主张关乎戏剧与心理的真实，而非一般性的劝诫。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Love is very penetrating, but it penetrates to possibilities rather than to facts.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, from Santayana's portrait of his teacher William James.

interpretation.en: The sentence comes from Santayana's portrait of William James, his teacher. He praises James's courtesy and generosity toward other people and theories, but says James's intuition outran his patience: he formed a quick, often flattering sketch of what others meant instead of grasping it exactly. The line generalises the point: sympathetic love sees what someone could be rather than what they are. It is a criticism wrapped in affection, and part of Santayana's case that James was more a romantic than a rigorous logician.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自桑塔亚那为他的老师威廉·詹姆斯所写的人物素描。他称赞詹姆斯对他人和各种理论的礼貌与宽厚，但说詹姆斯的直觉跑在耐心前面：他对别人的意思迅速勾勒出一幅常常带有美化的草图，而没有准确把握。这句话把这一点推而广之：带着同情的爱看到的是一个人可能成为什么，而不是他实际是什么。这是一种包裹在温情中的批评，也是桑塔亚那认为詹姆斯更像浪漫派而非严谨逻辑学家的论证的一部分。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Never was the human mind master of so many facts and sure of so few principles.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, on the open, unsettled state of modern thought.

interpretation.en: Santayana is summing up how America has affected philosophy: it has hastened the breakdown of inherited categories and brought every kind of idea together to be compared. The result is an alert insecurity, which the line captures: more facts known than ever, and fewer settled principles. He then asks whether this fluid state will produce a great new system, and says that would need genius, which circumstances cannot supply, though the material gathered might keep such a genius from going astray. The tone is cautiously hopeful rather than dismissive.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那在总结美国对哲学的影响：它加速了传统范畴的瓦解，又把各种观念汇聚一处相互对照。结果是一种警觉的不安定，这句话正概括了这一点：所知的事实前所未有地多，确定的原则却更少。他接着问，这种流动的状态能否结晶为一个伟大的新体系，并说那需要天才，而天才不是环境能提供的，不过这里积累的材料或许能让这样的天才少走弯路。语气是谨慎的期待，而非轻视。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Nothing so much enhances a good as to make sacrifices for it.
entries.work: The Sense of Beauty: Being the Outlines of Aesthetic Theory
entries.context: The Sense of Beauty, on how what people suffer for becomes dear to them.

interpretation.en: Santayana makes this remark while explaining how a political idea can come to be loved for its own sake. His example is democracy: it began as a means to happiness and good government, but because people struggled and sacrificed for it, the idea became vivid and dear, and began to seem good in itself. He says the same had happened earlier to feudal and royal order. The point is psychological and aesthetic rather than a judgement on democracy, and he is careful to say the French Revolution itself had moral, not aesthetic, causes.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那是在解释一种政治观念如何会因其自身而受人珍爱时说这句话的。他举的例子是民主：它起初只是通往幸福和良好治理的手段，但由于人们为之奋斗、为之牺牲，这个观念变得鲜明而可贵，开始显得本身就是好的。他说封建制和君主制早先也经历过同样的过程。这里讲的是心理和审美上的机制，而不是对民主本身的评判；他也特意说明，法国大革命本身的起因是道德上的，而非审美上的。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Great empty spaces bring a sort of freedom to both soul and body.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, on the American landscape and the American temper.

interpretation.en: Santayana is explaining the American temper by the emptiness of America, both physical space and a moral emptiness in which people move house and leave behind where they were born and what they were taught. The line says such open space frees body and mind alike. He goes on to describe what follows: self-reliance, trust in one's own experience, readiness to experiment, and little to lose. This is his outsider's sketch of a national character, offered as an interpretation rather than a measured finding.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那用美国的空旷来解释美国人的性情，既指物理空间的空旷，也指一种精神上的空旷：人们随意搬家，离开出生的地方，也离开所受的教导。这句话说，这样的开阔空间同时解放了身体与心灵。他接着描述随之而来的特点：自立、信赖自己的经验、乐于尝试、几乎没什么可失去。这是他以局外人眼光为一种民族性格所作的素描，是一种诠释，而非经过衡量的结论。

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Life begins to have some value and continuity so soon as there is something definite that lives and something definite to live for.
entries.work: The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense
entries.context: The Life of Reason, Volume One, on the moment life acquires direction.

interpretation.en: Santayana is describing the point at which life acquires value: when there is a definite living being and a definite aim it pursues. He says that philosophers like Fichte and Schopenhauer, with their doctrine that will comes first, were expressing this situation in mythical form. His own view is that valuing needs a starting point that cannot be derived from ideas alone; some interest or preference has to be given first. Value, in this reading, begins with a creature that wants something, not with abstract reasoning.
interpretation.zh: 桑塔亚那在描述生命获得价值的那一刻：当存在一个确定的生命体，以及它追求的确定目标。他说，费希特和叔本华主张意志第一性，是在用神话的方式表达这种情形。他自己的看法是，评价需要一个无法单从观念中推导出来的起点，必须先有某种兴趣或偏好。按这种理解，价值始于一个有所欲求的生物，而不是抽象的推理。

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Love of praise has in large measure served in place of love of rectitude.
entries.work: The Principles of Ethics
entries.context: The Principles of Ethics, on how the wish for reputation has stood in for real moral feeling.

interpretation.en: Spencer is arguing for being sparing with praise. He holds that the wish for reputation and glory, which he calls an ego-altruistic sentiment, has long done the work that genuine moral feeling was too weak to do. Love of praise thus served as a substitute for love of right conduct. Since he expects moral feeling to strengthen as society develops, he concludes that the appetite for praise should be discouraged. The argument depends on his evolutionary view of moral progress, which many later thinkers reject.
interpretation.zh: 斯宾塞在主张少给赞扬。他认为，对名声与荣耀的渴望，即他所说的利己兼利他情感，长期以来一直在替代真正的道德情感完成它力所不及的工作。对赞扬的喜爱由此充当了对正当行为之爱的替代品。由于他预期道德情感会随社会发展而增强，他得出结论：对赞扬的胃口应当受到抑制。这一论证依赖于他关于道德进步的进化论观点，后来的许多思想家并不接受这种观点。

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Do not expect from a child any great amount of moral goodness.
entries.work: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical
entries.context: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical, Spencer's advice to parents on moral training.

interpretation.en: This is one of Spencer's maxims for parents, and the surrounding text shows its basis: he claims that each child passes through the moral stage of the supposedly barbarous ancestors of civilized people, so cruelty, lying and theft are to be expected and will fade with growth. The reasoning relies on a recapitulation theory and on racial comparisons of children's faces to so-called savages that are now discredited and offensive. The practical advice, not to expect much moral goodness early, rests on that foundation and should be read with it in view.
interpretation.zh: 这是斯宾塞给父母的格言之一，上下文显示了它的依据：他声称每个孩子都要经历文明人那些所谓野蛮祖先的道德阶段，所以残忍、撒谎和偷窃都在意料之中，并会随成长而消退。这种推理依赖一种复演理论，以及把儿童面貌与所谓野蛮人相比的种族比较，这些如今都已被否定，且带有冒犯性。不要过早期待孩子有多少道德美德这一实际建议，正是建立在这一基础上，阅读时应当把这一点考虑在内。

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Do not regret the exhibition of considerable self-will on the part of your children.
entries.work: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical
entries.context: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical, on wilfulness in children as a sign of growing independence.

interpretation.en: Spencer tells parents not to regret strong self-will in their children. He reads it as the counterpart of a less coercive education: as adults tyrannise less, children assert their freedom more, and both signs point toward the discipline he favours, in which children learn to govern themselves by experiencing the natural consequences of their actions. He ties this to national character, saying the independent boy grows into the independent man, a claim framed in the confident terms of Victorian English progress.
interpretation.zh: 斯宾塞告诉父母，不必为孩子强烈的自主意志感到遗憾。他把这看作强制性较弱的教育的对应面：成年人越少专横，孩子就越多地伸张自由，这两种迹象都指向他所提倡的管教方式，即让孩子通过体验自己行为的自然后果来学会自我管理。他把这与民族性格联系起来，说独立的男孩长成独立的男人，这一说法带着维多利亚时代英国人对进步的自信口吻。

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: Love is pleasure, accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part III, from the definitions of the emotions.

interpretation.en: This is one of the formal definitions of the emotions at the end of Part III of the Ethics. Spinoza defines pleasure as the mind's passage to greater power or perfection, so love is simply that increase together with the thought of something outside as its cause. The definition is deliberately unromantic: it treats love as one case of a general mechanism, which lets him analyse jealousy, hatred and devotion in the same terms. The surrounding definitions of contempt and others show it is part of a systematic list, not a standalone saying.
interpretation.zh: 这是《伦理学》第三部分末尾对情感所作的正式定义之一。斯宾诺莎把快乐定义为心灵向更大力量或完满性的过渡，因此爱不过是这种增长，加上把某个外在事物当作其原因的观念。这个定义刻意不带浪漫色彩：它把爱当作一种普遍机制的一个实例，使他能用同样的术语分析嫉妒、仇恨和忠诚。周围对轻视等情感的定义表明，它是一份系统清单的一部分，而不是一句独立的格言。

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: He who is led by fear, and does good in order to escape evil, is not led by reason.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on acting from reason rather than fear.

interpretation.en: This proposition from Part IV contrasts two motives for doing good. Someone who acts well only to avoid punishment or harm is moved by fear, which for Spinoza is a passive emotion, a form of pain imposed by outside causes. Someone led by reason does the same good actions directly, because they understand them to be good. The surrounding text explains why reason's view of future goods is often weaker than present desires, which is part of why fear so often does the work instead.
interpretation.zh: 第四部分的这条命题对比了行善的两种动机。只为逃避惩罚或伤害而行善的人，是被恐惧推动的，而在斯宾诺莎看来，恐惧是一种被动情感，是外因强加的一种痛苦。受理性引导的人做同样的善事，是直接出于理解它们是善的。上下文解释了为什么理性对未来之善的认识往往敌不过当下的欲望，这也正是恐惧常常代为发挥作用的部分原因。

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: Love and desire may be excessive.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on when pleasure and desire become harmful.

interpretation.en: Spinoza has just argued that bodily pleasure can become harmful when it fixes on one part and crowds out the body's other capacities, and that even pain can be useful by checking such excess. This proposition extends the point to love and desire: they too can be excessive, when one object takes hold of the mind so strongly that it cannot attend to anything else. In his scheme the trouble is not feeling itself but feeling that narrows a person's power to act and understand.
interpretation.zh: 斯宾诺莎刚刚论证过：身体的快感如果集中于某一部分、排挤身体的其他能力，就会变得有害；甚至痛苦也可能因为抑制这种过度而有用。这条命题把这一点推广到爱和欲望：当某个对象过于强烈地占据心灵，使它无法顾及其他事物时，爱和欲望也会过度。在他的体系中，问题不在于情感本身，而在于缩小了人行动和理解之力的情感。

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: The mind's absolute virtue is therefore to understand.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on understanding as the mind's own virtue.

interpretation.en: The line comes from the proof of Proposition 28 in Part IV. Spinoza has argued that the mind is truly active only insofar as it understands; virtue, for him, means acting from one's own power, so the mind's virtue is simply understanding. The proposition then concludes that the highest thing to understand is God. Since Spinoza identifies God with the whole of nature, readers disagree about how religious this conclusion is, and it is often read as saying that the mind's best activity is understanding the order of everything.
interpretation.zh: 这句话出自第四部分命题二十八的证明。斯宾诺莎已论证：心灵只有在理解时才是真正主动的；在他看来，德性就是出于自身的力量而行动，所以心灵的德性就是理解。这条命题接着得出结论：最高的理解对象是神。由于斯宾诺莎把神等同于整个自然，读者对这一结论有多少宗教意味存在分歧，它常被理解为心灵最好的活动就是理解万物的秩序。

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: The highest good of those who follow virtue is common to all, and therefore all can equally rejoice therein.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on the highest good, which is lessened by no one else having it too.

interpretation.en: Just before this proposition, Spinoza admits that people are generally envious and troublesome to one another, yet argues that they gain far more than they lose from living together. The proposition gives the reason this can work: the highest good of those who live by reason is understanding, and one person's understanding does not reduce what is left for anyone else. Unlike wealth or fame, it is not a scarce prize, so it gives no ground for rivalry and can be enjoyed by all at once.
interpretation.zh: 在这条命题之前，斯宾诺莎承认人们通常彼此嫉妒、互相找麻烦，但又论证人们从共同生活中得到的远多于失去的。这条命题给出了这种共处之所以可行的理由：依理性生活的人，其最高的善是理解，而一个人的理解并不会减少他人可得的份额。它不像财富或名声那样是稀缺的奖品，所以不构成竞争的理由，众人可以同时享有。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: He who is only a traveller learns things at second-hand and by the halves, and is poor authority.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, on the difference between a traveller's knowledge and that of people who live in a place.

interpretation.en: In the chapter on higher laws, Thoreau reflects on fishing and hunting as his early way into close acquaintance with nature. He argues that fishermen, hunters and woodchoppers, who spend their lives outdoors, often observe nature better than philosophers or poets who come to it with expectations. A mere traveller only passes through, so his knowledge is secondhand and partial. Thoreau values science most when it confirms what such practical people already know.
interpretation.zh: 在《更高的法则》一章中，梭罗回顾钓鱼和打猎如何成为他早年亲近自然的途径。他认为，终生在野外的渔夫、猎人和伐木工，往往比带着期待接近自然的哲学家或诗人观察得更好。单纯的旅行者只是路过，所以他的知识是二手的、片面的。梭罗最看重的科学，是印证这些实干之人早已知道之事的科学。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Men do not fail commonly for want of knowledge, but for want of prudence to give wisdom the preference.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, Thoreau's account of a boat trip with his brother, on prudence and wisdom.

interpretation.en: Thoreau separates knowing from choosing: people usually go wrong not for lack of information but because they do not have the practical sense to put wisdom first. He adds that what needs knowing is simple, and then observes how easily any new routine settles in and is upheld as if it were exactly what was wanted. The passage is loosely connected and moves quickly between thoughts, so it reads as a set of reflections rather than a single argument.
interpretation.zh: 梭罗把知道与选择区分开来：人们通常犯错，不是因为缺乏知识，而是因为缺乏把智慧放在首位的实际判断力。他补充说，需要知道的东西很简单，又指出任何新的惯例都很容易扎根，并被维持下去，仿佛它正是人们想要的。这段文字结构松散，思绪跳跃很快，读起来更像一组随想，而不是一个完整的论证。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Nature is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Economy", on how much anxious care we could safely give up.

interpretation.en: In Economy, Thoreau argues that people take far more anxious care of themselves than they need to. Nature, he says, accommodates human weakness as well as strength, so much of the constant strain and vigilance is unnecessary and itself a kind of illness. He points out how much gets done without any one person's effort, and criticises a life lived on constant alert, unwilling to trust, and convinced there is only one way to live.
interpretation.zh: 在《经济篇》中，梭罗认为人们对自己的焦虑照料远远超过所需。他说，自然既适应人的坚强，也适应人的软弱，所以许多持续的紧张与戒备都是不必要的，其本身就是一种病。他指出，有多少事情并不靠哪个人的努力也照样完成，并批评那种时刻戒备、不肯信任、认定只有一种活法的生活。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Take your time, and set about some free labor.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Economy", on doing good without making a business of it.

interpretation.en: Thoreau is skeptical of organised philanthropy here, suggesting that a reformer's sadness often comes from his own private trouble rather than sympathy. His advice is wry: if one does good, do it without self-regard or announcement, rescue the drowning and then carry on with ordinary life, and do it unhurriedly as free, unpaid work rather than a profession. The tone is partly ironic, and the passage is often read as a criticism of moral busyness rather than of helping as such.
interpretation.zh: 梭罗在这里对有组织的慈善持怀疑态度，暗示改革者的忧伤往往源于自己的私人烦恼，而非对他人的同情。他的建议带着讥讽：如果行善，就不要自我标榜或张扬，救起落水者，然后照常过日子，从容地把它当作自由、无偿的劳动，而不是一门职业。语气部分带有反讽，这段话常被理解为批评道德上的忙碌，而非批评帮助本身。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine.
entries.work: On the Duty of Civil Disobedience
entries.context: Civil Disobedience, on refusing to lend oneself to an injustice one condemns.

interpretation.en: Thoreau sorts injustices in government into kinds. Some are ordinary friction that may wear away, and some may need a remedy worse than the evil. But if the law requires a person to be the agent of injustice to another, he says, break the law. The image of counter friction means using one's own conduct to resist the workings of the state rather than keep them running. His central concern, stated right after, is not to lend himself to the wrong he condemns.
interpretation.zh: 梭罗把政府中的不义分为几类。有些只是机器运转的寻常摩擦，或许会自行磨平；有些若要纠正，代价可能比弊端本身还大。但他说，如果法律要求一个人去充当对他人行不义的工具，那就违抗法律。反向摩擦的比喻，是指用自己的行为去阻碍国家机器运转，而不是助其运行。他紧接着点明核心关切：不让自己为自己所谴责的错误出力。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Nothing can rightly compel a simple and brave man to a vulgar sadness.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Solitude", on how nature keeps off melancholy.

interpretation.en: In Solitude, Thoreau claims that a person living close to nature, with senses intact, cannot fall into deep melancholy. A storm becomes music to a healthy ear, and the rain that stops his hoeing is good for the grass and therefore for him. The line means that ordinary dreariness has no real hold on someone simple and brave. This is a description of his own experience at the pond, and its confidence is personal rather than a general claim about sadness.
interpretation.zh: 在《独处》一章中，梭罗声称，一个亲近自然、感官健全的人不会陷入深重的忧郁。暴风雨在健康的耳朵听来是音乐，让他无法锄地的雨水对青草有益，因而对他也有益。这句话的意思是，庸常的沉闷无法真正控制一个简朴而勇敢的人。这是他对自己在湖畔生活的描述，其中的自信属于个人体验，而非关于悲伤的普遍论断。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: There are moments when all anxiety and stated toil are becalmed in the infinite leisure and repose of nature.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, on a midday rest on the river.

interpretation.en: Thoreau describes a midday rest on the river, the boat tied to a willow and melons being sliced. He presents noon as a time when work and reform are suspended and the mind drifts toward contemplation. He connects this mood to the lands of the East, which he romantically treats as homes of contemplation; that generalisation reflects his era's views rather than an accurate picture. The line itself is about the relief of leisure within a working day.
interpretation.zh: 梭罗描写在河上的一次午间休息：船系在柳枝上，人在切瓜。他把正午写成劳作与改革都暂停、心思飘向沉思的时刻。他把这种心境与东方各国联系起来，浪漫地把它们看作沉思之乡；这种概括反映的是他那个时代的看法，而非准确的描绘。这句话本身讲的是劳作日中闲暇带来的舒缓。

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Our life without love is like coke and ashes.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, in a long passage on friendship.

interpretation.en: This is from Thoreau's long reflection on friendship. He argues that clumsy, ignorant love is better than skill and wisdom without love, and that courtesy, wit and even goodwill do not satisfy the deepest human faculties if love is missing. Coke and ashes are what is left after burning, useful perhaps but without the fire. He ends by saying that refined but loveless hosts are worse than rough barbarians who offer warmth.
interpretation.zh: 这段出自梭罗关于友谊的长篇思考。他认为笨拙无知的爱胜过没有爱的技巧与智慧，礼貌、机智乃至善意，如果缺少爱，都满足不了人最深的能力。焦炭和灰烬是燃烧后剩下的东西，或许有用，却没有了火。他最后说，高雅却无爱的主人，还不如给人温暖的粗野蛮族。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: Truth must bring clear thoughts, as well as clear the way to action.
entries.work: The Meaning of Truth
entries.context: The Meaning of Truth, William James defending pragmatism's account of truth against its critics.

interpretation.en: James is describing the humanist view of truth associated with Dewey and Schiller: truth is not a copy of a finished reality but a collaboration with reality that brings about a clearer result. He openly admits the key terms are vague, and this line is his attempt to say what clearer must cover: both clear thinking and a clear path to action, a play on the word. He then says the only way to test the programme is to apply it to different kinds of truth, so the passage is a statement of a working hypothesis, not a finished doctrine.
interpretation.zh: 詹姆斯在描述与杜威、席勒相关的人本主义真理观：真理不是对一个现成实在的复制，而是与实在协作，促成更清晰的结果。他坦率承认其中的关键术语都很模糊，这句话是他试图说明更清晰必须涵盖什么：既要使思想清晰，也要为行动扫清道路，原文在这里玩了一个双关。随后他说，检验这一纲领的唯一方法是把它用于各类真理，所以这段话陈述的是一个有待检验的假说，而非完成的学说。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: There is the strangest lightness about the heart when one's nothingness in a particular line is once accepted in good faith.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, in the chapter on the self, on the relief of giving up a pretension.

interpretation.en: In his chapter on the self, James proposes that self-esteem equals success divided by pretensions, so it can rise either by succeeding more or by aspiring less. Giving up a pretension, he says, can be as great a relief as having it satisfied, and he cites evangelical theology's abandonment of salvation by works as the deepest example. The line describes the odd lightness that follows honestly accepting that one is no good at something. It is a psychological observation, not a recommendation to give up.
interpretation.zh: 在论自我的一章中，詹姆斯提出自尊等于成功除以抱负，所以自尊既可以靠更多的成功提高，也可以靠降低抱负提高。他说，放弃一项抱负，带来的解脱可以和实现它一样大，并举福音派神学放弃靠善行得救为最深刻的例子。这句话描述的是诚心承认自己在某方面一无是处之后那种奇特的轻松。这是一个心理学观察，而非劝人放弃。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: We must care more for our honor, our friends, our human ties, than for a sound skin or wealth.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, on how we rank the parts of the self: social and spiritual above material.

interpretation.en: James is describing how people commonly rank the different selves they might pursue: the body at the bottom, then material possessions, then the social self of reputation and relationships, with the spiritual self at the top. The sentence states the step from material to social. Although it is phrased as an obligation, in context James is largely reporting a hierarchy that people widely accept, so it is ambiguous how far he is endorsing it and how far describing it.
interpretation.zh: 詹姆斯在描述人们通常如何为可能追求的各种自我排序：身体在最底层，其上是物质财产，再上是由名誉和人际关系构成的社会自我，精神自我居于顶端。这句话陈述的是从物质自我到社会自我的这一级。虽然措辞像是一种义务，但在上下文中，詹姆斯主要是在报告一种被广泛接受的等级，所以他在多大程度上是赞同、多大程度上只是描述，并不明确。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: He who loves to balance nice doubts need be in no hurry to decide the point.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 2 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, Volume II, on questions that introspection alone cannot settle.

interpretation.en: James is discussing whether the effort of attention a person puts forth is fixed by prior causes or could have been greater or less, the question of free will. He argues that settling it would require measurements and laws far beyond human reach, leaving only fallible introspection and prior assumptions. The line is wry: anyone who enjoys weighing fine doubts has plenty of time, since the arguments on both sides will only grow longer. He is saying the question cannot be decided on scientific grounds, not that it is unimportant.
interpretation.zh: 詹姆斯在讨论一个人付出的注意努力是由先前原因决定的，还是本可以更多或更少，也就是自由意志的问题。他认为，要解决这个问题，需要远超人类能力的测量和规律，剩下的只有容易出错的内省和先验假设。这句话带着调侃：喜欢权衡细微疑问的人尽可以慢慢来，因为双方的论据只会越来越多。他的意思是这个问题无法在科学上得到裁决，而不是说它不重要。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: The best repentance is to up and act for righteousness, and forget that you ever had relations with sin.
entries.work: The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
entries.context: The Varieties of Religious Experience, where James describes the "healthy-minded" religious temper; the sentence sets out that view, which James examines rather than simply endorses.

interpretation.en: James is summarising the religion of healthy-mindedness, the temperament that attends to good and declines to dwell on evil, even denying it exists. On this view, worry about evil only adds to the disease, and even remorse can be a weakening impulse, so the best repentance is to act rightly and stop brooding on past wrongdoing. The sentence states that outlook in its own voice; James presents it sympathetically but goes on to argue that it is inadequate to the reality of evil, which the sick soul takes seriously.
interpretation.zh: 詹姆斯在概括健全心态的宗教，即一种关注善、不愿纠缠于恶、甚至否认恶存在的气质。按这种看法，为恶忧虑只会加重病情，连悔恨也可能是一种使人软弱的冲动，所以最好的悔改是去做对的事，不再沉溺于过去的罪过。这句话是以这种观点自己的口吻陈述的；詹姆斯对它抱有同情，但随后论证它不足以应对恶的现实，而病态灵魂恰恰正视这一现实。

entries.name: William James
entries.en: There is nothing to make one indignant in the mere fact that life is hard, that men should toil and suffer pain.
entries.work: Memories and Studies
entries.context: From "The Moral Equivalent of War", James's essay arguing for a peaceful outlet for martial virtues.

interpretation.en: In this essay James is looking for a peaceful substitute for the discipline and hardihood war produces. Here he makes the distinction behind his proposal: hardship as such is simply part of the human condition and nothing to be indignant about. What is unjust is that, by accident of birth, some people get nothing but toil and pain while others no more deserving never taste hardship at all. That unequal distribution leads to his idea of a conscription of young people to share the hard work of society.
interpretation.zh: 在这篇文章中，詹姆斯在为战争所培养的纪律与坚韧寻找和平的替代品。这里他提出了自己方案背后的区分：艰难本身只是人类处境的一部分，不值得愤慨。不公之处在于，由于出身的偶然，一些人一生只有劳苦和痛苦，而另一些并不更配得上的人却从未尝过艰辛。正是这种不均的分配，引出了他的设想：征召年轻人共同分担社会的艰苦劳动。

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Always determine, on every occasion, to speak the truth, and you will never be at a loss for words.
entries.work: Original Stories from Real Life
entries.context: Original Stories from Real Life, Wollstonecraft's book for children; the teacher Mrs Mason speaks to her pupils.

interpretation.en: In this book for children, the line is spoken by the teacher Mrs Mason to her pupils, a character through whom Wollstonecraft gives moral instruction. Mrs Mason defines honour as self-respect founded on truth, and argues that truthful people need not plan what to say, because a person who has acted rightly has nothing to construct or hide. She adds that a reputation for truthfulness earns respect even from those who dislike one, and that friendship is impossible without it.
interpretation.zh: 在这本写给孩子的书中，这句话出自教师梅森夫人对学生的教导，沃斯通克拉夫特借这个人物进行道德教育。梅森夫人把荣誉定义为以真实为基础的自尊，并论证诚实的人不必盘算该说什么，因为行事正当的人没有什么需要编造或掩饰。她还说，诚实的名声连不喜欢自己的人也会尊重，没有诚实就不可能有友谊。

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Love gilds all the prospects of life, and though it cannot always exclude apathy, it makes many cares appear trifling.
entries.work: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
entries.locator: OF FEMALES, FASHIONABLY EDUCATED, AND LEFT
entries.context: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, Wollstonecraft's first book, on taking the joys that cost nothing in innocence.

interpretation.en: Wollstonecraft is advising young women on attachments that cannot lead to marriage: guard against them early, since passions cannot be rooted out but should not be allowed near a precipice. Since sorrow cannot be avoided, she says, wisdom lies in enjoying the harmless pleasures available, and love brightens life and makes many cares seem small. She then turns to Swift as a man whose pride and contempt for ordinary human needs made him unkind, and insists that universal benevolence comes first. The praise of love is thus hedged by caution throughout.
interpretation.zh: 沃斯通克拉夫特在劝告年轻女性如何对待无法通向婚姻的感情：要及早防范，因为激情无法根除，但不应任其靠近悬崖。她说，既然悲伤无法避免，明智之举就是享受那些无害的快乐，而爱能照亮生活，使许多烦恼显得微不足道。随后她以斯威夫特为例，说他的骄傲和对常人需求的蔑视使他待人刻薄，并坚持普遍的仁爱是首要的。因此，她对爱的赞美通篇都带着审慎的限定。

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Love and compassion are the most delightful feelings of the soul, and to exert them to all that breathe is the wish of the benevolent heart.
entries.work: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
entries.locator: OF FEMALES, FASHIONABLY EDUCATED, AND LEFT
entries.context: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, on forbearance and kindness.

interpretation.en: Wollstonecraft is discussing forbearance: a benevolent mind suffers with others, makes allowance for their failings, and in this resembles a long-suffering God. The line praises love and compassion as the soul's best feelings and the wish to extend them to every living thing. But she immediately adds that meeting ingratitude is painful and that tender feelings often fall back into apathy, and concludes that the passions bring happiness only when governed by an educated reason. The passage is a balance between warmth and discipline, not simple praise of feeling.
interpretation.zh: 沃斯通克拉夫特在讨论宽容：仁慈的心与他人同受苦难，体谅他人的缺点，在这一点上与恒久忍耐的上帝相似。这句话称颂爱与同情是灵魂最美好的情感，以及把它们推及一切生灵的愿望。但她随即补充说，遭遇忘恩负义令人痛苦，温柔的情感也常常回落为冷漠，并得出结论：只有受到经过启蒙的理性统领，激情才能带来幸福。这段话是在温情与自律之间求取平衡，而非单纯赞美情感。

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Let people but watch their own hearts, and act rightly as far as they can judge, and they may patiently wait till the opinion of the world comes round.
entries.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
entries.context: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, on acting rightly without anxiety about appearances.

interpretation.en: This comes from a footnote in which Wollstonecraft rejects the idea that a person should avoid doing what they believe is right merely because ambiguous circumstances might make others suspect bad motives. That, she says, sacrifices substance for appearance. The line advises attending to one's own conscience and trusting that opinion will eventually catch up, and she adds that justice has too often been sacrificed to propriety, which she calls another word for convenience. The point fits the book's wider attack on judging women by appearances.
interpretation.zh: 这段出自一条脚注，沃斯通克拉夫特在其中反对这样一种看法：仅仅因为某些含糊的情形可能让别人怀疑自己动机不良，就不去做自己认为正确的事。她说，这是为了影子而牺牲实质。这句话主张关注自己的良心，并相信舆论终会转过来；她还补充说，正义太常被礼法牺牲，而礼法不过是方便的另一种说法。这一点契合全书对以外表评判女性的更广泛批判。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, caution and remorse, come upon us by turns, with ever-changing mood.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu (the Zhuangzi), in Herbert Giles's 1889 translation; from chapter II, on the endless round of moods.

interpretation.en: In the second chapter of the Zhuangzi, the text lists the moods that rise and fall in a person day and night, comparing them to music coming from empty hollows and mushrooms springing from damp. The point is that these states arise on their own and no one can find where they come from. The passage goes on to ask whether there is a true master behind them, and leaves the question open, as Zhuangzi often does; Giles's word Cause gives it a more philosophical tone than the original may carry.
interpretation.zh: 在《庄子》第二篇中，文本列举了人日夜起伏的种种情绪，把它们比作空窍中发出的乐声、潮湿处冒出的菌菇。要点是这些状态自行生起，没有人能找到它们从何而来。这段文字接着追问其背后是否有一个真正的主宰，却像庄子惯常那样不给答案；翟理斯译文用原因一词，使这段话带上了原文未必有的哲学术语色彩。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: There is no sorrow to be compared with the death of the mind.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, in a story where the character Confucius speaks to his disciple Yen Hui; Zhuangzi often puts his own ideas in Confucius's mouth.

interpretation.en: In this story the character Confucius is speaking to his disciple Yan Hui, who despairs of keeping up with his master; the words are Zhuangzi's invention, not the historical Confucius. Confucius says the worst sorrow is the death of the mind, worse than the death of the body, and then compares life to the sun rising and setting, with everything coming into and out of being in its light. The point seems to be that clinging to fixed forms deadens the mind, while moving with ceaseless change keeps it alive, though the passage is open to several readings.
interpretation.zh: 在这个故事里，说话的是作为人物的孔子，对象是因跟不上老师而苦恼的弟子颜回；这些话出自庄子的虚构，并非历史上的孔子所说。孔子说，最大的悲哀是心死，比身死更甚，接着把生命比作日出日落，万物在它的照耀下生成又消逝。其意思似乎是，执着于固定的形态会使心灵僵死，随不息的变化而动则使它保持生机，不过这段话可以有多种解读。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: The best language is that which is not spoken, the best form of action is that which is without deeds.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, from a passage on knowledge and its limits.

interpretation.en: The line belongs to a passage on the limits of knowledge, and the surrounding text mixes the Zhuangzi with Giles's notes, so the speaker is not clear from this excerpt. It expresses a recurring Daoist idea: the highest speech says nothing and the highest action does nothing deliberate, because words and purposeful deeds carve up what is whole. The next remark, that spread-out knowledge proves shallow, makes a related point about the vanity of trying to know everything.
interpretation.zh: 这句话属于一段讨论知识局限的文字，周围文本把《庄子》原文与翟理斯的注释混在一起，所以从这段摘录看不清说话人是谁。它表达了道家反复出现的观念：最高的言语不发一言，最高的行动不刻意作为，因为言辞和有目的的作为会割裂本为整体的东西。紧接着说知识铺得越开就越显浅薄，讲的是与此相关的道理：想要无所不知是徒劳的。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Those who make wealth their all in all, cannot bear loss of money.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, on how what we make everything of becomes what we cannot bear to lose.

interpretation.en: The passage observes that whatever people make into everything for themselves becomes what they cannot bear to lose: those who live for wealth cannot give up money, those who live for fame cannot give up renown, those who love power will not hand it to others. Such people are anxious while holding and miserable when losing, and never learn from the past. Giles's closing phrase, accursed of God, imposes a theistic sense; the original speaks of people punished by Heaven, an impersonal order rather than a personal God. The excerpt does not show who is speaking.
interpretation.zh: 这段文字指出，人把什么当作自己的一切，什么就成了他无法承受失去的东西：为财富而活的人放不下钱，为名声而活的人放不下名，贪恋权力的人不肯把权柄交给别人。这样的人得之则忧，失之则悲，却从不从过去吸取教训。翟理斯在结尾把他们译作受上帝诅咒的人，带进了有神论色彩；原文说的是受天惩罚的人，天是一种非人格的秩序，而非人格化的上帝。从这段摘录看不出说话人是谁。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Life must bring us from somewhere, and death must carry us back.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, on life and death as one ceaseless process.

interpretation.en: In this story the speaker is the character Laozi, answering a question about the state before birth; he first says his mind is bound and his mouth closed, then offers what is probably true. He describes the interplay of passive and active principles producing all things, and the line says that life brings beings out and death takes them back, in an endless series of beginnings and endings. Giles renders the source as a First Cause, which sounds more like Western theology than the original's tentative reference to something whose form is never seen.
interpretation.zh: 在这个故事里，说话的是作为人物的老子，他在回答关于出生之前状态的提问；他先说自己心有所困、口不能言，然后才说出大概的真相。他描述阴阳两种原理相互作用而生成万物，这句话是说，生把万物带出，死又把它们带回，开始与终结无穷无尽地相续。翟理斯把这个本源译作第一因，听起来更像西方神学，而原文只是试探性地指向某种从未显露形体的东西。

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: There is nothing more fatal than intentional virtue, when the mind looks outwards.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, in a passage on how virtue aimed at outward show destroys the power to look within.

interpretation.en: The line warns against virtue practised on purpose, with the mind turned outward toward approval, because looking outward destroys the capacity to look within. The following lines explain that such a person does what he approves of and condemns what he does not do, so virtue becomes a performance of judgment. The surrounding text interleaves Giles's commentary with the translation, so the exact boundaries of the original are uncertain here. The idea fits Zhuangzi's general suspicion of deliberate, display-minded morality.
interpretation.zh: 这句话告诫人们警惕刻意为之的德行，即心思向外、追求认可的德行，因为向外看会毁掉向内省察的能力。接下来几句解释说，这样的人做自己赞成的事，指责自己不做的事，于是德行变成了一种评判的表演。周围文本把翟理斯的评注与译文交织在一起，所以这里原文的确切边界并不清楚。这一观点契合庄子对刻意、炫示性道德的一贯怀疑。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects of Confucius, Book II, chapter 11, in James Legge's translation.

interpretation.en: Confucius names what qualifies someone to teach: holding on to what has already been learned while continually drawing new understanding from it. The point is that old and new knowledge are not separate stores; going back over the old is how the new appears. Legge's cherishing is one reading of a verb many translators take as reviewing or warming over, and the line is often read as saying that new insight comes out of revisiting the old, not merely alongside it.
interpretation.zh: 孔子在这里说明什么样的人可以为人师：守住已经学到的东西，并不断从中获得新的理解。要点在于旧知与新知并非两个分开的仓库，回顾旧的正是新理解产生的方式。理雅各把这个动词译作珍惜，是一种理解；许多译者理解为温习、重温，常见的读法是新的领悟正是从重温旧知中生出来的，而不只是与之并行。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book II, chapter 15, on learning and thinking.

interpretation.en: Confucius pairs two failures. Taking in teachings without reflecting on them yields nothing one can use; reasoning on one's own without the grounding of study leads into danger or confusion. The saying sits among others in Book II about what makes a cultivated person, and it treats study and reflection as needing each other. Legge's perilous translates a word that some read instead as being left in doubt or at a loss, which softens the warning.
interpretation.zh: 孔子把两种失败并列：只接受教导而不加思考，得不到可用的东西；只凭自己推想而没有学习作根基，就会陷入危险或困惑。这句话位于第二篇中谈论君子修养的一组语录之间，把学习与思考看作彼此依赖。理雅各译为危险的那个字，也有人理解为疑惑不定、无所适从，那样警告的意味就轻一些。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: If a man in the morning hear the right way, he may die in the evening without regret.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 8, on hearing the Way.

interpretation.en: Confucius measures how much hearing the Way is worth: a life that has grasped it, even for a single day, is complete enough that death that evening would not be a loss. Legge's right way translates dao, the Confucian term for the proper order of conduct and government. The line is usually read as a statement of how highly Confucius ranked understanding the Way above length of life; some commentators instead read it as a lament that the Way was not being heard in his own time.
interpretation.zh: 孔子在这里衡量闻道的分量：一个人只要领会了道，哪怕只有一天，人生也已足够完整，当晚死去也不算遗憾。理雅各译作正确之道的，就是儒家所说的道，指为人与治国的正当秩序。通常的读法是，孔子把领悟道看得比寿命更重；也有注家把它读作感叹当时的世道无人闻道。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 17, on learning from others' examples.

interpretation.en: Confucius treats other people as a mirror for self-cultivation. A worthy person gives a standard to try to reach; an unworthy one is not an occasion for judging them but a prompt to check whether the same faults are present in oneself. The weight falls on the second half: the failings of others are turned back into self-examination rather than criticism. The surrounding sayings contrast the superior man and the mean man, and this line shows how one moves from one toward the other.
interpretation.zh: 孔子把他人当作修身的一面镜子。遇到贤者，便以之为标准努力看齐；遇到不贤之人，不是借机评判对方，而是回头检查自己是否也有同样的毛病。重点在后半句：别人的过失被转成自我反省，而不是批评。前后的语录都在对比君子与小人，这一句说明人如何从后者走向前者。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: The superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 24, on the "superior man" (junzi), Confucius's ideal of the cultivated person.

interpretation.en: Confucius describes the junzi, the cultivated person, as someone who holds back in speech and puts effort into action. The contrast between words and deeds runs through the Analects, which repeatedly distrusts fluent talk and praises doing before speaking. Legge's slow does not mean dull; the sense is cautious and reluctant to promise more than one can perform.
interpretation.zh: 孔子描述君子：言语上有所保留，行动上用力去做。言与行的对比贯穿《论语》，书中一再不信任巧言，称赞先做后说。理雅各所译的慢并不是迟钝，而是谨慎，不肯许诺超出自己能做到的事。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 25.

interpretation.en: Confucius claims that goodness is never isolated for long: a person who practises it will draw others of like mind. The claim answers a worry that virtue might leave its holder alone or out of step with the world. It is usually read as a statement about moral influence, that a good example attracts companions, rather than a promise of popularity.
interpretation.zh: 孔子主张德行不会长久孤立：践行德行的人，必然会吸引志同道合的人。这是对一种担忧的回应，即德行可能让人孤立、与世不合。通常的理解是，这讲的是道德的感召力，好的榜样会招来同伴，而不是保证受人欢迎。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VI, chapter 18, on degrees of devotion to the truth.

interpretation.en: Confucius ranks three relations to what one studies: knowing it, loving it, and taking joy in it, with joy highest. The point is that understanding held at arm's length is less than understanding that has become part of what one cares about and finally enjoys. Legge supplies the truth as the object, but the original has only a pronoun, and commentators disagree whether it means the Way, learning, or goodness generally.
interpretation.zh: 孔子把人与所学之物的关系分为三等：知道它、喜爱它、以它为乐，以乐为最高。要点是，保持距离的理解不如融入自己所关切之事的理解，而最高的是乐在其中。理雅各补出真理作为宾语，但原文只有一个代词，注家对它究竟指道、学问还是善，看法不一。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 21; it goes on, "I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them."

interpretation.en: Confucius says that any small company contains teachers, and the full saying explains how: he copies the good he sees in his companions and steers away from the bad. Learning here does not depend on finding a master; every person met offers either a model or a warning. The line fits the Analects' wider picture of Confucius as someone who learned from whatever was at hand rather than from one fixed teacher.
interpretation.zh: 孔子说，几个人同行，其中必有可以为师的人；完整的语句说明了方法：学习同伴的长处，避开他们的短处。这里的学习不依赖于找到某位大师，所遇到的每个人不是榜样就是警示。这与《论语》中孔子的整体形象相合：他随处取法，而非只从一位固定的老师学习。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 29.

interpretation.en: Confucius asks whether goodness is far off and answers that it arrives the moment one truly wants it. The virtue here is ren, often rendered humaneness, which elsewhere in the Analects Confucius treats as very hard to attain and rarely grants to anyone. The two positions are usually reconciled by reading this line as about where goodness begins, in one's own will, rather than a claim that it is easy to complete.
interpretation.zh: 孔子问：仁难道很遥远吗？答案是，一旦真心想要，仁就到了。这里的德是仁，而在《论语》其他地方，孔子把仁看得极难达到，很少许人以仁。通常的调和方式是，把这句读作仁的起点在于自己的意愿，而不是说仁很容易完成。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: The superior man is satisfied and composed; the mean man is always full of distress.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 36, contrasting the superior man with the "mean man" (xiaoren).

interpretation.en: Confucius contrasts the junzi, who is at ease and broad-minded, with the xiaoren, the small or petty person, who is always anxious. The difference lies in what each is attached to: elsewhere the small man is described as thinking of gain and comfort, which are never secure, while the cultivated person's concern is with what is right, which outside events cannot take away. Legge's mean man means petty, not cruel.
interpretation.zh: 孔子把坦荡从容的君子与常怀忧戚的小人对照。区别在于各自所依附的东西：书中其他地方说小人心系利益与安逸，而这些从来不稳固；君子关心的是道义，外在事件夺不走它。理雅各所说的卑劣之人，意思是器量狭小，而非残忍。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VIII, chapter 17, on the attitude of a learner.

interpretation.en: Confucius describes the right temper for study as a double anxiety: feeling that the goal is still out of reach, and fearing to lose what has already been gained. The saying treats learning as something never secured, needing constant pursuit and constant review. It sits among unrelated remarks in Book VIII, so its immediate context offers little to narrow the reading.
interpretation.zh: 孔子描述求学应有的心态是双重的忧虑：觉得目标仍未达到，又担心失去已经学到的东西。这句话把学问看作永远不能稳握的事，需要不断追求，也需要不断温习。它在第八篇中与一些不相关的语录排在一起，上下文对理解帮助不大。

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book I, chapter 8, from a saying on the conduct of the scholar.

interpretation.en: This is the last of four short instructions Confucius gives on the conduct of the scholar: be serious, hold to loyalty and sincerity, choose friends carefully, and do not hesitate to correct one's faults. The emphasis is on not being afraid or reluctant to change once a fault is recognised. The Analects returns to this theme often, treating failure to correct a fault, rather than the fault itself, as the real failing.
interpretation.zh: 这是孔子关于士人修身的四条简短教诲中的最后一条：要庄重，以忠信为本，慎择朋友，有过错不要怕改。重点在于认识到过错后不畏惧、不迟疑地改正。《论语》常回到这个主题，认为真正的过失不是犯错本身，而是有错不改。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 33, in James Legge's translation.

interpretation.en: Chapter 33 is a string of paired contrasts, each setting an outward achievement against an inward one. In this first pair, understanding other people counts as shrewdness, but understanding oneself is ranked higher. The same pattern follows with strength over others versus mastery of oneself, so the chapter as a whole is usually read as moving the measure of worth from power over the world to the governance of oneself. The input labels this chapter 31, but the text is chapter 33.
interpretation.zh: 第三十三章是一连串成对的对比，每一对都把外在的成就与内在的成就并列。在这第一对中，了解别人算是明察，了解自己则被置于更高的位置。随后以同样的格式对比了胜过别人与战胜自己，所以整章通常被理解为把衡量价值的标准从支配外物转向自我治理。输入标注为第三十一章，实际文字属于第三十三章。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 33; it continues, "he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will."

interpretation.en: In chapter 33 this phrase sits among contrasts between outward and inward kinds of success. Wealth is redefined as being content with what one has, rather than as accumulation. It is immediately paired with a line praising persistent effort, which suggests the chapter is not recommending inertia; how the two halves fit together is read differently by different commentators. The input labels this chapter 31, but the text is chapter 33.
interpretation.zh: 在第三十三章中，这句话处在一系列外在成功与内在成功的对比之中。富足被重新定义为满足于自己所有，而不是不断积累。紧接着它的是一句称赞坚持力行的话，这表明这一章并不是在提倡停滞；两半句如何配合，注家的理解各不相同。输入标注为第三十一章，实际文字属于第三十三章。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: …the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 64, on great things growing from small beginnings ("li" is a Chinese measure of distance).

interpretation.en: This is the last of three images in chapter 64, after a great tree grown from a sprout and a tall tower raised from a heap of earth, all showing that large results start from small beginnings. The chapter then warns against grasping and forcing, and observes that people often ruin their work just before it is complete because they stop taking the care they took at the start. In context the line is as much about patience and care to the end as about the first step. Legge says commenced; the original is often read as saying the journey begins beneath the feet, a slightly different image.
interpretation.zh: 这是第六十四章三个意象中的最后一个，前两个是合抱的大树生于细芽、高台起于一堆土，都说明大的结果起于小的开端。这一章接着告诫不要强求和执持，并指出人们常常在事情快要完成时把它毁掉，因为他们不再像开始时那样谨慎。放在上下文中，这句话既讲第一步，也讲耐心和慎终如始。理雅各译作开始于一步；原文常被理解为旅程始于脚下，画面略有不同。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 9, on knowing when to stop.

interpretation.en: The chapter warns that riches cannot be guarded and that wealth and honour breed arrogance that brings its own ruin. This closing sentence offers the alternative: once the task is done, step back rather than stay to enjoy the fame. It is presented as the pattern of Heaven itself, which completes its work without clinging to it. Legge adds a reference to name and distinction that the shorter original only implies, and some translations simply say withdraw when the work is done.
interpretation.zh: 这一章告诫说，满堂金玉无法守住，富贵而骄会自招祸患。这最后一句给出另一条路：事情完成后就退身，而不是留下来享受名声。它被说成是天道本身的样子：成就万物而不占有。理雅各加上了名声显赫的意思，较简短的原文只是隐含此意，有些译本只说功成身退。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 23, on speaking little, since even heaven and earth cannot keep up violence for long.

interpretation.en: Chapter 23 opens by praising sparing speech as natural, then uses storms as evidence: a gale or downpour soon blows itself out. The text asks who produces such outbursts and answers Heaven and Earth, then concludes that if even they cannot sustain violent effort, people certainly cannot. The images thus argue for restraint in speech and action. Legge reads the opening as abstaining from speech; others read it as saying that few words are what is natural, and the chapter is one where translations differ noticeably.
interpretation.zh: 第二十三章开头称赞少言合乎自然，接着以风雨为证：狂风暴雨很快就会停息。文中问这些是谁造成的，回答是天地，然后得出结论：连天地都不能使这种猛烈的作为持久，何况人呢。这些意象由此论证言行都应有节制。理雅各把开头理解为不言；另一些译者理解为少言才合乎自然，这一章各译本之间的差异相当明显。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 24, on self-display and overreaching.

interpretation.en: Chapter 24 starts with two bodily images, standing on tiptoe and taking overlong strides, both of which make a person less stable rather than more. The chapter then applies them to self-display, self-assertion and boasting, which it says defeat their own purpose and are as unwelcome as leftover food or a growth on the body. The argument is that straining to appear greater than one is produces the opposite effect. The input labels this chapter 23, but the text is chapter 24.
interpretation.zh: 第二十四章以两个身体意象开头：踮起脚尖和跨大步，都会使人更不稳而不是更稳。随后这一章把它们用于自我炫耀、自以为是和自夸，说这些做法适得其反，就像剩饭或身上的赘瘤一样令人厌恶。其论点是，竭力显得比自己更大，只会带来相反的效果。输入标注为第二十三章，实际文字属于第二十四章。

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 15, on the old masters of the Way.

interpretation.en: This is the counterpart to the muddy-water image in the chapter on the ancient masters of the Way: stillness lets things clear, and movement in turn lets rest arise. Read together, the two lines describe a balance in which neither stillness nor activity is forced. The chapter goes on to say that those who follow this method do not seek to be full of themselves. The pairing is cryptic and has been read both as a description of the sage and as advice on timing. The input lists chapter 10; the text matches chapter 15.
interpretation.zh: 这是古之善为道者一章中浊水意象的对应句：静能使事物澄清，动又能使安定逐渐产生。两句合读，描述的是一种平衡，静与动都不强求。这一章接着说，持守此道的人不求盈满。这一对句子较为隐晦，既被理解为对圣人状态的描写，也被理解为关于时机的建议。输入标注为第十章，上下文与第十五章相符。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: The great man is he who does not lose his child's heart.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF THOSE OTHERS, THEY ARE NOT TO BE, chapter XII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book IV, Part II, chapter 12.

interpretation.en: This is a one-sentence chapter with no context around it. It is most often read as saying that the great person keeps the unfeigned, undivided heart of an infant, the moral sprouts Mencius believes everyone is born with, rather than losing it through calculation. Because the saying is so bare, its exact meaning is uncertain: some traditional commentators took the infant to stand for the common people, making it a remark about a ruler who keeps the heart of his people. Legge's child's heart follows the more common reading.
interpretation.zh: 这是只有一句话的一章，前后没有任何背景。它最常被理解为：大人保有婴儿那种不加伪饰、纯一无杂的心，也就是孟子认为人人生来就有的道德善端，而不会因算计而丧失。由于这句话太简短，确切含义并不确定：一些传统注家把赤子理解为百姓，于是这句话就成了讲君主不失其民心。理雅各的译法采用的是较常见的理解。

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: …when Heaven is about to confer a great office on any one, it first exercises his mind with suffering, and his sinews and bones with toil
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF SEVERAL EMINENT WORTHIES OF FORMER TIMES, Book VII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VI, Part II, chapter 15, on the hardships that came before great figures of antiquity took office.

interpretation.en: Mencius has just listed great figures of antiquity who rose from humble or harsh circumstances, such as a labourer, a man found at the seashore and one from the marketplace. From these examples he infers a pattern: before Heaven entrusts someone with great responsibility, it first tests him with mental suffering, physical toil, hunger, poverty and the frustration of his plans. He explains that these trials stir the mind, toughen the character and make up for what the person lacks. Heaven here is the Confucian sense of a guiding order, and the passage reads hardship as preparation rather than punishment.
interpretation.zh: 孟子刚刚列举了几位出身卑微或处境艰难的古代伟人，比如出身劳作者、从海滨被举用的人和从市井中被举用的人。从这些例子中他推出一个规律：天将要把重大责任交给某人时，一定先让他内心受苦、筋骨劳累，使他挨饿、贫困，并使他的作为处处受挫。他解释说，这些磨难能激发心志、坚韧性情，并增益他所欠缺的能力。这里的天是儒家所说的主宰秩序，这段话把苦难理解为准备而不是惩罚。

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is devoid of sensation, and that which is devoid of sensation is nothing to us.
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, number 2, as preserved by Diogenes Laertius.

interpretation.en: This is the second of the Principal Doctrines, which Diogenes Laertius copies out after his account of Epicurus's views on the gods. The argument is short: death is the breaking apart of the body and soul, what is broken apart feels nothing, and what feels nothing cannot be good or bad for anyone. It rests on Epicurus's atomism, in which the soul does not survive the body. Its aim is to remove fear of death, not to make death welcome, and later critics have asked whether losing future goods might still count as a harm even if it is never felt.
interpretation.zh: 这是《主要学说》第二条，第欧根尼·拉尔修在叙述伊壁鸠鲁关于神的看法之后抄录了它。论证很简短：死亡是身体与灵魂的分解，分解了的东西没有感觉，而没有感觉的东西对任何人都无所谓好坏。这一论证建立在伊壁鸠鲁的原子论之上，在他看来灵魂不会在身体之后存续。它的目的是消除对死亡的恐惧，而不是让人欢迎死亡；后世的批评者则追问，失去未来的种种好处，即使永远感受不到，是否仍算一种伤害。

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: It is not possible to live pleasantly without living prudently, and honourably, and justly
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, number 5, on pleasure and virtue being inseparable.

interpretation.en: Epicurus is often taken to have recommended indulgence, and this doctrine shows why that reading is wrong. He ties pleasure and virtue together in both directions: a pleasant life requires prudence, honour and justice, and a life with those qualities is pleasant. The reasoning, spelled out elsewhere in his work, is that wrongdoing brings fear of discovery and conflict with others, which destroys the calm he counts as pleasure. Virtue here is valued as the means to tranquillity, which is why later Stoic and Christian critics objected that he made goodness merely useful.
interpretation.zh: 人们常以为伊壁鸠鲁提倡纵欲，而这条学说说明了这种读法为什么不对。他把快乐与德性双向绑在一起：愉快的生活需要审慎、高尚和正义，而具备这些品质的生活也是愉快的。他在别处讲明了其中的道理：作恶会带来对被揭发的恐惧和与他人的冲突，从而毁掉他所说的快乐，即内心的平静。在这里德性被看重，是因为它通向宁静；也正因如此，后来斯多亚派和基督教的批评者指责他把善仅仅当作有用之物。

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: Of all the things which wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friendship.
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, on friendship (numbered 28 in this edition).

interpretation.en: Among the doctrines about how wisdom secures a happy life, this one ranks friendship above everything else wisdom provides. For Epicurus friendship belongs to the same project as removing fear: friends offer security and confidence that no amount of wealth or power can. Scholars still debate whether he valued friendship only for the safety it brings or also for its own sake, since his surviving sayings point both ways. This edition numbers the doctrine 28; most modern editions count it as 27.
interpretation.zh: 在讨论智慧如何保障幸福生活的几条学说中，这一条把友谊置于智慧所提供的一切之上。在伊壁鸠鲁看来，友谊与消除恐惧属于同一个目标：朋友带来的安全与信心，是财富和权力换不来的。学者们至今仍在争论，他看重友谊究竟只是为了它带来的安全，还是也因为友谊本身，因为他存世的言论两方面都有。这个版本把这条编为第28条，多数现代版本则算作第27条。

entries.name: Karl Marx
entries.en: The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles.
entries.work: The Communist Manifesto
entries.context: The opening sentence of the first section of The Communist Manifesto, by Marx and Engels.

interpretation.en: This is the opening sentence of the first section of the Manifesto, written by Marx and Engels together. It frames all of history as conflict between opposed classes, illustrated in the next paragraph by pairs such as free and slave, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman. That conflict, the text says, ends either in a revolutionary reshaping of society or in the common ruin of both sides. Engels later added a note to the English edition narrowing all history to written history, and historians have long disputed whether class struggle can explain history as fully as this sentence claims.
interpretation.zh: 这是《共产党宣言》第一部分的开篇句，由马克思和恩格斯共同写成。它把全部历史描述为对立阶级之间的冲突，下一段用自由民与奴隶、领主与农奴、行会师傅与帮工等成对的例子加以说明。文中说，这种斗争的结局，要么是整个社会的革命性改造，要么是斗争各阶级同归于尽。恩格斯后来在英文版中加注，把全部历史限定为有文字记载的历史；而阶级斗争能否像这句话所说的那样充分解释历史，史学界一直有争论。

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: …by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.
entries.work: The Nicomachean Ethics
entries.context: The Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 1: virtues are formed by practice, as skills are.

interpretation.en: Aristotle is contrasting virtues with natural capacities. People have sight before they use it, but virtues work the other way round: they are acquired by doing the acts first, as builders become builders by building. The claim is that character is formed by repeated action, which is why Aristotle stresses upbringing and habit, and why he holds that virtues are neither simply given by nature nor contrary to it.
interpretation.zh: 亚里士多德在把德性与天生的能力作对比。人先有视力，然后才使用它；德性则正好相反：要先去做相应的行为才能获得，正如人通过建造成为建筑师。他的主张是，品格是在反复的行动中形成的，因此他重视教养和习惯，并认为德性既非天生就有，也不违背自然。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …the unexamined life is not worth living
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates at his trial, explaining why he cannot stop examining himself and others.

interpretation.en: Socrates has already been convicted and is proposing his own penalty. He imagines being asked why he cannot simply go quietly into exile, and replies that keeping silent would disobey the god, and that daily discussion of virtue and examining himself and others is the greatest good for a human being. The famous line is part of that refusal: a life without such examination is not worth living. He expects the jury not to believe him, and the speech moves straight on to the matter of a fine.
interpretation.zh: 苏格拉底此时已被定罪，正在为自己提议刑罚。他设想有人问他为何不能安静地流亡他乡，他回答说，保持沉默就是违抗神，而且每天讨论德行、省察自己和他人，是人最大的善。这句名言正是这番拒绝的一部分：不经这种省察的生活不值得过。他料到陪审团不会相信他，随即话锋转到罚金上。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates' last words to the judges who voted to acquit him.

interpretation.en: These are among Socrates' closing words to the jurors who acquitted him. He tells them to face death with confidence, holding that nothing evil can happen to a good man in life or after it, since the gods do not neglect him. Because of this he says he bears no anger toward those who condemned him, since they have not really harmed him. The claim depends on his view that the only real harm is harm to the soul, which wrongdoing does and a death sentence does not.
interpretation.zh: 这是苏格拉底对判他无罪的陪审员所说的最后几句话之一。他请他们对死亡抱有信心，认为好人无论生前死后都不会遭遇恶，因为众神不会忽视他。正因如此，他说自己对判他有罪的人并无怒意，因为他们并未真正伤害他。这一主张建立在他的观点上：唯一真正的伤害是对灵魂的伤害，作恶会造成这种伤害，而死刑判决不会。

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing
entries.work: The Republic
entries.context: Plato's Republic, Book II, Socrates on the education of the young.

interpretation.en: In the Republic, Socrates is discussing how the guardians of the ideal city should be raised, and has just said that their training in music, which includes the stories told to children, must come before physical training. The point here is that early years matter most because character is still being formed and takes impressions easily. It leads straight into his argument that the city must control which stories children hear, a proposal that includes censoring the poets and is among the most debated parts of the book.
interpretation.zh: 在《理想国》中，苏格拉底正在讨论理想城邦的护卫者应如何培养，刚说过包括给孩子讲的故事在内的音乐教育必须先于体育训练。这里的要点是，早年最为关键，因为品格尚在形成，容易受到塑造。这直接引出他的论证：城邦必须控制孩子听到哪些故事，其中包括审查诗人，这是全书争议最大的部分之一。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Enchiridion of Epictetus, section 5.

interpretation.en: Epictetus locates the cause of distress in judgments rather than events. His example is death: if death were terrible in itself, Socrates would have found it so, so the terror lies in the opinion that death is terrible. From this he draws a lesson about blame: the untaught blame others, beginners blame themselves, and the fully instructed blame no one. The passage is one of the clearest statements of the Stoic view that emotions follow from beliefs.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德把痛苦的根源放在判断上，而非事件上。他以死亡为例：如果死亡本身可怕，苏格拉底就会觉得它可怕，所以可怕的是认为死亡可怕的那个看法。由此他引出关于归咎的教训：未受教化的人责怪别人，初学者责怪自己，学成的人谁也不责怪。这段话是斯多葛派认为情绪源于信念这一观点最清楚的表述之一。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The opening words of the Enchiridion of Epictetus.

interpretation.en: The Enchiridion begins with the distinction the rest of the handbook depends on. In our power are our own acts of mind: opinion, impulse, desire and aversion. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation and office. Epictetus adds that the first kind are by nature free and the second are weak and subject to others, and that confusing the two leads to frustration and blaming. Every later rule in the handbook applies this division.
interpretation.zh: 《手册》以一个区分开篇，全书都以此为基础。在我们能力之内的，是我们自己的心灵活动：见解、冲动、欲求与厌恶。不在我们能力之内的，是身体、财产、名声与官职。爱比克泰德补充说，前者本性自由，后者软弱且受制于人，把两者混淆就会导致挫折与怨尤。手册中后来的每条规则都是对这一区分的运用。

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Enchiridion of Epictetus, section 11, on loss as returning what was lent.

interpretation.en: Epictetus asks his students to change how they describe loss: not as something lost but as something given back. He applies this without softening to the death of a child or wife and to the seizure of property. To the objection that the taker was a bad man, he replies that it does not matter through whose hands the giver asked for it back. Things are to be cared for as belonging to someone else, like a traveller's inn. The teaching is often found harsh, and its force depends on the Stoic belief that all things are on loan from the gods.
interpretation.zh: 爱比克泰德要学生改变描述损失的方式：不说失去了，而说归还了。他毫不缓和地把这一点用于孩子或妻子的死亡，以及财产被夺。对于夺走者是恶人的反驳，他回答说，给予者经由谁的手要回去，无关紧要。人应当把事物当作属于别人的东西来照管，就像旅人对待客栈。这一教导常被认为严酷，它的说服力取决于斯多葛派的一个信念：万物皆是众神所借。

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF THE ART OF WAR, CHAPTER XVIII
entries.context: The Prince, chapter XVIII, on appearance and reality in a ruler's reputation.

interpretation.en: Later in chapter XVIII Machiavelli advises that a prince should always appear merciful, faithful, humane, upright and religious, above all religious. His reasoning is that people judge by sight rather than by touch: everyone can see a ruler, but few deal with him closely. The few who know the reality will not stand against the opinion of the many, who have the state behind them, and in the end people judge by results. The passage separates reputation from character and treats the management of appearances as part of ruling, which is a large part of why the chapter shocked readers.
interpretation.zh: 在第十八章后文，马基雅维利建议君主应当始终显得仁慈、守信、人道、正直和虔诚，尤其要显得虔诚。他的理由是，人们凭眼睛而不是凭手来判断：人人都能看见君主，却很少有人能近身接触他。少数了解真相的人不敢违抗多数人的看法，因为多数人有国家威严作后盾；而且人们最终是看结果来判断。这段话把名声与品格分开，把经营外表当作统治的一部分，这正是这一章令读者震惊的重要原因。

entries.name: Rene Descartes
entries.en: Good sense is, of all things among men, the most equally distributed
entries.work: Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences
entries.context: The opening sentence of Descartes' Discourse on Method; it goes on to note that no one wishes for more of it than they have.

interpretation.en: Descartes opens the Discourse by noting that everyone seems satisfied with their own share of good sense, and he takes this as a sign that the power to judge truly is equal in all people.
